Manifestation_Text: The widespread adoption of AI has rendered traditional academic integrity mechanisms and assessment systems ineffective; covert AI-generated academic misconduct has surged, delivering systemic shocks to macro-level academic governance structures, detection systems, and evaluation frameworks.
Mitigation_Text: The article strongly urges higher education institutions to 'rethink assessment design, clarify norms for acceptable AI use, and shift from punitive, detection-focused approaches toward integrity frameworks that reflect the realities of AI-enabled learning' (Section 3.4).

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated content suffers from serious deficiencies in accuracy and reliability, including fabricated citations, erroneous mathematical expressions, and scientifically unsound conclusions. Research finds that ChatGPT, when used as an academic writing aid, produces seemingly plausible yet factually incorrect references, citations, and scientific claims; moreover, its output quality is highly dependent on the correctness of its training data〞any errors embedded in the underlying data directly degrade the quality of scholarly outputs.

AI generates content based on limited and biased training data, potentially marginalizing or producing discriminatory representations of specific cultural, religious, or regional groups. Study participants explicitly identified the risk of ChatGPT generating anti-Islamic or Islamophobic content, reflecting how cultural biases in model training data pose a potential threat of erasure and homogenization to the knowledge systems of particular academic communities.

Deep AI integration undermines the foundational integrity and mutual trust within the academic community: students＊ and researchers＊ overreliance on ChatGPT suppresses their own reflective and critical thinking processes. The trust bond between faculty and students〞grounded in intellectual honesty within academic assessment〞is at risk of disintegration, and traditional academic mentoring and collaborative relationships are being distorted into one-way dependencies on algorithmic outputs.

The large-scale application of generative AI poses a systemic challenge to macro-level academic governance systems, including the blurring of intellectual property and copyright ownership, the risk of collapse in academic integrity evaluation frameworks, and the erosion of institutional safeguards for scientific originality by plug-and-play, template-based solutions (Boilerplate Solutions). The proliferation of AI-generated content is undermining the overall credibility of academic publishing and higher education evaluation.

The rampant dissemination of low-value, AI-generated content〞termed 'word salad'〞directly degrades the final efficacy and scientific quality of academic outputs, such as undergraduate and graduate theses.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Clarify usage boundaries and compliant scenarios: Academic institutions must explicitly define acceptable and unacceptable use cases of AI in their policies (e.g., survey results indicate acceptance only for language polishing, grammatical correction, or reference identification〞not for direct text or draft generation). Ｌ Universal AI literacy and limitation training: Provide faculty with specialized training on the capabilities and limitations of generative AI (supported by 57.1% of respondents), and deliver widespread education to students on academic integrity and responsible large language model (LLM) usage (supported by 62.4% of respondents), thereby enhancing frontline capacity to identify and resist low-quality AI-generated content. Ｍ Introduce technical detection support: Extend plagiarism-detection software functionality to include probabilistic assessment of whether a given text was AI-generated (supported by 55.3% of respondents).

Manifestation_Text: The delegation of student intellectual agency and the alienation of mutual trust in teacher每student assessment. Overreliance on generative AI (GAI) as an 'external aid' weakens students＊ capacity for independent research and original thinking, thereby jeopardizing the traditional teacher每student mentoring and evaluation relationship〞grounded in mutual human intellectual trust.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Restructure assessment and defense paradigms: Significantly increase the weight of 'thesis presentation and oral defense' in thesis evaluation (supported by 54.7% of respondents) and rigorously verify students＊ authentic mastery of their thesis content (supported by 51.2% of respondents), directly testing genuine intellectual engagement and restoring interpersonal trust. Ｌ Upgrade assignment design strategies: Supervisors should formulate thesis topics that demand greater creativity and are less amenable to direct resolution by LLMs (supported by 54.1% of respondents), compelling students to return to independent thought. Ｍ Strengthen process-oriented supervision: Equip faculty with concrete recommendations and intervention strategies to prevent academic misconduct during thesis supervision (supported by 47.1% of respondents).

Manifestation_Text: Systemic erosion of the credibility of higher education and the intrinsic value of academic degrees. The convenience afforded by AI for cheating broadly undermines macro-level academic governance systems, transparency, and the overall credibility of science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Comprehensive revision of top-level academic regulations: Universities must urgently revise existing anti-plagiarism policies to establish detailed standards delineating compliant versus non-compliant uses of AI tools such as ChatGPT (supported by 51.2% of respondents). Ｌ Transnational and multi-stakeholder collaborative governance: Call upon AI developers, educators, and students to jointly reassess the role of generative AI in education; simultaneously align national or European-level strategies, principles, and regulatory mechanisms with guidelines from transnational bodies such as the European Network for Academic Integrity (ENAI), ensuring safe, reliable, and sustainable AI deployment. Ｍ Fundamental re-examination of evaluation systems: A subset of respondents (31.2%) proposed abolishing the thesis requirement entirely (replacing it with alternative assessments), reflecting academia＊s systemic rethinking and restructuring of the prevailing singular written assessment model in response to technological challenges.

Manifestation_Text: Technological usage disparities lead to inequities in academic evaluation and resource allocation. Students using ChatGPT gain disproportionate advantages in assignments and theses, distorting grade assessments and the distribution of academic honors〞and marginalizing the efforts of diligent learners.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Institution-wide guidance and training: Higher education institutions must provide comprehensive guidance and training for both faculty and students on the responsible and ethical use of AI tools, thereby leveling knowledge and normative practice. Ｌ Emphasize diverse sources and personal effort: Instructors should require students to synthesize findings from multiple sources and locate qualified resources, and to rewrite and customize content in their own words〞ensuring that academic outputs authentically reflect individual intellectual labor.

Manifestation_Text: Defects in AI algorithms (hallucinations and biases) and students＊ 'secondary camouflage' behaviors degrade the quality and authenticity of academic output. AI-generated texts contain fabricated research information and biases; moreover, students employ additional AI paraphrasing tools to obscure AI traces, further undermining the scientific quality of academic content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Critical evaluation and cross-verification: The text emphasizes that students and educators must critically evaluate and cross-reference information obtained from AI tools to ensure its accuracy and credibility. Ｌ Upholding the primacy of classical research methods: Instructors stress that reliance on ChatGPT alone is insufficient; instead, classic research tools and techniques must be integrated to revise, rewrite, and tailor information.

Manifestation_Text: The mutual trust between teachers and students〞grounded in academic integrity〞is distorted by 'black-box' technologies and shortcuts to cheating. Students exploit AI paraphrasing tools unfamiliar to instructors to evade detection, pursuing 'undetectable shortcuts'; meanwhile, instructors, disempowered by the opaque nature of AI, lose a sense of control over teaching assessment, transforming pedagogical interaction into a strategic game of preventing academic misconduct.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establishing a transparency-based trust mechanism: Teacher interviewees propose that academic integrity is not compromised〞as long as students properly cite their work and explicitly state which parts were generated by ChatGPT〞thereby restoring mutual trust through transparent disclosure. Ｌ Conducting targeted capacity-building for teachers and students: Institutions must provide comprehensive support to eliminate instructors＊ knowledge gaps regarding AI tools, enabling both parties to rebuild collaboration and mutual trust within a shared ethical framework.

Manifestation_Text: Traditional academic integrity detection systems have become ineffective, and the rampant use of AI-assisted writing poses systemic threats to the reputation, professional image, and public safety of higher education institutions.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Developing clear university policies and codes of conduct: Teacher interviewees unanimously call for 'initiating university guidelines and conducts' to provide students and faculty with unambiguous usage instructions and ethical constraints, thereby safeguarding academic integrity within institutional parameters. Ｌ Catalyzing reform of academic assessment paradigms: The integration of AI compels academia to reevaluate course design and adopt novel assessment formats〞such as tests deliberately designed to be difficult for AI to answer〞thus restructuring the evaluation system at a systemic level.

Manifestation_Text: AI algorithmic defects ('hallucinations') and deficiencies in higher-order thinking degrade academic content quality. LLMs generate text based on statistical probabilities rather than retrieving verifiable sources, leading them to confidently produce false facts (e.g., fabricating a non-existent 'Tenant Protection Act of 1847' or inventing scholarly references). Furthermore, the generated texts lack the analytical depth and academic rigor required in higher education, remaining at a secondary-school writing level.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Cultivating critical AI literacies: Educators must guide students in understanding both the capabilities and limitations of LLMs within classroom instruction, training them to critically assess and verify AI-generated content rather than accept it uncritically. Ｌ Reframing assessment priorities: Assessment practices must place irreplaceable higher-order thinking skills〞analysis, synthesis, and evaluation〞at their core, ensuring students develop genuine disciplinary expertise and research competence.

Manifestation_Text: A crisis of mutual trust between teachers and students in academic assessment, coupled with the alienation of intellectual agency. Because LLMs generate uniquely different outputs each time, conventional plagiarism-detection software becomes entirely ineffective, leaving instructors unable to determine whether submitted work originates from the student themselves. Simultaneously, students＊ blind reliance on AI early in their degree programs impedes the development of their own writing, research, and critical thinking skills, thereby eroding the teacher每student trust bond rooted in human intellectual growth.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introducing alternative assessment modalities: Adopting flipped classrooms, multimedia assignments, oral presentations, in-person examinations, and viva-voce defenses directly verifies students＊ authentic understanding while circumventing interference from AI text generation. Ｌ Student每teacher co-exploration: Rather than simply banning technology, students should be engaged as collaborative partners in classroom inquiry〞for instance, jointly analyzing AI＊s flaws (e.g., verifying erroneous historical documents generated by AI in real time)〞to reconstruct academic trust through transparent and critical interaction.

Manifestation_Text: Systemic failure of traditional academic authorship and accountability mechanisms, alongside macro-level academic integrity governance systems. Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to write papers〞and even conduct peer review〞yet LLMs 'cannot bear legal or reputational responsibility for published material,' fundamentally undermining the accountability framework underpinning scholarly publishing. Concurrently, existing academic integrity review systems (e.g., plagiarism detection tools) have become entirely ineffective against generative AI, causing widespread disruption to macro-level academic governance structures.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Top-level policy and norm revision: Academic publishing organizations and professional associations (e.g., APA) must continuously update editorial guidelines and citation standards to explicitly define the boundaries of AI authorship and establish clear disclosure and citation requirements for AI-generated text. Ｌ Systemic shift in assessment paradigms: Educational institutions must move beyond merely 'banning' such technologies and instead rethink assessment systemically, shifting evaluation emphasis from 'final written outputs' to the assessment of 'higher-order cognitive skills and critical thinking processes' to meet the evolving demands of academic integrity management in the AI era.

Manifestation_Text: The underlying training data of generative AI (GenAI) contains political, racial, cultural, and gender biases, and is disproportionately centered on English and Western sources. Non-Western language data is severely constrained in terms of volume, contextual richness, and domain diversity, rendering models incapable of understanding, generating, or processing texts that reflect the cultural and linguistic nuances specific to these communities〞thereby marginalizing and homogenizing non-Western knowledge systems and cultural groups.

GenAI exhibits 'hallucination'〞generating seemingly high-quality, credible original content containing factual and data errors. Simultaneously, human raters produce false positives and false negatives when suspecting GenAI involvement, resulting in inaccurate and unreliable evaluation of students＊ learning outcomes〞directly diminishing the ultimate efficacy, authenticity, and scientific rigor of academic assessment.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Refocusing assessment design: Universities and national bodies, when formulating policies, must not rely solely on 'authentic assessments' as a panacea; instead, the core focus must shift to assessment design itself. Ｌ Introducing process-oriented assessment: Learning assessment must evolve from evaluating only 'final outputs' to emphasizing 'learning processes' and their relevance to workplace practice.

Manifestation_Text: Students exhibit uncritical deference to 'intellectual authority' when engaging with GenAI, lacking appropriate autonomy and critical thinking, and delegating responsibility for completing academic tasks to AI systems. Moreover, because educators cannot reliably distinguish between human- and AI-generated work, the trust-based evaluative bond between teachers and students〞grounded in mutual recognition of human intellectual agency〞is eroded, leading to misjudgments about students＊ actual learning status.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Paradigm shift toward synchronous interpersonal assessment: Implement a paradigm shift from asynchronous written assessments to 'synchronous interpersonal assessments,' such as interactive oral assessments and role-play-type assessments. Ｌ Guiding constructive use: Encourage students to use GenAI ethically and appropriately during assessment preparation, treating it as a learning tool for developing key employability skills〞thus rebuilding rational, contextually grounded understandings of AI tools through interpersonal interaction.

Manifestation_Text: The convenience and low cost of GenAI entice students to adopt a 'consequentialist approach'〞prioritizing task completion over adherence to academic integrity norms. Such circumvention of assessment procedures undermines the expected standards and conventions of academic writing and erodes the intrinsic value of higher education degrees, posing an 'existential threat' to the assessment systems and public credibility of the entire higher education sector.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Restructuring academic assessment systems: Recognize that traditional written assessments can no longer serve as reliable indicators of learning outcomes, and advance a macro-level institutional transformation〞from 'output-based' to 'performative and process-focused' assessment systems. Ｌ Systemic policy recalibration: At both national and university levels, GenAI policy development must dispel the policy myth that 'authentic assessment alone can fully resolve this issue,' and systematically align assessment design with the authentic demands of the world of work.

Manifestation_Text: The high false-positive rate of AI detection tools subjects students to unwarranted plagiarism accusations, resulting in unjust treatment and severely biased consequences in academic evaluation and scholarly reputation.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Abandon repressive approaches: Academic institutions should abandon the 'repressive approach'〞namely, unilateral bans and sole reliance on automated detection tools. Ｌ Shift toward preventive assessment design: Rethink the design of written assignments to ensure tasks are ones that generative AI cannot perform better than human learners, thereby eliminating reliance on detection tools and mitigating risks of misjudgment.

Manifestation_Text: Students outsourcing academic tasks to AI undermines the ability of educational assessments to accurately measure genuine skill development and knowledge acquisition, directly compromising the authenticity of academic output; meanwhile, factual inaccuracies and hallucinations inherent in AI models threaten the final quality of scholarly content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Redesign assessment tasks: Reconfigure written assignments to ensure they are tasks at which human learners outperform AI, thereby preserving the relevance, fairness, and validity of assessment. Ｌ Provide training on AI limitations: Explicitly incorporate misinformation and hallucination risks into AI ethics training to enhance the academic community＊s critical awareness of and capacity to identify AI＊s technical limitations.

Manifestation_Text: Students＊ covert use of AI without disclosure erodes the mutual trust between instructors and students grounded in authentic intellectual effort; meanwhile, instructors＊ reliance on unreliable AI detection tools for unwarranted accusations further alienates and fractures the bonds of trust and collaboration within the academic community.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Cultivate dialogical skills: Foster open, informed dialogue among educators, students, and administrators regarding ethical AI use, establishing a culture of transparency and shared understanding. Ｌ Reframe moral commitments: Recast academic integrity〞not merely as prohibition of dishonest behavior〞but as an active commitment to core moral values such as honesty, trust, and fairness, thereby restoring interpersonal trust.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of generative AI systematically devalues the worth and macro-level credibility of academic degrees conferred by higher education institutions; concurrently, existing academic governance systems and institutional policies lag significantly behind, placing the academic governance framework at risk of failure.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish preventive institutional mechanisms: Institutions must proactively develop mechanisms, structures, and training programs to foster a renewed preventive culture of academic integrity, replacing outdated reactive practices. Ｌ Institutionalize AI ethics training: Integrate comprehensive AI ethics training across the entire academic community to empower members to engage in reflective, context-sensitive, and autonomous decision-making. Ｍ Adopt a pragmatist ethical framework: Apply a pragmatist approach to redefine the moral principles and normative frameworks of academic integrity in the era of generative AI.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated academic content often contains factual errors, hallucinations, lack of depth, and inaccurate citations, leading to the dissemination of low-quality research and misinformation, thereby diminishing the scientific efficacy and authenticity of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Strengthen human supervision: Human supervision is indispensable in critical research domains such as medicine. Ｌ Introduce screening and detection tools: Researchers are beginning to integrate screening tools and analyze expert reviewers＊ evaluation logic to optimize monitoring of AI use. Ｍ Proactive intervention by search engines: Call upon more adaptive search engines to act as allies in actively preventing AI systems from generating false information. Ｎ Improve AI models: Emphasize the need to enhance AI models to increase their accuracy and reliability in academic text production.

Manifestation_Text: AI intervention undermines educational trust between teachers and students (reducing teachers to 'academic police'), weakens the trust bond among peer reviewers, and erodes interpersonal communication skills and traditional interpersonal learning modes.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reconceptualizing the teacher＊s role and fostering deep collaboration: Exploring whether AI can assume pedagogical roles to enable deeper human每AI or teacher每student collaboration, thereby transforming teachers from mere 'supervisors' into facilitators and guides; Ｌ Complementary assessment strategies: Employing assessments that demand analytical thinking and effective communication as supplementary approaches to students＊ use of AI systems, thereby preserving interpersonal interaction and ensuring authentic evaluation of competencies.

Manifestation_Text: AI has triggered a 'crisis of truth' in academia, undermining academic integrity systems, intellectual property regimes, authorship attribution mechanisms, and causing systemic damage to the overall credibility of scientific knowledge and the development of ideas.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establishing clear frameworks of responsibility and conduct: Developing explicit behavioral and operational frameworks within universities or research environments to define who is responsible for AI-assisted processes, outputs, and decisions; Ｌ Journal-level authorship policies: Scientific journals are beginning to issue authorship policy guidelines that explicitly assign publication responsibility to human authors; Ｍ Values-driven AI system design: Developers and researchers should prioritize designing new AI systems that integrate core values such as integrity, privacy, autonomy, and respect, to counteract academic misconduct and systemic risks.

Manifestation_Text: Inherent biases embedded in AI＊s underlying models, coupled with overreliance on AI, lead to homogenisation of ideas, marginalizing original and diverse academic perspectives and individual writing styles.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Value embedding and system design: Calling on developers and researchers to prioritize designing AI systems that proactively embed values such as integrity, autonomy, and respect to counteract bias and degenerative behavioral patterns; Ｌ Cultivating critical discernment: Proposing novel pedagogical approaches to integrating AI systems into student education〞aimed specifically at developing students＊ capacity for critical discernment regarding processes, actions, and tasks (especially in identifying AI-generated content and bias)〞thereby resisting intellectual homogenisation.

Manifestation_Text: Barriers to accessing AI tools and inequitable AI usage policies result in unfair distribution of educational opportunities and resources. A blanket ban on AI use penalizes students lacking informal access channels, whereas unrestricted use advantages already highly skilled students, exacerbating inequalities in academic resource allocation.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Policy-bounded allowance: Establishing clearly defined boundaries for AI use rather than imposing an outright ban; Ｌ Provision of infrastructure support: Ensuring equitable access through institutional or instructor-provided resources (e.g., shared lab accounts or low-bandwidth alternatives); Ｍ Delivery of AI literacy training: Introducing AI-literacy mini-modules to enhance tool-use capabilities among disadvantaged learners, thereby narrowing disparities in resource access.

Manifestation_Text: Over-assistance by AI systems (e.g., providing excessively detailed prompts or directly generating answers) fosters brittle understanding and dependency among students, introduces construct-irrelevant variance, thereby compromising assessment validity and diminishing the authenticity and quality of learning outcomes and scholarly output.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Incorporating process evidence (Process Evidence, EVB): Requiring submission of prompt fragments, code diff outputs (e.g., git diffs), and micro-experiment notes to render underlying learning and reasoning processes visible; Ｌ Adjusting feedback granularity (FMG): Enforcing AI feedback modes configured as 'explanation-first' and 'critique mode', requiring students to produce self-explanations and reflective responses to prevent superficial pattern-matching.

Manifestation_Text: Students outsource intermediate reasoning and problem-solving processes to AI (answer outsourcing), preventing instructors from identifying the true author of assignments and assessing students＊ authentic reasoning abilities〞thereby undermining the trust bond between instructors and students grounded in academic integrity and genuine competence assessment.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandate oral micro-defenses / mini-vivas: Verify students＊ authentic understanding (e.g., code logic) through 4每5 minute oral examinations, directly testing whether students truly master the knowledge and restoring interpersonal trust. Ｌ Establish clear integrity guardrails (IEG): Implement policies restricting AI use, requiring explicit attribution tags and disclosure of AI tool usage to rebuild transparent academic mutual trust.

Manifestation_Text: Generative AI can perfectly produce assignments aligned with authentic assessment rubrics, delivering systemic shocks to existing academic evaluation systems, authorship attribution mechanisms, and course management practices〞eroding the credibility of traditional assessment frameworks; meanwhile, high-friction regulatory regimes provoke avoidance behaviors among instructors and students.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Co-evolve assessment formats with guardrails: Integrate parameterized items, random seeds, brief oral examinations, and explicit attribution/disclosure requirements so that administrative frameworks evolve in tandem with AI capabilities. Ｌ Implement lean governance / low-overhead guardrails: Adopt lightweight management tools〞including one-page policies, checkbox-based attribution declarations, and templated micro-vivas〞to avoid avoidance behaviors triggered by high-friction regulations and ensure operational feasibility and scalability of academic governance.

Manifestation_Text: Advanced AI functionalities are restricted behind paywalls or exhibit English-centric design features, resulting in stratified student access to high-impact educational practices and exacerbating the digital divide and inequities in educational resource distribution.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Provide baseline institutional access to core AI capabilities to prevent the digital divide; Ｌ Offer multilingual and accessibility support; Ｍ Conduct regular Equity and Fairness Audits to detect and mitigate bias.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated examples or feedback embed linguistic or cultural biases, and systems exhibit English-centric characteristics, leading to marginalization or representational injustice for non-native English speakers or students from specific cultural backgrounds.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Use representative evaluation datasets; Ｌ Provide multilingual support; Ｍ Embed uncertainty signals and verification steps in AI-supported tasks to sustain epistemic vigilance.

Manifestation_Text: AI generates hallucinations, unverifiable citations, non-reproducible outputs, and fluent yet erroneous or biased explanations〞reducing the accuracy and epistemic quality of academic research and learning assessments.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Add uncertainty signals and verification steps in AI tasks; Ｌ Ask for process evidence, like prompt logs and draft history; Ｍ Mix in human oversight when using AI for evaluations; Ｎ Bring AI literacy into research methods teaching.

Manifestation_Text: If AI tools replace peer collaboration, they undermine students＊ sense of social inclusion; opaque classification, excessive monitoring, or intrusive analytics erode feelings of belonging and trust; blurring authorship boundaries in assignments and outsourcing reasoning processes undermines the mutual trust between students and instructors grounded in intellectual honesty.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Redesign assessment methods, like iterative drafting with version tracking, oral/interactive defenses, and real-world artifacts; Ｌ Make course-level policies clear on what's allowed and what needs to be disclosed, so expectations are clear; Ｍ Use privacy-by-design and proportional analytics to cut down on over-monitoring.

Manifestation_Text: Existing policy frameworks focus narrowly on institutional compliance while overlooking how students actually integrate AI into their learning, resulting in governance gaps; reliance on AI detectors constitutes a response that is neither robust nor educationally productive, delivering ineffective shocks and systemic misalignment to broader academic governance and assessment systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Adopt a four-pillar student-activity framework to unify fragmented discussions and support institutional decision-making; Ｌ Develop cross-pillar principles〞including Mandatory Disclosure with Process Evidence, privacy-by-design and proportional analytics, and equitable auditing; Ｍ Constructive alignment must explicitly incorporate AI governance to ensure coherence across learning activities, assessments, and support mechanisms in both ethical and pedagogical terms.

Manifestation_Text: Inequitable access to technology and the digital divide lead to unfair distribution of academic resources and opportunities. Privileged students〞who possess greater technological capital (e.g., paid large language models, professional writing tools, or institutionally licensed platforms)〞gain disproportionate cognitive and academic advantages, whereas students lacking such resources face heightened pressure, marginalization, or exclusion, thereby exacerbating stratified learning environments.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Equitable resource allocation and inclusive governance: Ensure ＆equitable resource allocation＊ at the governance level to address structural inequities that make dishonest behavior appear feasible; Ｌ Alignment with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Align governance structures with UN SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions), prioritizing inclusivity and ethical agency over competition and control.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic bias, linguistic privilege, and cultural exclusion marginalize and misjudge specific academic groups〞including multilingual students, international students, and students from collectivist cultural backgrounds. For example, rigid time limits and uniform scoring criteria in language assessments place multilingual students at a disadvantage; in collectivist cultures, ＆sharing answers＊ reflects solidarity but is misinterpreted as academic misconduct by institutional policies lacking intercultural awareness.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Interculturally informed integrity interpretation: Institutions must interpret and formulate integrity policies through intercultural lenses to avoid cultural exclusion; Ｌ Culturally inclusive expectations: Explicitly articulate culturally inclusive expectations within policies to eliminate ethical confusion and misjudgment arising from cultural differences.

Manifestation_Text: AI automation of core academic competencies bypasses the learning process and compromises the authenticity of academic output. Generative AI can perform fundamental academic tasks〞including summarization, synthesis, and argument construction〞at scale and with minimal friction, enabling students to circumvent foundational cognitive processes, undermining traditional learning metrics, and intensifying uncertainty regarding the authenticity of work and authorial identity.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Redesign assessment paradigms: Fundamentally shift assessment design toward ＆authentic, process-based, and formative assessments＊ that emphasize human judgment and learning processes, thereby reducing incentives to outsource tasks to automated reasoning systems; Ｌ Emphasize process orientation: Implement transparent, process-oriented AI-use policies that prioritize the learning process〞not merely the final output.

Manifestation_Text: Alienation of ethical scaffolding and erosion of trust bonds between students and educators/institutions. Ethical scaffolds originally designed to support learning〞such as instructor feedback and peer collaboration〞are displaced or distorted by unauthorized AI assistance, undermining the balance of the learning ecosystem and the ethical reciprocity between students and institutions. Moreover, punitive monitoring technologies provoke psychological resistance, further damaging interpersonal trust.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Cultivating institutional cultures that normalize disclosure and responsible AI use: Foster an institutional culture in which disclosure and responsible AI use are normalized, thereby rebuilding trust. Ｌ Shifting toward dialogic accountability: Move from punitive enforcement to 'dialogic accountability', jointly shared among learners, educators, and policymakers to uphold transparency and trust. Ｍ Supporting moral agency: Empower students to exercise moral agency when interacting with increasingly powerful AI tools, rather than relying solely on surveillance.

Manifestation_Text: Commodification of higher education and systemic disruption of academic governance frameworks. AI blurs the boundary between human and machine authorship, challenging traditional assumptions about originality and assessment integrity. Within the context of neoliberal governance and the commodification of higher education, learning is reframed as a market transaction; students adopt instrumental attitudes prioritizing credential acquisition, causing institutional success to diverge from its ethical purpose and eroding the social contract and moral foundations of higher education.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Systemic redesign: Abandon incremental adjustments and undertake systemic reconstruction using the 'Higher Education Integrity Ecosystem Model', conceptualizing integrity as an emergent property arising from the interplay of governance, assessment, culture, and agency. Ｌ Introducing reflexive governance mechanisms: Implement integrity audits and participatory policy design to ensure institutional adaptability to evolving AI technologies. Ｍ Calibrating enforcement and restorative measures: Combine preventive design, targeted detection, proportionate sanctions, and sustained ethics education to address systemic malicious violations and institutional vulnerabilities.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated content exhibits algorithmic bias and limitations in information retrieval scope〞for instance, producing anti-Islamic (or Islamophobic) content reflecting specific cultural or religious prejudices, and generating knowledge homogenization and marginalization due to constraints inherent in training data sources.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Developing clear AI ethics policies: Educational administrators and policymakers must establish institutional policies guiding the ethical application of conversational AI. Ｌ Advancing AI safety regulation and technical identification: Advocate for strengthened AI safety, AI regulation, and AI watermarking to trace and govern the generation of biased content.

Manifestation_Text: AI＊s 'hallucination' flaw leads to the generation of false, inaccurate, or empirically unsupported information, and fails to provide authentic citation sources〞directly compromising the authenticity, rigor, and scientific quality of academic research and scholarly writing.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandating human intellectual engagement and verification: The article emphasizes that 'human understanding' must intervene at every stage of research to ensure precision. Ｌ Standardizing attribution and acknowledgment of AI use: Require explicit attribution and acknowledgment of AI tool usage in research, preventing AI-generated content from being presented as human-authored scholarly output without disclosure.

Manifestation_Text: Students＊ overreliance on AI for 'quick and easy' answers results in superficial surface learning, dissolving the intellectual trust between students and instructors grounded in deep knowledge mastery and critical thinking; simultaneously, AI replaces human deep reflection, alienating intellectual agency within the academic research process.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Restructuring assessments: The article recommends increasing in-class assessments, oral assessments, and problem- or case-based applied assessments, reducing dependence on single post-class textual assignments. Ｌ Implementing continuous and concrete evaluation: Respondents propose that assessment procedures must not be 'lazy'; instead, tasks should be directed toward more concrete and ongoing formative assessment processes, directly verifying students＊ authentic understanding and restoring mutual trust between students and instructors.

Manifestation_Text: The low similarity scores of AI-generated text render traditional academic integrity detection systems (e.g., plagiarism detection technologies) ineffective, triggering widespread concerns regarding plagiarism, academic misconduct, copyright infringement, and intellectual property disputes〞thereby delivering a systemic shock to macro-level academic evaluation frameworks and academic integrity governance systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Top-level policy and institutional redesign: Research strongly calls on educational institutions and policymakers to draft clear policies regarding the use of AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT/AI tools) and to integrate responsible AI use into academic integrity norms. Ｌ Faculty training and capacity building: It is emphasized that faculty must be trained to distinguish between human- and AI-generated work and to effectively integrate AI into teaching and assessment〞thus safeguarding the baseline of academic integrity at the level of institutional implementation. Ｍ Regulatory intervention at the technical level: The adoption of AI watermarking and AI regulation mechanisms is advocated to assist academic systems in restoring their ability to identify originality at the technical foundation.

Manifestation_Text: Content generated by AI models may contain distorted responses stemming from flaws or biases embedded in training data, thereby reinforcing stereotypes about specific demographic groups and perpetuating social inequities within academic and learning contexts.

The unreliability of AI algorithms leads to the generation of inaccurate or misleading content〞for instance, erroneous citations or fabricated references〞which directly undermines research validity; students lacking the ability to assess source credibility and blindly relying on unverified AI-generated content face heightened risks of disseminating misinformation.

AI-mediated communication lacks emotional intelligence and empathy, resulting in reduced interpersonal interaction during learning; the integration of AI may degrade educational quality by diminishing meaningful interactions between teachers and students, thereby weakening the interpersonal bonds essential for fostering deep engagement and emotional support.

Generative AI＊s capacity to produce human-like content blurs the traditional boundary between students＊ original work and AI-assisted or AI-generated outputs, rendering concepts such as authorship, originality, and academic honesty ambiguous (e.g., rendering conventional definitions of plagiarism obsolete); simultaneously, a serious disconnect exists between institutional policy development and student awareness〞most students remain unaware whether their institutions have established relevant ethical regulations, thereby undermining macro-level academic integrity systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Development of clear institutional guidelines and comprehensive training: In response to student needs, academic institutions must provide explicit guidelines on AI use and deliver integrated training on compliance and appropriate tool usage within educational activities (as called for in Tierney et al.＊s research). Ｌ Integration of ethics-oriented pedagogy beyond binary frameworks: The authors emphasize that addressing institutional impacts requires moving beyond simplistic ＆allow-or-prohibit＊ dichotomies toward nuanced governance pathways that deeply embed ethical reasoning into generative AI pedagogy.

Manifestation_Text: Reliance on AI detection tools disproportionately negatively impacts vulnerable groups〞such as international students〞exacerbating inequities in academic evaluation and resource allocation.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Careful Implementation and Equitable Application: When introducing AI detection technologies, implementation must be conducted with care and accompanied by robust support, ensuring these tools are accessible, applied with equality, and beneficial to all students regardless of their background or geographical location.

Manifestation_Text: AI generates misinformation, fosters over-reliance, gives rise to novel forms of plagiarism (＆AI-giarism＊), and enables content manipulation〞directly undermining the authenticity and scientific quality of academic output.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish Ethical and Cautious Use Principles: It must be explicitly stipulated that the use of generative AI (GenAI) tools in scholarly contexts must be ethical and exercised with caution. Ｌ Cultivate Critical Evaluation Skills: Equip students with critical skills to assess GenAI-produced content, thereby supplementing algorithmic limitations with human oversight (Bearman et al., 2024).

Manifestation_Text: GenAI deconstructs traditional teacher每student roles and erodes the trust-based interpersonal bonds within the academic community that rest on human intellect〞for instance, students are highly reluctant to report peers for cheating, while inappropriate assistance to others or permitting others to plagiarize occurs frequently.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Foster a Culture of Trust and Accountability: Educational institutions must adopt robust measures to foster a culture of trust and accountability among students (Hill and Narine, 2023). Ｌ Conduct Structured Dialogue and Education: Formally integrate ethical discussions about GenAI technologies into academic integrity frameworks and deliver targeted integrity education to rebuild shared ethical understanding and mutual trust between instructors and students, and among students themselves.

Manifestation_Text: GenAI exerts systemic disruption upon traditional teaching and assessment systems, as well as upon the very concept of originality; many students directly submit AI-generated text for assessments, thereby upending established academic governance and evaluation mechanisms.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Redesign Assessment Paradigms and Digital Literacy: A fundamental rethinking is required regarding how and what is assessed, exploring ways to safeguard the originality of student work and leveraging assessment to cultivate digital literacy and uniquely human capabilities in the GenAI era (Lodge et al., 2023). Ｌ Strengthen Institutional Policy and Guidance: There is an urgent call for clear institutional policies and guidelines addressing misuse and safeguarding academic integrity, alongside structured ethical engagement support for students.

Manifestation_Text: Barriers to technology access lead to inequities in academic evaluation and resource allocation.

Defects in AI algorithms (e.g., hallucinations, inaccurate information) degrade the quality of academic and clinical education, undermining students＊ critical thinking and clinical decision-making abilities.
Mitigation_Text:
Ｋ Cross-verification and secondary validation: Empower users by requiring secondary verification and cross-referencing of information provided by ChatGPT.
Ｌ Incorporation of a reflective assessment component: Integrate a reflective element into assessments that focuses on the entire process〞from prompt formulation to output generation.
Ｍ Integration of domain-specific resources and annotations: Embed clinical pharmacy每specific resources and annotations within AI tools to reduce inaccuracies in information and citations.

Manifestation_Text: AI＊s lack of emotional resonance and authentic interaction alienates the core interpersonal communication and clinical collaboration bonds essential to medicine and pharmacy.
Mitigation_Text:
Ｋ Preservation of essential experiential learning components: Maintain a balanced integration of AI in education by preserving foundational elements of ＆hands-on learning and skill development＊ to ensure that interpersonal communication competencies are not fully displaced.
Ｌ Leveraging AI to develop communication evaluation criteria: Utilize AI tools to design objective, structured communication rubrics for Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs), thereby specifically enhancing and assessing critical interpersonal communication skills.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI triggers a systemic academic integrity crisis; existing detection tools are ineffective, and overarching governance policies lag behind, thereby undermining academic evaluation systems.
Mitigation_Text:
Ｋ Redesigning assessment frameworks: Thoroughly redesign current assessments vulnerable to generative AI (Gen-AI) influence by adopting holistic rubrics that evaluate competencies beyond written responses, and shifting curricular emphasis from content recall toward fostering active creativity and critical thinking.
Ｌ Delivering institution-wide AI ethics and competency training: Provide formal training for educators and students on the responsible and appropriate use of Gen-AI to enhance AI literacy and prevent both intentional and unintentional misuse.
Ｍ Establishing transparent and explicit institutional guidelines: Develop clear, publicly accessible guidelines and transparent assessment protocols that explicitly define the boundaries of compliant AI use, and mandate strict acknowledgment and disclosure of AI tool usage in academic publications and assignments.

Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Incorporate process-based evidence: Require submission of marked outputs, appendices, or selective interaction logs to verify the learning process. Manifestation_Text: The rupture of the teacher-student trust bond and the emergence of defensive concealment behaviors. Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implement proportionate and non-punitive mechanisms: Transparency mechanisms must be proportionate and explicitly avoid punitive or overly surveillant dynamics. Manifestation_Text: The 'black-box' nature and technical limitations of AI algorithms lead to deterioration and misrepresentation of academic content quality. Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduce human expert evaluation: While updating ethical frameworks, human expertise must be integrated to review and evaluate AI-generated content. Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Address data bias challenges: Explicitly designate the mitigation of data bias as a core issue within ethical guidelines, requiring proactive identification and discussion of potential biases when using AI (e.g., addressing challenges like privacy and data biases). Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Redefine academic norms: Call for redefining concepts such as plagiarism and co-authorship, and formulate comprehensive guidelines governing the use of LLMs throughout the research process. Manifestation_Text: The integration of AI has raised concerns about reduced face-to-face interaction and negative impacts on social environments; simultaneously, the widespread collection and analysis of students＊ personal data and learning patterns by AI systems have triggered concerns regarding unauthorized access and privacy breaches, undermining the bonds of confidentiality and mutual trust within the academic community (between institutions and students).
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Adopt a comprehensive approach to establish a robust ethical framework and enhance transparency in data processing, ensuring informed consent; Ｌ Educational institutions must implement comprehensive data protection policies, using data transparently and responsibly to safeguard students＊ privacy rights; Ｍ Integrate privacy-by-design principles and privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs) to embed privacy safeguards into AI systems from the outset; Ｎ Ensure equitable resource allocation to bridge disparities in AI-enabled educational practices and guarantee equal access to emerging technologies for all.

Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Issue institution-level academic integrity guidelines: Call upon universities and educational institutions to provide clear-cut guidelines and concrete examples that explicitly define the boundaries of permissible GenAI use and standards for plagiarism, thereby eliminating regulatory ambiguity. Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Diversification of research samples: The academic community is actively pursuing diversification of research samples to better reflect the human population overall, thereby advancing fairness and inclusivity in research. Ｌ Incorporating community engagement and democratic discourse: Drawing on the literature review (J. Jeon et al.), it is argued that AI research ethics standards must incorporate community engagement and democratic discourse to address the complexity arising from interactions between AI systems and social processes〞avoiding the reduction of ethics to generic checklists.

Manifestation_Text: The highly persuasive nature of AI-generated text renders conventional academic misconduct detection tools ineffective; simultaneously, students＊ misuse of AI for completing assignments suppresses critical thinking and directly compromises the authenticity of academic output and the ultimate quality of education and research.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reforming curriculum structure and assessment formats: Instructors are proactively modifying course structures and examination formats ('changing course structure and exams') to reduce student reliance on AI and to reassess genuine learning outcomes. Ｌ Implementing educational interventions to foster critical thinking: Based on the literature review citing M. Gerlich＊s findings, there is a call for 'educational interventions' designed to cultivate critical thinking skills related to AI technologies, thereby mitigating the cognitive costs associated with AI tool usage.

Manifestation_Text: Students＊ excessive 'cognitive offloading' onto AI leads to diminished intellectual agency and a marked decline in the quality and frequency of student每instructor interaction, thereby undermining the mutual trust and collaborative bonds within the academic community〞bonds traditionally rooted in human intellectual inquiry.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establishing clear usage standards to reconstruct academic authenticity: The article emphasizes that using technologies such as ChatGPT in academic life requires 'clear standards' to regulate technological use, ensuring academic processes remain authentic and aligned with core academic ethical values. Ｌ Adopting a balanced approach integrating ethics and practice: Drawing on S. Balakrishnan＊s research, the article stresses the need for a 'balanced approach' that addresses both ethical and practical concerns to enhance student每instructor interaction and improve overall learning outcomes.

Manifestation_Text: The widespread application of AI has exerted systemic pressure on traditional academic authorship norms, scholarly publishing evaluation systems, and institutional-level ethical oversight frameworks, resulting in ambiguous accountability mechanisms and regulatory gaps.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Improve citation and authorship standards: Scholars (e.g., M. Hosseini et al.) recommend revising the APA format to include the author, version, model, and date of use when citing ChatGPT, and to provide detailed documentation of interactions with large language models (LLMs) in the introduction, methods section, or appendix. Ｌ Develop institutional policies and educational curricula: Universities and colleges should establish clear regulations and educational courses to support students in using AI systems correctly and ethically. Ｍ Enhance AI ethics tools and auditing mechanisms: Drawing on J. Ayling＊s research, there is a need to close the current gap in AI ethics tools regarding auditing and risk assessment.

Manifestation_Text: Students＊ access to advanced generative AI tools varies due to disparities in economic resources. Under an ＆unrestricted use (Lane 2/All)＊ assessment model, students with better AI tools can complete assessments more easily or at higher quality, thereby gaining unfair competitive advantages in accessing limited academic and societal resources〞such as graduate admissions, scholarships, and employment opportunities.
Mitigation_Text: Implement and enforce uniform institutional restrictions on generative AI use for all students (i.e., adopt the ＆middle lane/Lane 3/Some＊ approach), rather than adopting an entirely unrestricted ＆all-allowed＊ model, thereby eliminating inequities in resource allocation arising from technological access barriers.

Manifestation_Text: Unrestricted AI use leads to reduced student academic engagement; assessment outcomes fail to authentically reflect students＊ knowledge mastery, skill development, and progressive learning processes, severely undermining the effectiveness and authenticity of assessment as a learning motivator. Moreover, inherent algorithmic flaws in AI detection tools (e.g., false positives) may lead to misjudgments, compromising the accuracy of academic integrity reviews.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reform assessment design: Adopt the ＆middle lane (Lane 3/Some)＊ strategy〞permitting AI use only under specific constraints (e.g., for research or brainstorming, not for direct writing)〞and integrate it with scaffolded skill instruction. Ｌ Employ multiple lines of evidence: Given the false-positive limitations of AI detectors, academic institutions should avoid sole reliance on such tools and instead require multiple corroborating evidence sources (e.g., document metadata, editing timestamps, source tracing, and oral discussions) to initiate academic misconduct investigations.

Manifestation_Text: Students blindly delegate intellectual agency to AI (e.g., directly inputting questions into AI and submitting the generated answers under their own names), thereby eroding authentic cognitive engagement and reflective learning processes; meanwhile, the ＆all-or-nothing (All-or-None)＊ governance model reflects a ＆defeatist attitude＊, undermining educators＊ trust in and expectations of students＊ academic integrity.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Policy communication and trust restoration: Clearly communicate assessment rules to students and conduct education grounded in the premise of trust〞that most students are willing to comply with established norms. Ｌ Introduce multi-layered defense and deterrence mechanisms: Apply the ＆Swiss Cheese Model＊ and the ＆Educational Integrity Enforcement Pyramid＊ to establish multiple procedural barriers and calibrated consequences for violations, thereby reinforcing and safeguarding academic integrity within the scholarly community.

Manifestation_Text: Tolerating students＊ passing assessments through unrestricted AI use〞which effectively constitutes cheating〞devalues the degree as a credible signal of the holder＊s knowledge and competencies, thereby seriously damaging the overall social reputation of higher education institutions and their graduates, and inflicting systemic harm on the academic evaluation system and its public credibility.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Process-oriented assessment monitoring: Introduce write-in assignment platforms (e.g., Cadmus) that enable assessors to view students＊ writing processes and drafts, and rapidly distinguish pasted content from typed text〞thereby enhancing assessment security at the system level. Ｌ Macro-level policy restructuring: Institutional AI policies must move beyond simplistic binaries of ＆blanket prohibition＊ or ＆blanket permission＊, and instead develop discipline-specific, task-appropriate frameworks and guidelines governing acceptable AI use.

Manifestation_Text: Unfair grade allocation and unequal access to tools resulting from ambiguous assessment criteria. In the absence of clear and transparent assessment standards, instructors rely on implicit judgments for grading, increasing arbitrariness and bias in evaluation; simultaneously, disparities exist among students in accessing generative AI tools.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop formalized assessment tools: Introduce standardized procedures such as explicit scoring rubrics or checklists to eliminate arbitrariness arising from instructors＊ implicit judgments. Ｌ Ensure regulatory clarity and evaluative safeguards: Explicitly define compliance requirements and evaluative safeguards in institutional policies to guarantee fairness in grade allocation.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated content obscuring authentic learning capacity, thereby undermining the validity of educational assessment and degrading the quality of final outputs. Assignments efficiently produced by students using AI often lack genuine understanding, reasoning, and deep learning; treating such outputs directly as evidence of learning severely compromises the authenticity and scientific rigor of academic assessment.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduce process-based evidence: Require submission of marked outputs, appendices, or selective interaction logs to verify the learning process. Ｌ Strengthen critical reflection and accountability statements: Require students to submit explicit reflective and verification statements, making transparency itself an integral assessment criterion〞not merely focusing on the final product.

Manifestation_Text: Erosion of the trust-based teacher每student relationship and emergence of defensive concealment behaviors. Fear of punishment, stigmatization, or informal sanctions prompts students to adopt concealment or strategically selective disclosure〞transforming the educational environment into a 'low-trust environment' where pedagogical relationships devolve from learning facilitation into control and surveillance.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implement proportionate and non-punitive mechanisms: Transparency mechanisms must remain proportionate and explicitly avoid punitive or overly surveillant dynamics. Ｌ Shift toward a 'declaration-of-responsibility' governance model: Move away from attempting to 'prove usage' toward ensuring that usage is 'traceable and defensible', establishing a trust framework grounded in learning orientation and pedagogical alignment.

Manifestation_Text: Failure of traditional academic accountability mechanisms and systemic misalignment between macro-level 'policy每practice'. The integration of generative AI disrupts foundational assumptions underlying conventional grading and attribution of performance; meanwhile, institutional policies often remain at the level of abstract ethical principles or recommendations, lacking translation into concrete, assessable tasks〞resulting in an implementation vacuum within macro-level governance systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Advance operational paradigm shifts at the institutional level: Translate abstract transparency principles into concrete, assessable tasks. Ｌ Integrate compliance assessment mechanisms: Systematically embed compliance assessment methods (e.g., clearly specified requirements, spot-check verification) into macro-level assessment design to bridge the institutional gap between policy and practice.

Manifestation_Text: Academic output authenticity and quality degradation caused by AI hallucinations and non-compliant use. Students directly generate assignment content using generative AI and apply only 'light editing' (e.g., changing a few words) to obscure its origin〞or even fabricate 'fake references'. Moreover, students themselves acknowledge that generative AI is not a reliable source; overreliance directly diminishes the ultimate efficacy of learning and research outputs.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Enhance AI literacy: Position AI literacy as a potential means to alleviate academic integrity pressures, helping students recognize the limitations and appropriate boundaries of generative AI. Ｌ Implement structural assessment reforms: Go beyond declarative guidelines by redesigning assessment mechanisms〞for instance, conducting portions of assessments under conditions where generative AI is unavailable〞to physically and procedurally constrain misuse and ensure the authenticity of assessed content.

Manifestation_Text: Blind delegation of intellectual agency and the erosion of mutual trust within the academic community. Students reduce academic integrity to an individual, ad hoc act of 'avoiding detection', rather than recognizing it as a shared moral character of the scholarly community. The integration of generative AI (GenAI) severely undermines the core requirement of 'ownership' in academic work; students＊ over-dependence on algorithms stunts their learning and intellectual development, while the mutual trust between instructors and students〞grounded in authentic intellectual effort〞is distorted into a zero-sum 'anti-cheating' game.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reaffirming the intrinsic value of academic integrity: Reframe academic integrity not as 'rules for passing assessments', but as a holistic and intrinsic facet of being a Higher Education student. Ｌ Co-constructing contemporary learning ethics: Call upon scholars and learners to jointly co-construct learning ethics suited to the GenAI era, thereby restoring the academic community＊s moral consensus and collaborative bonds.

Manifestation_Text: Systemic collapse of traditional academic governance and evaluation systems. The widespread adoption of GenAI has rendered conventional mechanisms for sanctioning academic misconduct〞relying on 'rule lists, honor codes, and plagiarism detection'〞nearly ineffective due to the near-impossibility of detection. Higher education is thus trapped in an 'ethical impasse' and 'philosophical and practical confusion'; terminology guidelines issued by existing national or international academic integrity networks (e.g., ENAI, TEQSA) have become obsolete in the face of GenAI, and macro-level public confidence in academic evaluation has been severely undermined.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Shifting from 'cheating management' to 'assessment validity': Policymakers must abandon the futile practice of endlessly expanding lists of prohibited behaviors and instead prioritize the validity and security of assessments. Ｌ Driving 'structural' reform of assessment mechanisms: Replace discourse-based or declaration-based guidelines〞reliant solely on student self-reporting〞with redesigned assessments that naturally elicit the desired academic behaviors (i.e., the desired behaviour emerges naturally from the assessment design), thereby institutionalizing resilience against GenAI misuse at the foundational level.

Manifestation_Text: AI＊s instantaneous generation of text〞devoid of the iterative human thinking process〞directly violates the essential requirements of 'authenticity' and 'originality' in academic and publishing content, resulting in a substantive downgrade of intellectual investment in scholarly output.
Mitigation_Text: Develop and deploy the 'Writer's Integrity' framework, which verifies whether content has undergone genuine human cognitive engagement and iterative refinement by capturing behavioral metrics such as typing speed, edit frequency, and paste ratio〞thereby safeguarding the intellectual quality and authenticity of scholarly output.

Manifestation_Text: The indistinguishability of AI-generated text undermines the trust bond〞rooted in 'human original intellectual contribution'〞among academic supervisors, journal reviewers, publishers, and authors, triggering a severe crisis of interpersonal trust in academic mentoring, peer review, and publishing scrutiny.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Issuing and sharing the 'Writer's Integrity Certificate': Provide supervisors and reviewers with transparent logs containing writing-behavior metrics and revision histories, serving as objective evidence to rebuild interpersonal trust. Ｌ Reshaping user cognition and trust expectations: Analogize the monitoring function of this framework to online proctoring systems used in remote examinations, clarifying to users that it constitutes a necessary safeguard for upholding academic standards〞not malicious surveillance〞thus alleviating interpersonal defensiveness and resistance.

Manifestation_Text: The failure of current AI detection tools (characterized by high false-positive and false-negative rates, and susceptibility to semantic paraphrasing evasion), coupled with the proliferation of AI-generated content, is systematically weakening the macro-level governance systems through which academia and publishing uphold information authenticity and scientific credibility.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ A systemic paradigm shift in detection: Advocate a transition from 'product-based text analysis' to 'process-based writing monitoring'. Ｌ Building a multi-stakeholder certification ecosystem: Integrate this framework broadly into macro-level academic governance institutions〞including universities and publishers〞via open-source code, commercial licensing, partnership agreements, and subscription models, thereby establishing an institutionalized anti-forgery infrastructure. Ｍ Embedding detection and provenance mechanisms into foundational models: Citing Knott et al. in the text, call upon developers of base models to make reliable detection mechanisms a mandatory condition for model release, and align them with content authenticity initiatives such as the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA), ensuring normative governance of AI content generation and traceability from the source.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic flaws in AI detection tools (e.g., high false-negative rates) and human reviewers＊ overreliance on AI directly undermine the accuracy and quality of peer review and internal ethical review.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Uphold the irreplaceability of human evaluation: Reviewers must carefully evaluate AI-generated information to ensure final decisions are based on accurate and in-depth assessment. Ｌ Establish the principle of 'AI as assistant, not replacement': Provide clear recommendations to researchers in editorial conclusions, emphasizing that human evaluation remains indispensable; AI tools should support, not supplant, professional human judgment.

Manifestation_Text: The introduction of AI-assisted peer review systems has given rise to novel forms of academic misconduct (e.g., fabrication of citations or verbatim plagiarism), while existing academic evaluation systems〞overly reliant on metrics such as the h-index and journal impact factor〞are highly vulnerable to systemic erosion through citation manipulation and inappropriate authorship practices (e.g., gift, honorary, or guest authorship), thereby undermining macro-level academic governance and resource allocation systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduce automated detection algorithms and platform integration: Develop and integrate tools such as the CIDRE algorithm (to detect anomalous citation behavior), Scite Reference Check (to verify references), and AI-integrated submission platforms (e.g., AIRA) to automatically intercept misconduct during submission and review processes. Ｌ Strengthen authors＊ ethical responsibilities and disclosure requirements: Researchers must fully disclose conflicts of interest and ethical approvals, and strictly avoid unethical practices such as guest authorship and plagiarism. Ｍ Promote continuous R&D of AI detection tools: Future research should prioritize enhancing AI tools＊ capacity to identify complex publication ethics issues〞such as concealed authorship concerns and undisclosed conflicts of interest.

Manifestation_Text: AI algorithmic flaws (e.g., hallucinations, factual errors) and limitations of AI detection tools compromise the authenticity and scientific quality of scholarly content. AI-generated text may appear authoritative yet contain errors, omissions, or biases; meanwhile, current AI content detection tools suffer from both false positives and false negatives and struggle to identify conceptual plagiarism or semantically altered images.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reinforce final human oversight by editors and authors: Experts unanimously stress the necessity of strict human oversight for AI-generated content; authors must critically assess AI outputs and revise them based on domain-specific knowledge. Ｌ Combine auxiliary technical screening with expert review: AI detection tools should be used cautiously and cannot replace human editorial judgment; for images, emerging AI-based image verification tools must be integrated with expert editorial review and explicit author declarations.

Manifestation_Text: Authors＊ excessive reliance on AI and the delegation of intellectual agency erode the trust bond within the academic community〞grounded in human originality and accountability. AI＊s involvement may enable authors to evade substantive intellectual contribution to their work, placing academic trust among readers, editors, and authors at risk.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandate transparent disclosure of AI use: Following guidelines such as those from the ICMJE, authors must explicitly declare in the cover letter and manuscript the names and versions of AI tools used, their specific purposes, and affirm that human authors have reviewed and edited the content and assume full responsibility. Ｌ Institutional-level ethics training: Institutions should provide training or guidance on the use of AI in medical writing to help researchers uphold academic integrity while leveraging AI tools, thereby avoiding blind delegation of intellectual agency.

Manifestation_Text: The rapid penetration of AI technologies has exposed the lagging nature and systemic gaps in traditional academic publishing management systems, ethical statements, and author guidelines, delivering institutional-level shocks to the overall credibility of the scientific literature and the scholarly evaluation system.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Comprehensive revision of top-level ethical guidelines and author handbooks: Journals must update their 'Instructions for Authors' to explicitly incorporate provisions on AI use and text/image plagiarism, and uniformly adopt the latest positions of COPE and ICMJE to standardize industry-wide expectations. Ｌ Build a structured journal editorial governance framework: The article recommends journals implement a six-pillar structured framework〞including mandatory AI disclosure, AI similarity screening, transparent threshold policies, image verification workflows, regular ethics training, and an explicit prohibition of AI as an author〞to systematically close loopholes enabling AI misuse at the procedural level.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated academic texts suffer from 'hallucinations'〞fabricating references, presenting superficial content, and lacking originality〞thereby directly undermining the scientific quality and authenticity of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandatory peer review and human evaluation: Any AI-generated output must undergo rigorous peer review prior to application in critical decision-making or subsequent publication; during detection, automated analytical tools must be combined with human evaluation. Ｌ Strengthening citation verification mechanisms: Journal editors and researchers are encouraged not to overlook meticulous verification of references and citations, employing specialized technical tools (e.g., the 'Correct citation' check mentioned in Table 4 of the text) to validate the authenticity of AI-generated content.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI tools has triggered widespread academic plagiarism and delivered systemic shocks to macro-level governance frameworks〞including traditional copyright regimes, citation norms, and academic integrity evaluation systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establishing clear regulatory frameworks and policies: Academic and research institutions must implement explicit measures, guidelines, policies, and rules to govern AI use within controlled educational environments, safeguarding academic integrity. Ｌ Comprehensively enhancing AI literacy: Providing ongoing training for faculty and staff on ethical AI use, fostering collaboration between educators and AI experts, and designing more effective pedagogical strategies. Ｍ Introducing third-party review and assessment adjustments: Adopting third-party review mechanisms and appropriately reducing conventional written assignments to mitigate plagiarism incentives at the source of the evaluation system.

Manifestation_Text: Overreliance on AI leads to the degradation of human reasoning capacity (i.e., 'rational obsolescence'), eroding the intellectual agency and critical thinking that underpin academic research and education.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implementing targeted measures to protect human reasoning: Prioritizing 'measures to preserve human reasoning' as the central regulatory strategy (as indicated in Table 3 of the text, supported by 21 cited studies) to ensure human agency remains central to research. Ｌ Cultivating motivational environments and academic integrity culture: Fostering educational environments that stimulate intrinsic motivation (motivational environments), encouraging students to use AI responsibly rather than relying on it passively. Ｍ Promoting practice-based methods in controlled settings: Educators should adopt AI-integrated pedagogical approaches, guiding students to use AI tools in safe, controlled environments to ensure alignment between teaching activities and educational values.

Manifestation_Text: Erosion of the academic trust bond and a crisis of authorial identity and trust.
Systemic disruption to core academic publishing institutions (e.g., peer review) and to the overall credibility of science.

Technological barriers and unequal resource distribution have fragmented the global scholarly ecosystem into a 'two-tier system', placing researchers in constrained regions at systemic disadvantages〞and subject to algorithmic injustice〞in academic publishing, literature verification, and international competitiveness.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Foundational mitigation at the user level: Researchers in constrained regions should consistently cross-verify AI-suggested references against authoritative databases such as Scopus, treat large language models (LLMs) strictly as idea generators, and prioritize manual literature searches (Section 8). Ｌ Macro-level resource allocation and policy prioritization: Funding bodies should tie research grants to the use of certified verification tools, thereby institutionalizing support to offset resource disadvantages faced by researchers in under-resourced regions (Section 12).

Manifestation_Text: Geographic inconsistencies and region-specific content censorship distort, fabricate, or marginalize knowledge systems〞particularly those originating from specific territories, addressing sensitive topics, or produced by independent scholars.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Algorithmic transparency and independent verification: The scientific community must require publishers and AI providers to ensure algorithmic transparency and subject detection and generation systems to independent validation, preventing their use for discriminatory or politically motivated filtering (Section 12). Ｌ Establishment of clear appeal procedures: Clear appeals processes must be provided for submissions that are flagged or filtered, safeguarding independent scientists and marginalized scholarly perspectives from unwarranted suppression (Section 12).

Manifestation_Text: The 'hallucination' mechanism of AI generates widespread fabricated citations, spurious data, and error cascades, directly undermining the authenticity, accuracy, and ultimate scientific efficacy of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Publisher-led validation at submission stage: Implement mandatory AI-assisted reference validation, integrating real-time database checks (e.g., CrossRef/DOI), retrieval-augmented grounding (RAG grounding), and uncertainty scoring (Sections 10 and 12). Ｌ Hybrid human每AI review mechanisms: Introduce human editorial review for cases flagged by the system as potential hallucinations (Section 12). Ｍ Technical architecture optimization: Developers should adopt probabilistic uncertainty estimation methods〞such as semantic entropy〞to flag potentially fabricated content in real time during inference (Section 5).

Manifestation_Text: Misuse of AI distorts academic evaluation metrics (e.g., h-index), fuels the proliferation of paper mills, and risks transforming publishers＊ monopolies over AI verification tools into a 'censorship-industrial complex', thereby delivering institutional shocks to macro-level scholarly governance and the overall credibility of science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Cross-publisher collaboration and integrity auditing: Establish cross-publisher consortia to share verification models and require journals to publish annual 'integrity audits' disclosing hallucination detection rates (Section 12). Ｌ Accountability mechanisms within the scholarly community: Scholars, academic societies, and research institutions must hold publishers accountable to ensure verification tools are not exploited for commercial gain or knowledge monopolization, thereby upholding the scientific community＊s decisive stewardship of the scholarly record (Section 12 and Abstract). Ｍ Policy revision and mandatory disclosure: Enforce mandatory AI-use watermarking, automated statistical integrity checks, and strict adherence to author verification protocols and AI-use disclosure policies (Section 10).

Manifestation_Text: The 'hallucination' flaw inherent in AI algorithms〞combined with the high verisimilitude of generated text〞directly threatens the authenticity and scientific quality of scholarly publications, enabling low-quality or false content to infiltrate the academic system.
