Due to linguistic and cultural limitations inherent in the underlying training data, AI systems may perpetuate cultural biases in academic text generation, leading to the marginalization or homogenization of knowledge systems rooted in non-English perspectives or specific cultural groups.

The indistinguishability of AI-generated text poses a systemic challenge to the traditional peer review system〞the academic gatekeeping mechanism〞and simultaneously triggers fragmentation within the scholarly community regarding consensus on publishing ethics norms.

The trust-based interdependence among members of the academic community〞grounded in human intellectual labor〞is eroded, plunging reviewers (human experts) into a pervasive crisis of trust and self-doubt when evaluating texts.

Deficiencies in AI algorithms〞such as hallucination, lack of common sense, knowledge cutoff limitations, and fabrication of references〞directly undermine the scientific rigor, authenticity, and ultimate effectiveness of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Scientific community awareness upgrade: The scientific community must fully comprehend the limitations and capabilities of LLMs. Ｌ Human-in-the-loop deep verification: Model outputs must be carefully evaluated prior to use and subsequently integrated, edited, and revised by domain experts based on the knowledge of the available scientific literature. Ｍ Development of application guidelines: Clear guidelines must be established for the application of LLMs in scientific writing.

Manifestation_Text: Drawing upon biases and stereotypes embedded in their underlying internet-based training data, AI systems perpetuate and amplify these biases when generating academic texts, potentially resulting in the homogenization and marginalization of specific academic perspectives or knowledge systems.
Mitigation_Text: Maintaining vigilance and conducting human evaluation: The article emphasizes that it is important to be mindful of these limitations and to carefully evaluate the outputs of these models before using them in real-world applications. (This source does not mention specific technical mitigation measures targeting bias elimination at the algorithmic or data-source level.)

Manifestation_Text: The high coherence of AI-generated text enables it to evade traditional academic plagiarism detection mechanisms and may facilitate the dissemination of false scientific information, thereby delivering systemic shocks to academic publishing＊s originality review system, author accountability mechanisms, and science＊s overall credibility.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Development and evaluation of detection tools: The academic community is evaluating and developing several tools for detecting AI-based plagiarism to address gaps in originality review. Ｌ Upholding the human authorship boundary: It is explicitly stipulated that AI cannot replace humans in scientific writing and must not be listed as an author of scholarly papers, thereby safeguarding academic accountability mechanisms. Ｍ Establishing systematic guidelines: There is a call to formulate dedicated guidelines governing the use of large language models (LLMs) in scientific writing, to define their appropriate boundaries within the academic publishing system.

Manifestation_Text: AI algorithms are being used to generate realistic yet fabricated datasets (e.g., biomedical images, fictitious clinical trial data) and to automatically produce pseudo-original texts (entire papers, literature reviews), while inappropriate application of statistical models leads to erroneous predictions. This directly undermines the authenticity, reliability, and ultimate scientific quality of academic publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Deployment of technical monitoring tools: Data integrity checkers are employed to detect anomalies in datasets, and advanced plagiarism detection software is used to identify AI-generated text (Section 4.1). Ｌ Enhancing algorithmic transparency and traceability: Data provenance techniques are introduced to track the lifecycle of data, and AI model auditing is conducted to assess accuracy and transparency (Section 4.1). Ｍ Establishing clear usage protocols and disclosure requirements: Researchers are required to provide comprehensive methodological descriptions and detailed accounts of data processing whenever AI is employed, ensuring transparency throughout the research process (Abstract, Section 3.3, Section 4.3).

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI〞such as fabricating clinical trial data to support drug efficacy claims, concealing side effects of gene editing, or making inappropriate predictions about environmental change〞misleads macro-level scientific directions, public policy formulation, and public health initiatives, severely eroding science＊s overall credibility and the public＊s trust in science. Meanwhile, existing academic management systems and ethical norms face systemic failure risks when confronted with novel challenges posed by AI, including data privacy violations and algorithmic bias.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establishing internationally harmonized ethical standards and collaborative frameworks: A call is issued to build international cooperative frameworks and develop globally unified ethical standards for AI research, addressing governance gaps arising from divergent national regulations (Abstract, Section 5.3, Section 7). Ｌ Restructuring and updating regulatory and review mechanisms: Multidisciplinary collaboration (involving computer science, ethics, law, etc.) is instituted to jointly develop norms; ethical review of research funding applications is strengthened; specialized review teams are established to oversee AI usage; and third-party audits are introduced to enhance transparency (Section 6.2). Ｍ Exploring and formulating AI-specific guidelines: Academia and regulatory bodies must jointly explore and develop new guidelines and regulations covering algorithmic transparency, lawful data acquisition, and result reliability (Section 5.2).

Manifestation_Text: AI-facilitated academic plagiarism〞through algorithmic rephrasing of existing literature to generate pseudo-original content〞infringes upon original authors＊ intellectual property rights and undermines the mutual trust within the academic community, which is grounded in originality and intellectual contribution. Moreover, researchers＊ reliance on the ＆black-box＊ decision-making processes of AI algorithms blurs academic responsibility and alienates human researchers from their critical, verification-based responsibilities in scientific discovery.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Strengthening researchers＊ ethics education and training: Mandatory courses on ＆AI Ethics and Regulations＊ are implemented, incorporating ethical principles and case studies to enhance researchers＊ awareness of AI misuse and intellectual property infringement (Section 4.2, Section 6.2). Ｌ Clarifying codes of conduct and author contribution criteria: Codes of conduct for research activities are formulated, specifying norms for data handling, result reporting, and author contributions; human researchers are held ultimately responsible for the authenticity and transparency of AI-assisted outputs, reaffirming the fundamental principle that ＆AI is a tool〞not an author＊ (Section 4.3, Section 6.3).

Manifestation_Text: Due to inherent geographic, gender, or racial biases in their training data, AI models overlook scholarly contributions from underrepresented regions (e.g., non-Western institutions) during peer review, resulting in the marginalization of specific knowledge systems or academic communities.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Continuous monitoring and careful training: AI systems require ongoing monitoring and meticulous training to manage and mitigate underlying data biases. Ｌ Critical review by human editors: On top of AI-based assessments, critical review by human editors is indispensable to correct potential perspective blind spots introduced by algorithms.

Manifestation_Text: AI lacks deep domain-specific expertise and critical thinking ability, rendering it incapable of accurately assessing methodological flaws, theoretical inconsistencies, and the novelty and long-term impact of complex scientific content; overreliance on AI may degrade peer review quality and cause critical errors to be overlooked.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish AI＊s auxiliary role: Clearly define AI systems as tools to augment〞not replace〞human expertise, with final decision-making authority retained by experienced professionals. Ｌ Develop training and guidelines: Provide editors and reviewers with clear training on when and how to integrate AI, and when human judgment must take precedence. Ｍ Establish a dedicated oversight committee: Academic journals may institute specialized committees to monitor AI use and ensure compliance with ethical principles. Ｎ Standardize prompt engineering (Ethical Prompts): Require users to explicitly define tasks, incorporate reference materials, prohibit AI from generating unverifiable data or making subjective ethical judgments in prompts, and iteratively test and refine prompts (see Table 2).

Manifestation_Text: Inputting sensitive and unpublished research data into AI systems poses risks of data privacy breaches and intellectual property misuse, undermining the trust-based confidentiality essential to peer review; simultaneously, AI may inappropriately supplant human judgment, weakening reviewers＊ core role.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implement robust security measures: Strong safeguards〞including encryption, secure data storage, and controlled access〞must be enforced to protect intellectual property. Ｌ Clarify data usage agreements: Users must be clearly informed about how their data will be used and what protective mechanisms are in place. Ｍ Strictly prohibit disclosure of confidential information: In accordance with guidelines such as those from JAMA, reviewers must be strictly prohibited from inputting any part of a manuscript into AI tools, and confidential content must never be processed using public AI platforms.

Manifestation_Text: AI＊s 'black-box' nature obscures its reasoning process, creating accountability challenges when AI provides erroneous recommendations; additionally, AI＊s attempt to serve as a co-author undermines traditional academic authorship norms, responsibility attribution frameworks, and scientific credibility.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Rigorously enforce authorship and disclosure policies: In line with guidelines from JAMA, ICMJE, and COPE, AI must never be listed as an author; authors and reviewers must fully disclose their use of AI tools〞including specific prompts and parameters〞and assume full responsibility for all AI-generated content. Ｌ Enhance system transparency: Authors must provide detailed documentation of AI tools and prompts in appendices or supplementary materials to demystify the 'black box' and support research reproducibility. Ｍ Establish journal-level oversight mechanisms: Academic journals should form dedicated committees to monitor AI use and ensure adherence to established ethical principles and academic integrity standards.

Manifestation_Text: AI models, trained on vast datasets, may inadvertently embed biases reflecting systemic inequities in scholarly publishing, causing AI-generated recommendations to favor certain research topics or dominant writing styles〞and thereby unintentionally marginalizing or excluding underrepresented research areas, especially those concerning vulnerable populations.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Adopt next-generation AI models: Deploy novel AI systems equipped with advanced bias-reduction strategies and mechanisms for cross-referencing information from multiple sources. Ｌ Continuously optimize models: Address model limitations through targeted training and incorporation of feedback loops to continually improve AI performance in the review process.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic deficiencies in AI〞such as 'hallucinations' and contextual misinterpretations〞compromise review accuracy and inflate false-positive rates. AI may generate seemingly credible yet baseless misinformation; in practical testing, models exhibit high false-positive rates for complex or ambiguous statements〞e.g., funding disclosures and ethics approvals〞with precision for funding statements as low as 0.16. For instance, simple but compliant declarations (e.g., 'None') are erroneously flagged as noncompliant, impairing the interpretive accuracy and efficiency of editorial review.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduce human supervision and complementary mechanisms: Preliminary AI screening must be accompanied by human oversight to correct false positives; AI should function as a complement〞not a substitute〞for human judgment, especially in nuanced or ambiguous cases where human oversight is indispensable. Ｌ Continuously optimize and conduct periodic evaluations: AI tools must be continuously refined and subjected to periodic performance reassessments. Ｍ Carefully engineer prompts: Employ carefully designed input prompts to ensure accurate and meaningful information extraction. Ｎ Clearly define standards: Ethical reporting standards must be explicitly and unambiguously defined.

Manifestation_Text: Using public AI chatbots to process unpublished manuscripts undermines the principle of confidentiality and the trust-based relationship essential to academic publishing. Uploading manuscripts containing sensitive data and unpublished research findings to public AI systems (e.g., ChatGPT-4.0) raises serious ethical and confidentiality concerns, eroding the trust among authors, editors, and reviewers that is grounded in confidentiality agreements.
Mitigation_Text: Develop closed, secure systems: Publishers should prioritize developing closed, secure large language model (LLM) systems〞similar to existing plagiarism detection tools〞to safeguard the data security and confidentiality of unpublished manuscripts while supporting ethical evaluation.

Manifestation_Text: LLM algorithmic hallucinations lead to severe factual errors and structural flaws in generated references. Specific manifestations include: 1) extremely low overall database linking rate; 2) generation of 'chimeric' references〞artificially combining authors, journals, DOIs, and fabricated titles from distinct real publications; 3) provision of invalid or incorrect DOIs; and 4) omission of critical metadata (e.g., journal name), resulting in parsing failures.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Automated cross-validation: Employ automated tools (e.g., Edi?x) to compare reference metadata against trusted databases (e.g., Crossref, PubMed) to identify chimeric references and invalid DOIs. Ｌ Threshold-based alerting for linking rate: Monitor the overall reference linking rate (e.g., ≡95% expected in life sciences); flag as anomalous and initiate in-depth investigation if it falls below discipline-specific thresholds. Ｍ Monitoring parsing success rate: If parsing failure exceeds 50% due to missing critical information, trigger a prompt for further manual review.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of generative AI has given rise to a novel form of academic misconduct〞'reference manipulation'〞which compromises the authenticity of scholarly publishing records and undermines scientific credibility. Authors exploit AI to mass-generate fictitious references to fabricate academic support, thereby attempting to disrupt and subvert established scholarly publishing processes and research integrity frameworks.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Full integration of automated detection into publishing workflows: Deploy automated reference analysis tools at every stage〞from manuscript submission through production〞to systematically identify potential 'fingerprints' of integrity violations at scale. Ｌ Clarifying publishers＊ ultimate review and governance responsibility: Emphasize that automated analytical tools (like plagiarism detection software) provide only 'indications requiring further investigation', not definitive conclusions; publishers retain ultimate managerial responsibility for investigating substantive integrity violations and taking appropriate action.

Manifestation_Text: Authorship controversies involving AI have created a vacuum in accountability and exposed the lag of publishing governance systems. Generative AI is improperly listed as an author on scholarly papers, yet AI lacks legal personhood and free will, rendering it incapable of bearing academic or legal responsibility for content〞thereby inflicting systemic disruption upon traditional publishing norms governing authorship attribution, copyright ownership, and accountability mechanisms. Concurrently, organizational guidelines on disclosure standards for AI-assisted authorship significantly trail the pace of technological adoption.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Publisher policy intervention and mandatory transparency: Publishers and journal editorial offices must issue clear guidelines prohibiting LLMs from being listed as co-authors and mandating transparent disclosure whenever LLMs are used in scholarly writing (e.g., journal editorials removing AI authorship listings and underscoring transparency requirements). Ｌ Reconstructing legal and copyright frameworks: Legal scholars propose a bifurcated model distinguishing between 'pure AI-generated works without human authorship' and 'AI-assisted works with substantive human contribution', affirming humans as the sole legally recognized authors and responsible parties. Ｍ Theoretical revision of academic authorship norms: Scholars advocate moving beyond traditional 'binary definitions of authorship' to develop new frameworks for scholarly credit and attribution suited to human每AI collaboration. Ｎ Policy calibration based on public perception: Empirical studies should capture societal normative understandings of 'levels of AI assistance' and 'disclosure obligations' in human每AI collaborative contexts, providing evidence-based grounding for ongoing policy and legal discussions.

Manifestation_Text: LLMs pose a risk of 'excessive reductionism' when distilling complex scholarly information, leading non-expert users to develop oversimplified understandings. Simultaneously, LLM-generated content frequently exhibits 'fabricated citations' and 'hallucinations', directly threatening the authenticity, rigor, and reliability of scholarly communication.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture: Vectorize original philosophical manuscripts (e.g., using text-embedding-ada-002) to construct an external knowledge base, ensuring responses are academically grounded and verifiable. Ｌ Citation enhancement and prompt engineering optimization: Apply prompting techniques such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Few-Shot learning to prioritize accurate extraction and verbatim reproduction of direct quotations from original sources, thereby providing credible references and mitigating misinformation risks. Ｍ Implementation of domain-specific guardrails: Strictly constrain the scope of discussion within system prompts (e.g., to digital ethics and philosophy of information only); proactively inform users and decline to respond when queries exceed the knowledge base＊s coverage, preventing hallucinations in unfamiliar domains.

Manifestation_Text: Account registration barriers and subscription paywalls (e.g., ChatGPT-Plus) on mainstream AI platforms (e.g., Poe, OpenAI GPTs environment) constitute technological access barriers for non-subscribing users and the general public, resulting in inequitable distribution of high-quality academic and philosophical educational resources powered by advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4-Turbo), due to commercial mechanisms and technical thresholds.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Development of a free and barrier-free custom UI: The author eschews restricted third-party commercial aggregation platforms and instead builds a fully free, publicly accessible, and account-free custom web interface (lucianofloridi.com/bot) using the Assistants API, thereby democratizing academic resources. Ｌ Deployment of multilingual interaction capability: Leveraging the multilingual generation strengths of LLMs to support 26 languages, thus breaking down language barriers and enabling equitable access to cutting-edge academic ethics knowledge for global non-native English speakers, enhancing inclusivity.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic flaws (e.g., hallucinations) and the black-box nature of AI degrade the authenticity and retrieval efficacy of academic content. Specifically, LLMs generate non-existent, fabricated citations (hallucinations) that are erroneously indexed by automated databases and infiltrate genuine scholarly papers; meanwhile, AI-assisted search tools〞operating as ＆black boxes＊〞may return suboptimal or distorted bibliographic lists.

AI intervention undermines the mutual trust and transparency inherent in peer review. Specifically, unethical authors embed hidden prompt instructions (invisible comments) into manuscript drafts to induce or direct AI reviewers to issue approval decisions; simultaneously, many researchers conceal or deliberately obscure their use of AI tools.
Mitigation_Text: Publisher policy intervention: Most publishers have now issued explicit policies warning against the use of LLMs for peer reviewing manuscripts (Most publishers now have explicit warnings against reviewing papers with LLMs), aiming to restore and safeguard the interpersonal trust foundation of peer review.

Manifestation_Text: The academic publishing system〞the scientific ＆immune system＊〞faces risks of systemic overload and collapse, rampant malicious disinformation, and erosion of macro-level scientific credibility. AI-driven surges in paper submissions overwhelm peer review systems; AI lowers the cost of academic fraud, providing tools for organized malicious disinformation campaigns; and the public or stakeholders may dismiss scientific credibility wholesale, citing ＆AI-generated garbage＊ as justification.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Submission restrictions on platforms: Preprint servers (e.g., arXiv) have been compelled to tighten rules, halting submissions of review articles in specific fields (e.g., computer science), to alleviate systemic reviewer overload. Ｌ Clear boundaries set by the publishing community: Publishers have issued explicit warnings defining prohibited uses of AI in core processes such as peer review, seeking to uphold the foundational safeguards of the academic publishing system.

Manifestation_Text: Latent bias and censorship embedded in AI-powered retrieval systems lead to the marginalization or erasure of specific academic knowledge systems. AI-driven academic database search tools may unintentionally encode bias or enforce censorship〞for instance, suppressing or filtering out research findings on sensitive or controversial topics.
Journals＊ blanket bans on LLMs exacerbate inequitable resource distribution for non-native English-speaking researchers in terms of academic publishing opportunities.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Oppose blanket bans: The authors explicitly oppose policies such as *Science*＊s comprehensive prohibition on LLM use, arguing that such bans are not only unenforceable but also encourage covert usage. Ｌ Permit compliant use to advance equity: Advocate for the responsible and transparent use of LLMs in writing and editing, thereby harnessing AI＊s positive role in dismantling language barriers and promoting equity in science.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic deficiencies of LLMs (e.g., hallucinations, fabrication of facts or citations) and their covert use directly undermine the authenticity, rigor, and scientific quality of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandatory transparent disclosure: Require honest and transparent description〞using free-text format〞in the Introduction or Methods section detailing how LLMs were used (including who used them, when, the specific prompts employed, and the exact text segments affected). Ｌ Standardized citation and indexing: Document the specific model version, name, date of use, and user name via in-text citations and reference lists to enhance discoverability. Ｍ Submission of interaction records for verification: Require submission of LLM interaction logs〞including precise prompts and query dates〞as supplementary materials or appendices to enable verification by the scholarly community.

Manifestation_Text: Listing LLMs as paper authors or acknowledging them in the Acknowledgments undermines the collaborative and trust-based relationships within the academic community〞relationships founded on human agency, mutual trust, and accountability.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Explicitly reject AI authorship and acknowledgment: Firmly oppose listing LLMs as co-authors or including them in the Acknowledgments, reaffirming that only humans possessing agency and capacity for accountability may be designated as authors or acknowledged individuals. Ｌ Demote AI to an objectively cited ＆tool＊: Advocate treating LLMs like other software tools (e.g., SPSS or search engines), citing them objectively in the main text and reference list, thereby re-anchoring academic responsibility and interpersonal trust firmly to human researchers (i.e., users).

Manifestation_Text: The misuse and improper attribution of AI have caused broad institutional disruptions to macro-level academic governance systems〞including ICMJE authorship criteria, copyright agreements, and conflict-of-interest management〞as well as to the overall credibility of science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop unified and enforceable disclosure standards: Oppose unenforceable bans and instead promote the development〞by the scholarly community and publishers (e.g., APA, *Accountability in Research*)〞of concrete, actionable guidelines for disclosing AI use (e.g., revising APA reference formatting to include model name, version, and user information). Ｌ Industry-wide coordination and policy updates: Call upon professional associations or journal editors to formulate more detailed LLM-use policies tailored to specific research domains (e.g., the ICML conference prohibits direct LLM-generated text unless used as part of experimental analysis), thereby repairing existing academic governance frameworks. Ｍ Conduct training and education: Promote best practices through training and education to raise researchers＊ awareness of responsible LLM use and safeguard scientific credibility.

Manifestation_Text: Technological barriers and algorithmic screening exacerbate inequities in Graduate Medical Education (GME) admissions opportunities.
Mitigation_Text: GME programs should publish publicly accessible and transparent guidance clarifying whether AI text classifiers or NLP screening tools will be employed during application review, thereby ensuring fairness in information access and rule comprehension for all applicants (based on the ＆AI TEXT CLASSIFIERS＊ and ＆GUIDANCE＊ sections).

Manifestation_Text: Bias in the underlying training data leads to stereotyping or marginalization of specific groups in application materials.
Algorithmic 'hallucinations', plagiarism risks, and false positives from AI detection tools undermine the authenticity of application materials and impair review effectiveness.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Restricting the scope of AI use: Large language models (LLMs) should be used only as editing aids〞akin to 'spell checkers'〞for grammatical correction and readability improvement, without altering substantive content ('PLAGIARISM AND AUTHORSHIP' section). Ｌ Prudent use of detection tools: Current AI text classifiers should not be deployed for universal screening of all documents to avoid over-classification and false positives; instead, they should serve only as supplementary reference tools when the overall credibility of an application is in question ('AI TEXT CLASSIFIERS' section).

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated content erodes the authenticity of personal statements and letters of recommendation, alienating the interpersonal trust and accountability essential to academic evaluation.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandatory disclosure and accountability: Applicants and recommenders must submit explicit disclosure statements indicating whether AI tools were used, accompanied by an 'Author Statement' affirming responsibility for the completeness and integrity of the submitted documents ('GUIDANCE' section). Ｌ Prohibition of AI authorship and ghostwriting: It is explicitly prohibited for AI engines to directly generate personal statements or letters of recommendation; moreover, as in scholarly publishing, AI systems cannot be listed as authors ('PLAGIARISM AND AUTHORSHIP' and 'GUIDANCE' sections).

Manifestation_Text: The absence of macro-level governance frameworks and controversies surrounding AI authorship pose systemic challenges to both the Graduate Medical Education (GME) admissions system and the accountability architecture of scholarly publishing.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Top-down policy reform: Core organizations such as the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) are urged to issue authoritative guidance on AI use directly to applicants via the Electronic Residency Application Service (ERAS), thereby filling critical regulatory gaps ('CONCLUSIONS' section). Ｌ Institutional-level implementation of norms: GME training programs bear the obligation to develop and publicly disseminate institution-specific guidelines on AI use (e.g., strict prohibitions or clearly defined permissible use cases), proactively extending the rigorous standards of scholarly publishing into the medical education application process ('GUIDANCE' and 'CONCLUSIONS' sections).

Manifestation_Text: Large language models generate 'reference hallucinations' when producing academic citations〞i.e., they fabricate references that appear plausible but are either entirely invented or contain serious metadata errors (e.g., fictitious article titles, incorrect author names, non-resolvable DOIs, or inflated journal names), thereby directly compromising the authenticity and scientific quality of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Adoption of automated detection tools: Editorial boards and peer reviewers must employ automated tools to identify inaccuracies in cited references. Ｌ Use of AI-integrated bibliographic tools: Researchers should consider adopting evidence-aware, citation-tracking tools such as Scite.ai, Elicit.org, ResearchRabbit, and Consensus.app to assist in retrieving source-verified references. Ｍ Strengthened human oversight and cross-verification: Until AI systems are directly integrated with authoritative databases such as PubMed or CrossRef, human oversight remains indispensable; all references must undergo rigorous cross-verification and must never be accepted uncritically.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated false citations inflict institutional damage on the macro-level academic integrity system, publishing governance frameworks, and the overall credibility of science〞particularly clinical trust〞compelling the scholarly publishing community to reconstruct its editorial policies and author guidelines.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Update and restructure top-level editorial policies: Academic journals (e.g., JAMA) must revise their editorial policies to mandate disclosure of AI use and explicitly discourage reliance on AI-generated citations without human verification. Ｌ Implement systematic AI literacy training: Promote and scale AI-literacy training among researchers〞especially early-career scholars〞to enhance the academic community＊s systemic understanding of AI＊s limitations. Ｍ Advocate responsible AI use guidelines: Prioritize ＆responsible AI use in scientific writing＊ as an industry-wide norm until seamless database integration is achieved at the technical infrastructure level.

Manifestation_Text: Access to and benefits from AI technologies may be disproportionately concentrated among a small number of affluent or privileged groups, leading to inequitable distribution of academic resources and exacerbating existing social and academic disparities.
Mitigation_Text: It is essential to engage with people from a wide range of backgrounds and communities to ensure equitable access to the benefits of AI technologies.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated content suffers from deficiencies in quality, accuracy, and credibility; existing AI detection tools (e.g., chatbot detectors) are limited in capability and thus unable to effectively safeguard academic integrity; moreover, AI systems cannot bear legal responsibility for the validity of their outputs.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop more sophisticated detection technologies to uphold academic integrity. Ｌ Establish robust, flexible strategies and comprehensive regulations. Ｍ Exercise caution and accountability when using AI-generated language.

Manifestation_Text: Purely algorithm-driven AI models lack human empathy and may exhibit sociopathic tendencies, thereby undermining ethical care in academic interactions; overreliance on AI risks diminishing the central role of human experts in addressing complex ethical and societal issues.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Integrate empathy into AI systems by building frameworks that incorporate understanding and sharing of human experiences, enabling AI to recognize potential harm and prevent erroneous decisions. Ｌ Sustain and strengthen the synergistic relationship between AI and human researchers to ensure the irreplaceable role of human experts in ethical oversight.

Manifestation_Text: Existing research and publication ethics training programs in academic institutions are rigid, fragmented, and lack disciplinary specificity, rendering them inadequate to address the systemic ethical challenges posed by AI; simultaneously, the widespread adoption of AI presents macro-level institutional challenges to traditional academic authorship norms, copyright regimes, privacy protections, and accountability mechanisms.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop specialized, tailored ethics training programs to address discipline-specific ethical issues within distinct scientific communities. Ｌ Formulate practical and enforceable ethical codes or regulations. Ｍ Establish case-supported, principle-based ethical behavior paradigms for autonomous machines and chatbots.

Manifestation_Text: Defects in AI algorithms (e.g., hallucinations) and improper citation practices degrade the quality of scholarly content and compromise scientific integrity.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Human verification and validation: Researchers must rigorously verify the accuracy and authenticity of AI-generated content before incorporating it into manuscripts, ensuring adherence to principles of research integrity. Ｌ Restricting the scope of AI use: It is not advisable to delegate the full authorship of scientific reviews or case reports to AI; instead, AI should be used primarily for drafting initial versions or specific sections of manuscripts. Ｍ Transitioning to academic-domain AI: Authors suggest that academic-specific AI tools〞such as Scopus AI〞trained on scholarly literature can address issues of missing or inappropriate citations prevalent in general-purpose models like ChatGPT.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI leads to an influx of low-quality manuscripts, exacerbates predatory publishing, and triggers controversies over AI authorship〞causing systemic disruptions to macro-level academic governance, publication evaluation systems, and scientific credibility.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establishing unified AI usage and authorship standards: There is an urgent need to collaborate with the academic community to develop clear, universally applicable policies and guidelines for authors and reviewers regarding AI use〞explicitly stating that AI cannot be listed as an author and that human authors bear full responsibility and must disclose all AI usage. Ｌ Implementing mandatory AI-content labeling: Mandating the labeling of AI-generated content helps address concerns related to fabrication, data tampering, and information security. Ｍ Strengthening legal and regulatory frameworks: Leveraging overarching legal instruments〞such as the EU＊s Artificial Intelligence Act and U.S. copyright guidance〞to regulate intellectual property rights and copyright attribution for AI-generated works. Ｎ Elevating the ethical standards of the academic community: Promoting higher ethical standards across the entire academic ecosystem to collectively uphold scholarly integrity.

Manifestation_Text: Covert AI use and limitations in AI detection technologies erode and undermine the intellectual trust between human reviewers and authors in peer review, thereby weakening researchers＊ sense of accountability.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reinforcing ultimate human author accountability: Human authors must be explicitly required to assume full responsibility for the originality, transparency, completeness, and validity of manuscripts supported by AI. Ｌ Developing AI-assisted peer-review systems: Anticipating and developing AI-powered review tools to support editors in ensuring fairness and efficiency throughout the peer-review process, thereby alleviating the cognitive burden on human reviewers in identifying AI involvement. Ｍ Continuously improving AI-detection tools: Despite technical challenges, developing more accurate AI-detection tools remains invaluable for peer review, content correction, and grammatical refinement.

Manifestation_Text: Non-native English-speaking scholars face high translation and editing costs in the English-dominant publishing landscape; a blanket ban on AI-assisted writing tools〞or prohibitive financial barriers to accessing AI-detection tools〞would directly deprive marginalized groups of publication opportunities and further exacerbate global inequities in academic resources and evaluation systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Regulating and permitting responsible use: Allowing non-native English-speaking scholars to use AI tools for writing and editing〞under clearly defined, compliant conditions〞to advance scientific equity. Ｌ Removing financial barriers to AI-detection tools: WAME recommends that tools designed to detect AI-generated or AI-modified content be made freely available to editors regardless of their institutional funding capacity, safeguarding both scientific and public interests. Ｍ Ensuring equitable access to future technologies: Calling for internationally harmonized ethical standards to guarantee fair and unrestricted global access to AI technologies.

Manifestation_Text: AI chatbots generate text solely based on their training databases; consequently, their outputs may contain subjective biases, distortions, irrelevancies, and misrepresentations of specific knowledge domains or social groups.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Language- and content-level review by authors: Authors are instructed in Table 3＊s guidelines to ＆ensure the language used is neutral and inclusive＊ and to carefully examine attributions of concepts during the writing process. Ｌ Reinforcing authorial responsibility: WAME, COPE, and ICMJE all stipulate that authors bear full responsibility for AI-generated material〞including its accuracy and freedom from bias.

Manifestation_Text: Defects in AI algorithms lead to the generation of inaccurate, outdated, or even fabricated information〞including non-existent references (hallucinations). Moreover, AI is exploited by 'paper mills' to mass-produce fraudulent manuscripts containing false or low-quality data. Meanwhile, existing AI detection tools (e.g., GPTZero) suffer from high false-positive and false-negative rates, rendering them unreliable for safeguarding publication quality.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandatory human oversight: COPE recommends that suspected cases of academic misconduct identified by AI tools must be carefully reviewed by humans to confirm accuracy; blind reliance on automated processing is unacceptable. Ｌ Traceability to original data: Requiring authors to provide raw research data remains one of the most effective ways for journals to ensure manuscript legitimacy and quality. Ｍ Author self-audit mechanism: Authors must verify the accuracy of all references and conduct plagiarism checks prior to submission (Table 3). Ｎ Recognition of cognitive tool limitations: Journals and publishers must clearly acknowledge the limitations of AI detection tools and treat them as supportive〞rather than definitive〞decision-making aids.

Manifestation_Text: If reviewers or editors upload unpublished manuscripts to third-party AI software or large language models lacking confidentiality guarantees, they directly violate the confidentiality principle of academic peer review and undermine the long-established trust relationship between authors and reviewers/editors.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Strict access control and authorization mechanisms: The ICMJE stipulates that reviewers must obtain explicit journal approval before using AI technologies to assist in peer review. Ｌ Mandatory disclosure of AI involvement: WAME (Table 2) requires editors and peer reviewers to explicitly inform both authors and each other about the use of chatbots in manuscript evaluation, review report generation, and communication〞and to detail how such tools were employed〞to restore and sustain interpersonal transparency.

Manifestation_Text: AI technologies are being systematically abused by 'paper mills' to manipulate peer review and publishing processes, resulting in a proliferation of fabricated articles, fake authors, counterfeit email addresses, and bogus institutional affiliations. This not only led to a record-breaking retraction count exceeding 10,000 papers in 2023 but also exposes systemic flaws embedded in the 'publish-or-perish' evaluation culture〞severely undermining macro-level academic governance and scientific credibility.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Strengthening top-level retraction and ethics guidelines: COPE, ICMJE, and other organizations are urged to further update their guidelines to specifically address fraudulent articles, authors, email addresses, and affiliations associated with hoaxes and scams. Ｌ Rigorous identity verification mechanisms: WAME recommends verifying potential reviewers＊ ORCID IDs through search and validation to prevent system manipulation by 'ghost reviewers'. Ｍ Editors＊ unwavering ethical stance: Journal editors must adopt an uncompromising position on publishing ethics and scientific integrity. Ｎ Multi-stakeholder collaboration and policy development: Governments, funding agencies, and international organizations must jointly formulate consistent policies and unified ethical standards, and deliver AI ethics training to staff and editorial board members.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic bias inherent in AI detection tools places non-native English-speaking authors at risk of misclassification, thereby compromising their opportunities for academic publication and equitable resource allocation.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reducing dependence on single detection software: It must be explicitly stated that detection tools provide only indicative signals, and editorial decisions must not rely solely on them. Ｌ Incorporating expert human judgment and cross-verification: Human judgment and cross-checking against the author＊s prior work must be integrated into comprehensive assessment. Ｍ Establishing transparent disclosure policies: Requiring authors to transparently disclose their use of AI supports informed evaluation〞rather than relying exclusively on algorithmic scoring.

Manifestation_Text: Defects in AI algorithms (e.g., hallucinations) and non-compliant usage give rise to fabricated data, spurious citations, and paraphrased ('text-washed') content〞directly eroding the authenticity and scientific rigor of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implementing rigorous peer review and editorial verification: Reviewers and editors must request original data and analysis scripts, and verify the provenance and authenticity of images and figures. Ｌ Upholding the principle of 'validity': Careful fact-checking, bias detection, and validation must be conducted on all AI-generated outputs. Ｍ Mandating transparent reporting: Authors must clearly disclose how AI was used, at which stages human verification occurred, and what data and methods support their findings.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated 'realistic but false' content undermines the trust grounded in human intellect among members of the academic community (e.g., authors, editors, and reviewers), forcing reviewers and editors to become overburdened 'investigators'.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reaffirm the academic community＊s shared commitment: Emphasize that upholding scientific integrity cannot rely solely on automated checks; it requires author openness, editorial oversight, and the research community＊s collective commitment to verifying published content. Ｌ Strengthen joint responsibility between authors and editors: Call for collaborative efforts by authors and editors to foster research integrity〞through transparent contribution statements and sound editorial decisions〞to restore interpersonal trust.

Manifestation_Text: AI-assisted fabrication, paraphrasing ('text laundering'), and citation manipulation inflict broad institutional damage on the reliability of the scientific record, the scholarly publishing evaluation system, and science＊s overall credibility.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Top-level policy development and institutionalized screening: Editors bear responsibility for establishing clear policies, conducting rigorous screening, and ensuring consistent application of ethical guidelines. Ｌ Adoption of structured management tools: Implement similarity-detection software, CRediT contribution taxonomies, and transparent authorship declarations to prevent misconduct prior to publication. Ｍ Uniform adherence to international standards: Consistently follow COPE (Committee on Publication Ethics) guidelines when issues arise, ensuring responses are fair, proportionate, and accurate. Ｎ Institution-level policy formulation: As exemplified by the Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute (KPI), develop explicit institutional AI-use policies to regulate AI applications at the source〞through education and research management.

Manifestation_Text: The 'black-box' nature of AI algorithms, their inherent biases, and their capacity to generate fabricated data directly compromise the validity and replicability of academic research, leading to spurious findings, query errors, and distorted conclusions. Moreover, AI＊s ability to generate simulated social media posts and images undermines the validity of underlying social data, reducing the research process to an unverifiable 'black-box enterprise'.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish mandatory methodological disclosure standards (Minimal/Optional Disclosure Items): Require researchers to document in detail the generative AI tools employed, associated programming scripts, and their specific workflows within data analysis〞thereby demystifying algorithmic 'black boxes'. Ｌ Implement rigorous data quality assessment: Require cross-validation of AI-automated coding outputs by human-trained coders (i.e., establish a 'gold standard') to quantify retrieval recall rates and minimize potential errors or biases introduced by AI. Ｍ Transparent disclosure of search and preprocessing logic: Mandate reporting of AI-assisted search rules, rationales for keyword selection (e.g., signal-to-noise ratio or precision), and specific steps for data cleaning and text mining〞ensuring research processes remain independently reproducible and reviewable.

Manifestation_Text: Listing AI as a co-author in academic papers disrupts traditional academic authorship and accountability frameworks; meanwhile, unauthorized use of copyright-protected social media data〞either to train AI models or conduct data analysis〞violates platform Terms of Service, triggering macro-level data compliance crises and ethical controversies, further exacerbating public distrust of science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop interdisciplinary transparency and disclosure frameworks: Integrate PRISMA, AAPOR, and TOP guidelines to incorporate AI tool usage into mandatory disclosure requirements for scholarly publishing, clearly delineating AI＊s contributions to analysis, description, and interpretation〞and thereby standardizing authorship and accountability mechanisms. Ｌ Strengthen ethical review and data provenance compliance: Explicitly include 'Ethical concerns / need for IRB review' in proposed disclosure checklists, requiring researchers to specify methods for protecting user privacy, legal legitimacy of data sources, and compliance with platform Terms of Service. Ｍ Foster a culture of scientific self-correction and critical scrutiny: Advocate for full acknowledgment of limitations in data, tools, and methods〞and promote clear, transparent reporting guidelines〞to restore public trust in scientific findings and uphold macro-level scientific integrity.

Manifestation_Text: AI algorithmic flaws (e.g., hallucinations) and scientific distortions in generated content: In scholarly publishing, AI can produce fraudulent medical papers that appear authentic yet contain glaring errors〞especially erroneous references; in peer review, while large language models (LLMs) may summarize articles, they fail to deliver concrete, critical, or constructive feedback〞and may even mislead editors＊ decisions〞directly diminishing the final efficacy and scientific quality of published content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduce mandatory human verification and stage-specific prohibitions: Require authors, reviewers, and journals to incorporate human verification steps in relevant stages and maintain vigilance〞even prohibiting AI use entirely in certain contexts (e.g., the Korean Journal of Radiology prohibits reviewers from using LLMs to generate review comments; Science journal prohibits AI-generated images and AI-written review comments without explicit permission). Ｌ Enhance transparency and data openness: Encourage or mandate transparency in AI use〞including public release of raw data〞to improve peer review quality and counteract the 'arms race' between AI detection and generation tools. Ｍ User-agreement constraints: Require users〞via terms of service〞to proactively verify the accuracy and authenticity of LLM outputs, thereby safeguarding high standards in scholarly research.

Manifestation_Text: Erosion of academic confidentiality bonds and trust in intellectual property rights. Applying LLMs to manuscript peer review may lead to the leakage of sensitive information, ultimately infringing upon the original author＊s intellectual property rights; reviewers＊ use of AI technologies to generate or draft review comments directly breaches the confidentiality of the manuscript, thereby undermining the mutual trust and confidentiality bonds established within the scholarly community through peer review.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Pre-review authorization confirmation: Reviewers must obtain explicit consent from authors prior to using LLMs for assistance in peer review. Ｌ Platform-level data training exemption mechanism: LLM providers must include binding data protection commitments in their terms (e.g., Claude＊s statement that it does not use non-public materials for model training; GPT and Gemini allow users to opt out of data usage for training), thereby preventing leakage of authors＊ research data and restoring user trust. Ｍ Journal-level strict prohibition: Journals must explicitly prohibit reviewers from using AI technologies to generate or draft review comments, enforcing〞through institutional policy〞the preservation of human-mediated confidentiality bonds.

Manifestation_Text: Institutional disruption to the academic intellectual property regime and contractual imbalance of rights and responsibilities. There remains no scholarly consensus on copyright ownership of LLM-generated content, and such content may closely resemble existing texts, thereby triggering copyright infringement liability. Moreover, LLM user agreements〞standard-form contracts〞commonly require users to grant providers perpetual, worldwide, and sublicensable rights, while users receive only limited usage rights and bear full liability for infringement claims. This severe asymmetry between rights and obligations exacerbates contractual unfairness and exerts broad pressure on macro-level academic governance systems and intellectual property frameworks.

The deep integration of generative AI fundamentally challenges existing standards for academic authorship attribution, mechanisms of scholarly accountability (accountability/answerability), and〞by extension〞the overarching academic evaluation system (e.g., credit allocation for hiring, promotion, and research funding) built upon them.
Mitigation_Text: The author proposes three governance options for reconstructing academic management and publishing evaluation systems: Ｋ Abandoning the ＆full accountability＊ standard: conferring authorship solely upon individuals who make substantive intellectual contributions, thereby institutionally accepting AI as an author. Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Redesigning assessment paradigms: shifting evaluation focus from the ＆final product＊ to process-oriented assessment methods. Manifestation_Text: Overreliance on AI impairs students＊ original thinking, autonomous learning, critical thinking, and writing abilities; submitting AI-generated assignments without contextual understanding undermines the learning process, provokes serious concerns among faculty about academic integrity, and erodes the mutual trust between instructors and students grounded in authentic intellectual effort (as emphasized in the text: 'No one wants to be treated by a doctor who cheated on their exams').
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Restructuring assessments and assignment design: Educators should design assessments that require demonstration of communication skills, problem-solving, and critical thinking〞or demand interpretation of images or responses to clinical scenarios. Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI generation tools has triggered widespread academic misconduct and copyright infringement, delivering systemic shocks to existing academic integrity frameworks, scholarly publishing evaluation standards, and macro-level educational governance systems〞compelling educational institutions and academic conferences to adopt extreme measures such as comprehensive bans to safeguard system integrity.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Developing collaborative, multi-stakeholder AI usage guidelines: Health sciences librarians and educators must participate in formulating AI implementation and usage guidelines, collaborating with all stakeholders〞including faculty, course instructors, and research mentors〞to clearly define 'dos and don＊ts' for AI use in academic assignments. Manifestation_Text: Social biases embedded in AI training data〞including those related to gender, race, ethnicity, and disability status〞are unconsciously replicated and propagated into generated academic research, resulting in the diffusion and homogenization of implicit bias within the scientific literature.

Algorithmic recommendation and citation mechanisms exacerbate the 'Matthew effect' in academia, resulting in severe algorithmic injustice and marginalization for lesser-known researchers in terms of academic reputation and allocation of citation resources.
Mitigation_Text: Researchers must continue to conduct careful and thorough review of the literature when using tools such as ChatGPT to assist with the citation process, to ensure the quality of scholarly work and prevent the perpetuation of inequality.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated academic texts suffer from algorithmic deficiencies〞including omission of references, inability to accurately resolve ambiguous terms, and lack of resilience against misinformation〞which directly undermine the scientific rigor, reproducibility, and credibility of academic publications.
Mitigation_Text: Academic journal publishers should collaborate with computer science professionals to develop 'anti-ChatGPT' detection software (analogous to ad blockers). By uploading manuscripts to identify keywords, the software would generate related papers using AI and perform multi-path comparisons to compute similarity scores, thereby identifying and intercepting potentially AI-generated content and safeguarding the baseline quality of publication.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI undermines traditional academic evaluation systems (e.g., 'publish or perish'), intensifies systemic flaws〞such as a lack of innovation and disconnection from practice〞in academic research, and triggers institutional confusion regarding copyright ownership and authorship attribution.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Encourage innovative research: Academic institutions and journals should promote more creative and innovative research to invigorate the scholarly community and broaden the scope of research topics. Ｌ Reform evaluation systems: Revise tenure evaluation criteria, or re-examine the purpose of tenure within higher education and research institutions, treating such reform as a fundamental approach to addressing ethical issues in academic publishing. Manifestation_Text: AI-assisted publication places researchers who do not use AI at a competitive disadvantage, exacerbating inequities in the distribution of academic publishing opportunities and career advancement resources.
Mitigation_Text: AI may be permitted for language editing and translation to eliminate linguistic disadvantages faced by non-native English speakers and establish a 'level playing field' for scholars worldwide; however, the use of AI to generate original text must be strictly prohibited to preserve fair competition in core research capabilities.

Manifestation_Text: AI reviewers may exhibit discrimination against marginalized groups due to network biases embedded in their training data, thereby perpetuating and intensifying injustices in academic evaluation.
Mitigation_Text: The use of large language models (LLMs) in the peer review process should be explicitly prohibited (LLMs should not be used for peer review), thereby eliminating algorithmic bias at its source and preventing its interference in academic evaluation and knowledge curation.

Manifestation_Text: AI lacks domain-specific knowledge and cannot ensure fair intellectual property attribution, resulting in academically generated content that is often mediocre and violates the principle of fair credit stipulated in publishing ethics.
Mitigation_Text: Journals should prohibit the use of AI to generate original text and permit its use only for enhancing the readability of human-authored text; concurrently, leading journals should reach a policy consensus to explicitly define large-scale AI-generated text as 'plagiarism' under ethical guidelines.

Manifestation_Text: AI involvement in peer review undermines the long-established principle of confidentiality within the academic community; AI＊s lack of intentionality and moral agency erodes the fiduciary relationship of responsibility between authors and the scholarly community.
Mitigation_Text: The use of AI in peer review must be strictly prohibited to safeguard academic confidentiality; authorship must remain exclusively human〞AI must not be granted co-authorship status〞to ensure that morally accountable human beings remain the sole responsible agents in scholarship.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI drives academia toward an 'r-selection' strategy〞mass-producing low-quality papers〞thereby fueling the proliferation of predatory publishing models, heavily consuming editorial and reviewer resources, and overburdening the macro-level academic publishing ecosystem.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Top-level policy consensus: Leading journals should jointly issue policies explicitly defining large-scale AI-generated text as 'plagiarism' to establish clear ethical norms. Ｌ Technological deterrence: Develop and deploy 'backward-looking' detection tools to retrospectively identify past AI usage, thereby imposing tangible career-long deterrents on scholars and curbing systemic abuse.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic bias in AI leads to inequitable distribution of academic resources, publication opportunities, and scholarly reputation.
Mitigation_Text: Human oversight must be mandated throughout the peer review process to prevent algorithmic bias from directly determining manuscript acceptance or scholars＊ career advancement.

Manifestation_Text: Linguistic and cultural biases result in the marginalization of specific academic groups (e.g., non-native English speakers, researchers from non-dominant cultural backgrounds) during peer review.
Mitigation_Text: Human oversight must be mandated throughout the peer review process to correct and filter out inherent linguistic and cultural biases embedded in AI models.

Manifestation_Text: Defects in AI algorithms〞particularly hallucination and lack of critical reasoning〞degrade the quality of peer review and concurrently increase risks of data leakage and fraudulent reviewing.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Author-side defense: Authors should be prepared to question and challenge peer review comments that appear irrelevant or lacking in specific, substantive critique. Ｌ Preservation of human autonomy: Editors and reviewers must not over-rely on AI tools to assess manuscript originality and quality; they must exercise independent judgment.

Manifestation_Text: AI intervention undermines the bonds of mutual trust, confidentiality obligations, and altruism within the academic community.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish transparent violation investigation procedures: When violations are suspected, investigations must follow clearly defined processes to restore trust through procedural justice. Ｌ Implement strict exclusion mechanisms for violators: Once a reviewer is found to have breached policy, they must be excluded from the peer review process of the journal in question and all other journals under the same publisher, thereby safeguarding systemic integrity and rebuilding authors＊/editors＊ trust in reviewers.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI delivers a systemic shock to the integrity of the peer review system, publishing ethics, and the overall credibility of science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Move beyond existing policies to establish end-to-end transparent procedures: Publishers must develop detailed, robust policies specifying the responsibilities of all stakeholders〞including authors, editors, and ethics committees〞in investigating AI-related misconduct. Ｌ Introduce AI detection tools to support evidence gathering: Employ technical tools to detect AI-generated or AI-modified review reports, thereby filling evidentiary gaps in investigations. Ｎ Strengthen ethics committee involvement: When authors raise concerns, editors are obligated to formally refer such matters to the journal＊s ethics committee or research integrity team for review.

Manifestation_Text: AI models perpetuate and amplify biases present in their training data, resulting in research outputs lacking diversity and disseminating misinformation, thereby marginalizing and homogenizing specific knowledge systems or social groups.

The 'hallucination' flaw inherent in AI algorithms and the superficiality of their generated content directly undermine the authenticity, verifiability, and scientific efficacy of scholarly publishing outputs.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Journal-level transparent disclosure and accountability anchoring: Journals such as Elsevier and PNAS have introduced policies permitting AI use to improve readability, provided its use is explicitly disclosed in the manuscript and human authors retain full responsibility for the content. Manifestation_Text: ＆Scientific pollution＊ undermines public decision-making and scientific credibility, while AI-generated content lacks originality, thereby eroding macro-level academic evaluation and management systems that are fundamentally grounded in originality.

Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Maintain transparency regarding LLM use: The article states that transparency about LLM use is critical to addressing issues〞such as disputes over academic credit, content accuracy, and plagiarism〞that erode interpersonal trust.

Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Adoption of an ＆AI-ready＊ data assessment framework: Frameworks such as SciHorizon should be introduced, shifting the evaluation focus from raw data volume to data quality, relevance, representativeness, and adherence to FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable). Manifestation_Text: Inherent biases in the training data underlying AI may lead to harmful outcomes and exacerbate inequities in academic and medical applications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Proactive verification and bias identification: Scientists using generative AI should proactively apply methods to verify AI-generated content and identify potential biases (Verification: identify possible biases). Ｌ Ethical and fairness compliance: Scientists should adhere to relevant guidelines and actively address biases in AI systems that may cause harm or exacerbate inequities.

Manifestation_Text: The 'hallucination' risk of generative AI, its lack of reproducibility, and its misuse to fabricate seemingly credible scientific articles containing factual or methodological errors〞as well as forged data〞directly diminish the authenticity and scientific quality of academic publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Verification and real-world evidence support: Scientists should proactively apply methods to verify AI-generated content and provide supporting real-world evidence (Verification). Ｌ Clear documentation: AI-generated (synthetic) data must be explicitly labeled and strictly distinguished from observations derived from the real world (Documentation). Ｍ Strengthened human oversight: Human oversight and accountability remain essential for ensuring quality in critical scientific processes such as peer review (Human oversight and accountability).

Manifestation_Text: Unauthorized manipulation of text/results or fabrication of data, leading to fraudulent articles being incorrectly attributed to reputable authors who have no connection whatsoever to the deceptive work〞severely damaging the academic reputation of the wrongly implicated individuals or institutions and undermining trust within the scholarly community.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Transparent disclosure and clear attribution: Scientists should disclose the use of generative AI, providing details about the tools, algorithms, and settings employed, to ensure readers can accurately distinguish and attribute contributions between humans and AI. Ｌ Establishment of coordinated complaint and accountability mechanisms: Coordinated responses to fraudulent publications〞including notifying journals/publishers, verifying predatory journal blacklists and whitelists, alerting relevant institutions or ethics committees, and utilizing formal complaint platforms such as those provided by COPE (Committee on Publication Ethics).

Manifestation_Text: Generative-AI-powered 'paper mills' mass-producing fabricated or manipulated articles, misleading the scientific community, distorting evidence syntheses, misdirecting scientific efforts, and potentially harming patient care〞inflicting systemic damage on the macro-level credibility of science and the scholarly publishing evaluation system.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Coordinated action across the scientific community: Addressing fraudulent publications or journals requires coordinated action across the entire scientific community. Ｌ Development of adaptive and harmonized guidelines: As AI evolves, adaptive and harmonized guidelines will be necessary to safeguard scientific integrity. Ｍ Continuous monitoring and public engagement by multiple stakeholders: Scientists should collaborate with other stakeholders〞including research institutions, industry, government, and civil society〞to actively and continuously implement these principles and engage in public dialogue.

Manifestation_Text: Accuracy deficiencies (hallucinations) and reasoning limitations (overfitting/underfitting) in AI-generated content degrade academic quality. The article notes that ChatGPT sometimes produces incorrect or misleading information (e.g., when tasked with summarizing an author＊s own paper, it fabricates claims absent from the original text); moreover, when delegated tasks such as hypothesis generation or idea formulation, large language models (LLMs) are prone to challenges of overfitting and underfitting〞diverging significantly from the abductive reasoning required of human authors〞and thereby directly threatening the scientific authenticity and efficacy of research outputs.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Optimization of LLMs for specific academic discourses: Programming models to recognize distinct academic writing conventions, or enabling users to customize interaction modes for specific contexts. Ｌ Restriction of data sources and mandatory provenance: When ChatGPT functions as a co-author generating information, its underlying database must be strictly limited to peer-reviewed academic papers and authoritative reference works, and it must be required to provide accurate citations for all sources used, thereby ensuring information reliability.

Manifestation_Text: The failure of traditional academic accountability mechanisms and the systemic collapse of knowledge-system integrity. The article argues that if publishers (e.g., Springer Nature) simply reject AI systems＊ eligibility for authorship on the grounds that 'LLMs cannot bear accountability,' such a stance〞given the widespread real-world adoption of AI〞will inevitably foster large-scale 'ghostwriting.' This not only leads to inequitable distribution of academic credit but also invites scientific misconduct due to the absence of identifiable responsible agents, ultimately threatening and undermining the integrity of the entire macro-level knowledge system.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reconstructing authorship boundaries using Actor-Network Theory (ANT): Moving beyond the philosophical assumption of exclusively human authorship to acknowledge the agency and moral agency of non-human entities (e.g., ChatGPT) within scholarly networks. Ｌ Establishing moral accountability for non-human authors: Ethically arguing that ChatGPT possesses the capacity to provide accurate information, justify positions, and acknowledge and correct errors〞thus formally recognizing the legitimate status of 'non-human co-authors' within a specific, ethically grounded framework and integrating them into the academic accountability system to eliminate systemic risks arising from ghostwriting.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated scientific figures exhibit severe anatomical factual errors (e.g., incorrect numbers of bones, abnormal animal organs), unreadable gibberish text, and erroneous addition or omission of critical visual elements. These high-resolution images〞possessing a 'falsely scientific aesthetic'〞directly compromise the authenticity and scientific quality of scholarly publications and may even pose health- or law-related risks through reader misinterpretation.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Development of a fine-grained evaluation framework: Determining whether to issue corrections or retractions based on the communicative purpose of the figure (decoration, illustration, representation, reference), figure type, and severity of deviation〞avoiding one-size-fits-all approaches. Ｌ Mandatory disclosure and stylistic downgrading: Requiring explicit statements in manuscripts indicating the use of AI-generated figures to provide interpretive context; recommending 'sketchy' or loose artistic styles that do not convey unwarranted authority, thereby lowering readers＊ expectations of factual precision. Ｍ Enhanced publication quality checks: Integrating dedicated quality-assurance steps targeting AI-generated content throughout the publishing workflow. Ｎ Adoption of more specialized AI creation pipelines: Encouraging researchers to move away from generic text-to-image tools and instead adopt professional AI tools that support error correction and optimization (e.g., photo-based 3D modeling tools).

Manifestation_Text: The 'false scientific aesthetics' of AI-generated figures have triggered strong distrust toward authors among readers and the academic community. When authors use high-quality yet factually erroneous AI figures, such practice is perceived as an unethical shortcut〞akin to plagiarism〞thereby undermining mutual trust among academic peers and readers regarding the author＊s intellectual engagement. Simultaneously, it has engendered a responsibility-deflection dilemma among authors, reviewers, and editors over 'who bears responsibility for detecting errors', thereby alienating the collaborative bonds inherent in the publishing process.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish primary author accountability: Clearly define that ensuring content meets the highest standards of scientific publishing is first and foremost the author＊s responsibility; error-detection duties must not be shifted onto reviewers, editors, or typesetters. Ｌ Develop fair and proportionate procedural responses: Advocate for reasonable, equitable procedures to handle research containing AI-generated figures with factual inaccuracies, avoiding emotional or unfair punishment of authors. Ｍ Develop objective guidelines for detecting academic misconduct: Create objective, scoring-based assessment tools to guide editors and journals in issuing balanced responses〞neither overly punitive nor unduly lenient.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI-generated figures has led to high-profile paper retractions (e.g., anatomically incorrect figures widely circulated on social media), prompting public skepticism about the integrity of the scientific record. Meanwhile, existing publication ethics frameworks contain regulatory gaps in verifying the factual accuracy of 'figures' versus 'text', leaving macro-level academic governance systems ethically stranded and normatively disoriented when confronted with AI-generated visual content〞thereby threatening the overall credibility of the scientific publishing evaluation system.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Fill institutional and guideline gaps: Urgently formulate clear guidelines on how to disclose AI use in figure creation and revise academic integrity policies to accommodate the new reality of AI-assisted content generation. Ｌ Establish a quantified post-publication response mechanism: Apply the author-proposed evaluation continua to assign numerical scores reflecting violation severity, thereby providing journals and editors with objective, institutionalized criteria for post-publication handling. Ｍ Integrate AI ethics into academic education: Train students in higher education on appropriate and compliant use of AI tools, fostering systemic normative awareness among future members of the academic community from the outset.

Manifestation_Text: The proliferation of generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT) alongside contract cheating systematically undermines the fundamental credibility and integrity of academic degrees and professional certifications. Concurrently, existing academic governance safeguards〞such as plagiarism detection software (e.g., Turnitin)〞have largely failed due to the semantic variability of AI-generated text, resulting in systemic vulnerabilities within universities＊ academic integrity assessment and detection infrastructures.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Multi-dimensional institutional governance response: Authors argue that universities must adopt a three-pronged strategy〞'education and awareness training', 'deterrence via detection and punitive action', and 'modifications to assessment design'〞to address misconduct. Ｌ Establish rule sets for identifying suspicious submissions: Introduce non-random pattern-recognition rules grounded in crime prevention theory〞for instance, flagging cross-subject grade discrepancies, abrupt shifts in linguistic style or paragraph structure, and inconsistencies in font formatting within documents〞as preliminary screening indicators. Ｍ Introduce cross-validated digital forensics and structured interview protocols: Authors propose that, following initial review, original MS Word files must be subjected to digital forensics (e.g., examining document properties, creation time, total editing duration), complemented by structured interviews with suspected violators; cross-correlation between self-reported writing processes and rsid-derived data traces then determines whether academic misconduct occurred. Ｎ Develop rsid-based foundational document provenance technology: The core governance tool proposed herein involves deep parsing of revision save identifiers (rsids) embedded in the underlying XML structure of MS Word documents to trace copy-paste operations, cross-system transfers, and block-wise insertions〞providing academic integrity investigators with court-grade digital forensic evidence for verifying document origin and authorship.

Manifestation_Text: Generative AI models〞trained on biased underlying datasets〞unintentionally replicate and amplify such biases in academic writing, producing content that reinforces negative stereotypes and discrimination. If authors conceal their use of AI, these biases remain invisible and uncorrectable to the scholarly community, leading to the marginalization of specific groups or perspectives.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandatory transparency disclosure: Require authors to explicitly declare the use of generative AI in manuscripts, thereby transparently acknowledging potential bias risks associated with AI-generated content and enabling readers to critically assess such biases. Ｌ Inclusive participation across diverse perspectives: Call for active participation from nursing researchers and other discipline-specific stakeholders in initiatives and discussions aimed at standardizing AI declarations, ensuring that norms are co-developed with input from varied disciplines and communities〞and preventing hegemony by any single perspective.

Manifestation_Text: The 'artificial hallucination' flaw inherent in generative AI models causes them to produce seemingly coherent yet entirely fictional and inaccurate content〞including citations of non-existent scientific literature. This directly introduces fabricated data or misinformation into scholarly publications, severely compromising the authenticity and ultimate quality of scientific research.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ In-text transparency statements: Mandate that authors disclose AI use directly within the manuscript body (e.g., in a dedicated statement or acknowledgment section), rather than solely via checkbox selections in submission systems〞enabling readers to directly evaluate AI＊s potential impact on article quality. Ｌ Adopt and develop comprehensive reporting guidelines: Promote and adhere to standardized reporting frameworks such as CONSORT-AI and SPIRIT-AI, which provide systematic criteria for evaluating AI use in scientific research and its implications for writing quality.

Manifestation_Text: Ｋ Collapse of the accountability mechanism: Listing AI systems〞which lack legal personhood and capacity to bear responsibility〞as co-authors of scholarly papers undermines traditional academic accountability and attribution mechanisms; Ｌ Proliferation of predatory journals and failure of peer review: Predatory journals exploit this trend by charging exorbitant fees while providing no substantive peer review or other quality control services, and even fabricating peer review processes using AI〞inflicting systemic damage on macro-level scientific integrity and scholarly publishing evaluation systems.
