Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Extending AI disclosure requirements to the peer review stage: Mandating that journal reviewers explicitly declare their use of generative AI tools, thereby enhancing the assessment of review quality, distinguishing legitimate journals from predatory ones, preventing the academic community from inadvertently supporting predatory journals, and exposing their deceptive marketing claims regarding AI use. Ｌ Institutionalizing and standardizing AI declarations: Elevating AI usage statements to the same institutional importance as the IRB (Institutional Review Board) approval statements introduced in the 1990s in medicine, making them a cornerstone of responsible scholarly conduct and globally standardized ethical practice. Ｍ Strictly defining AI＊s non-author status: Following recommendations from international bodies such as the ICMJE (International Committee of Medical Journal Editors), formally rejecting AI as an author in scholarly publications and upholding the fundamental principle that humans must bear ultimate responsibility for the scientific integrity of published content.

Manifestation_Text: Hallucinations and tortured phrases generated by generative AI (GAI) distort scientific content. Erroneous information (hallucinations) produced by GAI, as well as meaningless synonymous terminology (tortured phrases) introduced during GAI-assisted text generation, directly compromise the precision of scientific representation, rendering research claims devoid of 'repeatable efficacy' and thereby diminishing the authenticity and ultimate scientific quality of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establishing a common analytical framework: Authors advocate developing a common framework for scholarly text integrity analysis to enhance detection capabilities for LOTS (Language-Only Textual Symptoms), including GAI hallucinations. Ｌ Collaborative screening and terminological standardization: Encouraging shared responsibility among authors, peer reviewers, and editors to carefully scrutinize such errors and ensure only standardized scientific terminology is published.

Manifestation_Text: Systemic literature contamination and failure of publishing quality control systems caused by GAI misuse. LOTS errors〞including 'tortured phrases' and 'hallucinations'〞generated by GAI have already widely infiltrated and compromised numerous indexed journals claiming to uphold peer review and copy-editing-related quality control. This systemic accumulation of errors renders the publication of factually unsupported claims 'epistemologically and socially irresponsible', inflicting institutional damage on the integrity of the scientific literature and the credibility of scholarly publishing evaluation systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Proactive governance by databases and platforms: Calling on major academic databases such as PubMed to adopt a hands-on, proactive stance in correcting and screening for these errors, rather than relying solely on disclaimers. Ｌ Practicing virtue ethics and shared responsibility: Urging biomedical engineers and the broader academic community to adopt a virtue ethics approach, treating the resolution of such normative issues as a professional duty and establishing a 'shared responsibility' mechanism to reduce LOTS. Ｍ Developing a unified text integrity framework: Advocating for the establishment of a common framework for scholarly text integrity analysis to systematically resist GAI＊s erosion of the scholarly publishing ecosystem.

Manifestation_Text: AI intervention disrupts traditional academic authorship identification systems and accountability mechanisms, and triggers novel forms of academic misconduct. Lacking human moral emotions (e.g., guilt, shame) and legal subjecthood, AI fails to satisfy the ICMJE＊s core criterion that authors must assume accountability for all aspects of a manuscript. Simultaneously, human scholars may engage in 'free-riding' by listing AI as guest/honorary authors to attract attention, or concealing its use as a 'ghost author'. Such abuses undermine macro-level academic integrity management systems and publishing evaluation frameworks.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Publication bans by publishers: Major commercial and academic journals (e.g., JAMA, Nature, Science, Wiley) and preprint platforms (e.g., arXiv) have explicitly prohibited AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) from being listed as co-authors. Ｌ Revision and reconstruction of top-level guidelines: Calling upon authoritative international scholarly ethics organizations〞including the ICMJE, COPE (Committee on Publication Ethics), and CSE (Council of Science Editors)〞to re-examine, revise, and update existing authorship guidelines, clearly delineating AI＊s functional scope and rights boundaries in scholarly publishing, and issuing specific guidance addressing AI-related 'honorary authorship' and 'ghost authorship'. Ｍ Clarifying human fallback responsibility: Where AI cannot assume responsibility, human co-authors must bear the ethical and legal consequences arising from errors introduced due to AI＊s inherent limitations.

Manifestation_Text: Inherent limitations of AI algorithms and automated generation may compromise the accuracy and scientific quality of scholarly publications. AI-generated manuscripts may enter legitimate or predatory journals under conditions where humans conceal AI＊s contribution as a 'ghost author'; moreover, AI＊s intrinsic weaknesses or limitations may introduce errors into manuscripts, directly undermining the factual authenticity of published scholarly content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandating final human quality assurance and accountability: Given AI＊s inability to experience shame or bear consequences, the article emphasizes that when errors attributable to AI appear in a publication, human co-authors must explicitly assume corresponding ethical and legal responsibilities ('human co-authors assume the ethical and legal responsibilities on behalf of ChatGPT'), thereby compelling rigorous human scrutiny of AI-generated content. Ｌ Strictly restricting AI＊s authorial status: Prohibiting AI authorship through journal and publisher policies prevents humans from offloading quality assurance responsibilities onto AI systems, ensuring that all published content is ultimately endorsed by human scholars capable of accountability.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic and bibliometric biases lead to inequitable allocation of academic resources (e.g., funding, promotion, hiring). For example, AI-based evaluation tools that omit information on 'career breaks' may introduce design bias against women; if trained on historical data reflecting gender or racial patterns, such tools may reinforce existing societal biases (existing bias), placing women or ethnic minorities at a disadvantage in senior position recommendations or academic assessments.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Enhance transparency to support appeal mechanisms: Ensure openness and transparency in data collection and analysis processes, enabling evaluated individuals to examine key assumptions and calculations in TARA data and challenge erroneous or inappropriate computations where necessary (Sections 1 and 2). Ｌ Introduce explainable AI (XAI) for human intervention: Adopt white-box AI algorithms that allow domain experts to understand the decision-making process and manually adjust erroneous outputs generated by AI due to limitations in training data (Section 2.3.2).

Manifestation_Text: Knowledge systems from non-English-speaking countries, niche disciplines, and specific geographic regions are systematically marginalized and erased in academic evaluation. For instance, major citation databases exhibit a strong bias toward English-language literature, leading to severe underestimation of research from non-English-speaking countries and locally focused studies (e.g., national politics, native flora and fauna); simultaneously, publication-volume bias disadvantages research in niche or geographically specific areas (e.g., ecologically unique but sparsely studied regions) during evaluation.

Limitations in AI training data and algorithmic opacity (the 'black-box' problem) undermine the accuracy and scientific rigor of academic evaluations such as peer review. For example, if a peer-review AI system is trained exclusively on physics papers and reports, it will fail to identify critical ethical issues when applied to health-related research, thereby directly diminishing the quality of peer review and the scientific efficacy of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandate disclosure of training data sources: Require explicit disclosure to evaluated individuals regarding the types of data used to train AI software, enabling assessment of its cross-domain applicability and accuracy, and preventing deterioration of review quality due to misaligned training data (Section 2.2).

Manifestation_Text: The extreme complexity and opacity (black-box nature) of AI algorithms pose institutional challenges to the credibility and accountability of macro-level academic evaluation systems. For example, state-of-the-art AI algorithms〞including deep learning, support vector machines (SVMs), and ensemble decision trees〞exhibit extremely high dimensionality and node complexity, rendering their decision-making processes entirely uninterpretable. Such opacity impedes algorithm owners＊ ability to assume responsibility for decisions, thereby undermining natural justice within academic evaluation systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop and deploy explainable AI (XAI): Promote the use of 'white-box' AI models (e.g., linear regression, limited rule sets, or simple decision trees) in research evaluation to ensure human experts can comprehend the decision-making process and uphold accountability (Section 2.3.2). Ｌ Adhere to the 'simplicity' principle and adopt reproducibility as an alternative: Design TARA systems in accordance with the principles of the Leiden Manifesto, maintaining analytical processes simple and transparent; where unavoidable complexity precludes transparency, full reproducibility shall serve as an acceptable alternative to sustain systemic credibility (Section 2).

Manifestation_Text: AI is being used to generate fabricated research content, posing risks of data falsification and invention of non-existent results〞leading to scientific fraud, misleading statistics, and content saturation in biomedical research, and directly compromising the authenticity and scientific quality of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Journals must rigorously verify author credentials and contributions: Scientific journals must strictly ensure authorship is based on genuine contribution〞for example, verifying whether an author＊s academic training background aligns with the subject matter or discipline of the research (to detect and prevent AI-assisted writing or cross-disciplinary authorship trading). Ｌ Establish retraction and reporting mechanisms: Oversight bodies responsible for regulating research activities should establish dedicated committees to retract journal articles involving repeated fraudulent publication and set up formal channels for reporting misconduct in scientific research.

Manifestation_Text: Paper mills leveraging AI tools mass-produce academic papers for sale and authorship attribution, distorting academic publishing metrics and university rankings, facilitating fraudulent research funding applications, wasting valuable resources, and causing long-term damage to the reputation and productivity of research institutions〞thereby delivering broad institutional shocks to macro-level academic governance systems and the overall credibility of science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Institutions rigorously investigate fabricated academic credentials: universities, hospitals, and research institutions〞as key stakeholders〞must strictly scrutinize publications and affiliations that may artificially inflate individual academic records. Ｌ Implement stringent disciplinary sanctions: universities must institute disciplinary measures against scientific misconduct. Ｍ Governments formulate macro-level policies: governments must develop relevant policies and establish sanctioning mechanisms to regulate research integrity at the national institutional level. Ｎ Promote transparency and accountability across the entire sector: the global scientific community must collectively advance transparency, accountability, and ethical conduct in scientific publishing to safeguard the foundational principles of scientific research and its global credibility.

Manifestation_Text: Abuses such as AI-assisted writing and academic cheating have delivered widespread institutional shocks to macro-level academic governance systems, educational evaluation frameworks, and the fundamental baseline of academic integrity〞triggering collective moral outrage among the public and prompting national-level reconstruction of academic integrity policies.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Policy revisions at national and institutional levels: bottom-up affective counterpublic movements exert pressure to compel institutional responses, culminating in the revision and issuance of new academic integrity guidelines and reform measures by the state in 2024. Ｌ Responsive adjustments by platforms and regulators: in response to virally spreading public sentiment, national authorities and platform actors implement reactive policy adjustments〞including issuing new administrative guidelines, temporarily modifying content moderation thresholds, or recalibrating visibility algorithms〞to balance public affective feedback with institutional stability.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated false content (e.g., deepfakes), algorithmic deception, and acts of plagiarism and ghostwriting in academic and cultural domains directly undermine the authenticity of information, degrade the ultimate quality of academic and cultural outputs, and severely erode public trust in the information ecosystem.

The misuse of AI technologies (e.g., voice cloning, memory resurrection) disrupts emotional bonds, consent mechanisms, and identity formation between the living and the deceased, while simultaneously undermining human-intellect-based mutual trust in educational and academic contexts〞sparking serious controversies regarding ethical and emotional exploitation.

High training-cost barriers concentrate large-model R&D resources within industry-leading enterprises, placing smaller research institutions at risk of marginalization and exacerbating inequities in the distribution of academic and technological resources.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Lowering training-cost barriers: drawing on the Theory of Contestable Markets, continuously reduce training-cost barriers to optimize resource allocation; Ｌ Advancing open-source strategies: encourage open-source and free-access approaches (e.g., the DeepSeek open-source model cited in the text) to break technological monopolies, foster low-cost collaboration, and shift innovation paradigms from oligopolistic competition toward mass-driven innovation.

Manifestation_Text: Large language models are trained on underlying data containing noise and probabilistic errors, thereby exposing and amplifying existing biases and discriminatory patterns. This leads to the distortion of users＊ values and the reinforcement of public cognitive biases, resulting in representational injustice and homogenization in knowledge generation.

Generative AI may produce 'factual hallucinations' (statements contradicting objective facts) and 'faithfulness hallucinations' (outputs inconsistent with context), generating fabricated facts or misleading text〞directly undermining the authenticity, effectiveness, and credibility of scholarly and publishing content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Technical safeguards and provenance tracking: Introduce watermarking technology to embed imperceptible identifiers into AI-generated text and other content, enhancing traceability and platform-level review capabilities; Ｌ Policy and governance coordination: Leverage existing regulations and norms in a coordinated manner to ensure compliance and transparency in the application of AI-generated content (AIGC) technologies.

Manifestation_Text: Generative AI has triggered widespread debate regarding copyright ownership of generated content and the question of whether AI can be considered an original author. When training data is used without authorization, the intellectual property status of generated outputs becomes ambiguous, posing systemic challenges to existing academic copyright management systems, authorship attribution frameworks, and societal legal norms.

AI-generated 'synthetic' content carries risks of fabrication, forgery, hallucination, or deepfakes, directly compromising the authenticity and scientific quality of scholarly content; meanwhile, current AI detection tools (e.g., similarity-checking tools) cannot deliver 100% accuracy and frequently yield false positives, thereby impairing the quality assessment of scholarly outputs.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Propose the aiTARAS framework (Academic Integrity and Transparency in AI-assisted Research and Specification): Require authors to provide multi-layered transparency statements detailing the specific location, purpose, and prompts used for AI assistance, and mandate critical human review, verification, and correction of AI-generated content to address potential biases and hallucinations. Ｌ Journal policy updates: Academic journals must revise editorial policies to explicitly define appropriate conditions for AI use and encourage transparent reporting by authors on the extent of their AI utilization.

Manifestation_Text: AI intervention undermines the trust and collaborative bonds within the academic community〞bonds traditionally grounded in human morality, emotion, and responsibility. Specifically: AI lacks human emotional traits such as guilt, shame, and remorse, rendering it incapable of assuming or resolving authorship-related conflicts; furthermore, AI＊s unauthorized harvesting of unpublished ideas from the web〞without proper attribution〞constitutes infringement upon original authors＊ intellectual property rights and breaches academic trust.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Explicit rejection of AI authorship: Authors strongly assert that generative AI should not be credited as a co-author, citing the four criteria established by authoritative bodies such as the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) to emphasize that only humans can bear legal and ethical responsibility. Ｌ Establishment of ultimate human accountability: Through the aiTARAS framework, a mandatory final human approval statement must be appended in all AI-assisted scenarios, clearly affirming that 'the final content, conclusions, and claims are solely the responsibility of the human authors', thereby restoring the accountability linkage.

Manifestation_Text: The widespread application of AI has imposed institutional shocks on macro-level academic governance systems, the traditional 'publish or perish' evaluation culture, and educational assessment frameworks. AI has become an 'invisible stakeholder' in the publishing process, rendering conventional human-centric evaluation methods〞such as written essays or reports〞ineffective in accurately measuring students＊ genuine understanding or original thinking, thereby undermining the foundational integrity of scientific evaluation systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Restructuring of macro-level evaluation systems: Calling on the academic community to critically re-examine and reform the 'publish or perish' academic system〞one that incentivizes publication at all costs. Ｌ Innovation in educational assessment paradigms: Moving beyond traditional anti-AI measures (e.g., oral examinations) toward experiential and project-based assessments, alongside strategic use of technology, with emphasis on evaluating authentic skills difficult for AI to replicate〞such as practical application and reflective capacity. Ｍ Establishing novel review and identification mechanisms: Advocating for the development of new mechanisms to accurately detect AI usage and breaches of academic ethics, and enhancing content quality scrutiny within peer review processes.

Manifestation_Text: Delegation of academic tasks to AI engenders 'cognitive debt' and deteriorates the quality of scholarly output. Scholars increasingly rely on AI for writing papers, leading to 'technology-induced cognitive decline (TICD)' and long-term 'cognitive debt', manifesting as suboptimal performance at neural, linguistic, and behavioral levels. Moreover, the salient content rapidly generated by AI distracts scholars＊ sustained attention, activates intuitive, automatic 'System 1' processing, and reinforces cognitive biases (e.g., overvaluation of AI outputs), thereby eroding scholars＊ capacity to produce high-quality academic papers through authentic reasoning and impeding substantive scholarly dialogue.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Upholding a 'low-tech' ethical baseline: Scholars should refuse to delegate any academic task to AI and remain committed to exercising the full range of human intellectual capacities in performing cognitive work. Ｌ Returning to pen-and-paper drafting: Grounded in neurocognitive research, drafting ideas and taking notes by hand yields superior brain activation and learning outcomes, followed by transcription into digital format. Ｍ Rejecting 'prompt engineering' as an instructional objective: Educators should not substitute writing instruction with efforts to increase prompt complexity, as this disrupts sustained task engagement and fails to cultivate genuine judgment and intellectual virtue.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI exacerbates institutional distortions and goal displacement within academic evaluation systems. The extensive use of large language models (LLMs) in academic publishing represents a concentrated eruption of the academic community＊s 'perverse incentives', wherein macro-level institutional arrangements conflate the 'means' of scholarship (e.g., publishing papers, pursuing bibliometric indicators) with its 'ultimate ends' (i.e., advancing human flourishing through the exercise of reason), plunging the entire academic system into a systemic crisis characterized by technocratic governance and metric obsession.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reforming academic policies and incentive structures: Calling on decision makers in academic policy to fundamentally transform existing evaluation criteria〞from rewarding 'competitive metrics' (e.g., publication output) to rewarding 'intellectual virtue'. Ｌ Conducting systematic 'low-tech' reflection across academia: Encouraging the academic community to re-examine the relationship between means and ends in individual and collective intellectual labor, and to reconstruct a more 'human-centred' macro-governance paradigm amid accelerating technocratic trends.

Manifestation_Text: AI systems harvest and utilize human-created content (e.g., academic papers, creative works) without generating any traceable traffic, citations, or recommendation metrics ('no-footprint condition'), resulting in severe losses for content creators in terms of academic reputation (e.g., citations, visibility) and economic resources (e.g., traffic monetization, income), thereby exacerbating the digital divide.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Proposing and deploying the Chujoyi-TraceNet (CTN) socio-technical framework, integrating real-time content interaction tracking, dynamic licensing agreements, geospatial usage mapping, and attribution metadata. Ｌ Introducing blockchain-based licensing and metadata watermarking technologies, enabling authors to determine where and to what extent their works have influenced LLM outputs〞thereby ensuring fair attribution and equitable economic compensation.

Manifestation_Text: Large language models (LLMs), trained on vast volumes of internet and historical data, inherit and amplify societal biases related to gender, race, politics, and culture, perpetuating stereotypes in generative outputs〞including those in academic publishing. Simultaneously, the unauthorized harvesting of copyright-protected works risks erasing or homogenizing the distinctive expressions of specific human creators.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establishing a robust traceability framework that strengthens AI system accountability through transparent attribution, enabling users to verify the credibility of AI-generated information and thereby reducing the dissemination of biased or misleading content. Ｌ Prioritizing mechanisms that ensure appropriate recognition, transparency, and accountability in AI development, fostering a more sustainable and equitable knowledge economy.

Manifestation_Text: The probabilistic nature and black-box characteristics of large language models (LLMs) can lead them to generate factually incorrect or misleading information (i.e., hallucinations); their lack of transparency makes it difficult for users to trace the decision-making process or verify knowledge sources, thereby directly undermining the quality, authenticity, and scientific credibility of content in academic publishing and the broader digital information ecosystem.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandate the inclusion of source references or citations in AI-generated content to ensure that AI-assisted research adheres to appropriate citation practices. Ｌ Implement end-to-end traceability〞linking content access, transformation, and attribution〞to mitigate risks of misinformation and unverified knowledge dissemination, thereby restoring academic and ethical standards.

Manifestation_Text: AI＊s unauthorized use of intellectual property and failure to attribute original creators undermines the traditional economic models and governance frameworks underpinning academic publishing, journalism, and the creative industries〞frameworks that rely on reader engagement, citation practices, and licensing revenues. This devalues human intellectual labor, threatens job security for knowledge-based professions, and inflicts systemic damage on the macro-level scientific credit system and the sustainability of the knowledge economy.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop multi-dimensional 'human reintegration' strategies that provide structured models for displaced human contributors, enabling LLMs to participate ethically online while leaving meaningful digital footprints. Ｌ Policy and regulatory coordination: Provide policy-relevant insights to LLM developers and regulatory bodies, aligning with guidelines from organizations such as UNESCO and the European Union〞emphasizing fairness, accountability, and transparency〞to foster human-AI symbiosis in the creative economy and support Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 9 and 10.

Manifestation_Text: Technological barriers and high detection costs exacerbate academic inequity in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), and the proliferation of AI further aggravates cheating problems in resource-constrained regions.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Low-cost technological provision: A globally accessible, affordable, secure, sustainable, and responsible solution must be co-created by multiple stakeholders. Ｌ Inclusive international collaboration: Technology developers such as OpenAI are urged to expand their collaborative engagement with the education sector beyond the United States to include academic stakeholders worldwide〞especially those in LMICs. Ｍ Develop cost-effective and trusted detection tools to identify dishonest AI usage globally.

Manifestation_Text: Academic quality deterioration caused by algorithmic flaws in AI (e.g., hallucinations, generation of false information) and inherent knowledge limitations directly threatens the authenticity and accuracy of scientific output.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Enhance information transparency and policy definition: Academic institutions and publishers must explicitly define the unacknowledged use of AI-generated text as academic misconduct in their policies. Ｌ Capacity-building for all stakeholders: Universities should widely deliver academic integrity training for faculty and students to raise awareness of LLM limitations and clarify appropriate, compliant usage boundaries. Ｍ Position AI as an assistive tool: Treat it as a 'learning companion' for idea generation, while ensuring final refinement and editorial oversight remain firmly in human hands. Ｎ Enforce mandatory citation and disclosure requirements: Prior to the maturation of technical detection tools, users must record the date of content generation, the prompts used, and limit direct quotations to no more than one paragraph.

Manifestation_Text: The uncritical delegation of academic trust and intellectual agency to algorithms undermines traditional teaching and assessment mechanisms〞systems historically grounded in mutual human intellectual trust〞leading to their collapse and distortion.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reconstruct academic assessment paradigms: Academic institutions are advised to fundamentally shift existing evaluation methods〞from assessing 'final short-form papers' to assessing 'critical thinking demonstrated throughout the writing process.' Ｌ Mandate oral examinations/interviews: Elevate oral exams or interviews from supplementary to primary assessment components in thesis or code-based evaluations, thereby directly testing and verifying students＊ genuine understanding of knowledge and code functionality, and restoring interpersonal bonds of trust.

Manifestation_Text: Institutional disruption to traditional scientific credit and accountability mechanisms, coupled with the lag and regulatory vacuum of existing academic governance systems in responding to disruptive technologies.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Top-level policy revision: Academic institutions must urgently review and revise their research integrity policies to explicitly define undisclosed use of AI-generated text as a violation and clearly communicate the core values being breached to all stakeholders. Ｌ Collaborative development of citation standards: Academic institutions must work closely with journal editors, publishers, and other industry stakeholders to jointly formulate effective and unified standards for disclosing and citing AI tools. Ｍ Upholding the authorship boundary: Aligning with the stance of leading journals, large language models (LLMs) must be explicitly excluded from authorship positions to preserve human agency in scientific accountability. Ｎ Redefining scholarly achievement: Multiple stakeholders must collaboratively redefine what constitutes scholarly achievement and impact, and develop new metrics and methodologies to assess them, in response to systemic transformations brought about by AI.

Manifestation_Text: Academic communities in the Global South and non-native English-speaking regions face disproportionate compliance burdens and structural inequities.

Deficiencies in AI algorithms and ＆anthropomorphic＊ rewriting distort scientific terminology and introduce factual errors, generating epistemologically unfounded ＆pseudo-knowledge＊ that directly degrades the scientific quality of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implementing critical information practice education: Explicitly teach students〞within information literacy curricula〞how to critically evaluate AI-generated content and its inherent limitations (Critical Information Practice), thereby enhancing users＊ ability to identify AI-related flaws. Ｌ Returning to process-oriented assessment: Move away from overreliance on technical detection (＆technical policing＊) toward assessment frameworks that prioritize information provenance and authentic intellectual engagement, thus safeguarding scholarly quality at its source.

Manifestation_Text: The integration of AI tools undermines intellectual trust within the academic community, resulting in fractured authorship identity and alienation of trust bonds between students and instructors or among peers.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implementing process-oriented assessments: Restore authentic academic trust〞previously eroded by surface-level textual reliance〞by focusing on genuine knowledge engagement throughout the research and writing process. Ｌ Strengthening information ethics and knowledge construction education: Integrate explicit instruction on information philosophy (e.g., why authentic sources matter) and knowledge construction (e.g., how active participation in information practices cultivates cognitive capacity) into scientific writing and information literacy courses, thereby reconstructing scholarly identity and ethical foundations.

Manifestation_Text: The macro-level ＆publish-or-perish＊ evaluation pressure, when combined with AI humanizers, leads to ＆systemic information corruption＊, undermining the scholarly publishing evaluation system, information traceability mechanisms, and the overall credibility of science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reforming academic evaluation and assessment paradigms: Authors emphasize that information integrity cannot be restored solely through technical detection; instead, a return to ＆process-oriented assessments＊ is essential〞prioritizing information provenance and authentic intellectual engagement. Ｌ Restructuring information literacy and scientific writing pedagogy: Systematically integrate information philosophy, knowledge construction, information ethics, and critical information practice into formal curricula to institutionally reinforce the academic community＊s commitment to information integrity. Ｍ Policy responses from journal publishers: In light of the widespread adoption of AI-assisted writing tools, journals must formulate and refine corresponding publication policies and editorial review guidelines (as elaborated in the ＆Implications to scientific writing and integrity＊ section at the end of the paper).

Manifestation_Text: AI paraphrasing tools (AI humanizers) distort scientific terminology, introduce factual errors, and generate 'pseudo-knowledge' lacking epistemological foundations.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Return to process-oriented assessment: The author argues that information integrity cannot be restored solely through technical policing; instead, assessment must shift toward 'process-oriented assessments' that emphasize information provenance and authentic knowledge engagement. Ｌ Enhance information literacy education: Explicitly integrate 'critical information practice' into information literacy instruction, teaching users how to evaluate AI-generated information and understand its limitations.

Manifestation_Text: Academic writing becomes alienated into superficial performance, undermining authorial identity and eroding the trust-based bond among scholars grounded in human intellect.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reconstruct information ethics awareness: Explicitly teach 'philosophy of information' and 'information ethics' within information literacy curricula, enabling scholars to deeply appreciate the essential role of information provenance in scholarly communication. Ｌ Strengthen the knowledge construction process: Educational interventions must shift from purely technical skill training to 'knowledge construction', emphasizing the irreplaceable role of human participation in information processing for cognitive development.

Manifestation_Text: Macro-level academic governance systems are subject to malicious gaming, resulting in systemic 'epistemic pollution' of institutional repositories and scientific records.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Move beyond single-point technical regulation: The author explicitly calls for moving away from reliance on 'technical policing alone' to restore information integrity, advocating instead for systemic reform of evaluation mechanisms. Ｌ Implement process-oriented assessment reform: Academic institutions must adopt 'process-oriented assessments', focusing on information provenance and authentic knowledge engagement to fundamentally dismantle the systemic incentives for misconduct driven by 'publish-or-perish' culture.

Manifestation_Text: Inherent biases in AI predictive analytics and automated processes〞and AI＊s capacity to amplify pre-existing biases in training data〞lead to biased and potentially discriminatory research outcomes, threatening fair representation of specific populations or knowledge systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Algorithmic fairness review and ongoing assessment: Develop and implement fair algorithms, and conduct continuous, vigilant evaluations of AI tools to ensure inclusivity in the research environment (Section 3). Ｌ Mandatory dataset bias review: Institutional Ethics Committees (IECs) formulate ethical guidelines requiring researchers to critically assess and report the fairness of AI tools used, and rigorously examine the representativeness and bias of datasets employed to train AI models, thereby ensuring fairness and equity in research outcomes (Section 7).

Manifestation_Text: The absurdity and factual inaccuracies of AI-generated content〞as well as its circumvention of peer review〞directly undermine the authenticity and scientific quality of academic publications (e.g., AI-generated images containing garbled text and anatomically nonsensical structures have passed peer review and been published).
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reinforce human authors＊ fact-checking responsibility: Publishers explicitly stipulate that authors must verify and assume responsibility for the factual accuracy of AI-generated content, thereby preventing plagiarism and fabrication (a shared requirement across publishers including APA, Frontiers, and PLOS, as shown in Table 2). Ｌ Implement tiered restrictions and disclosure requirements: Academic journals enforce differentiated restrictions and mandatory disclosure requirements for AI-generated content to safeguard the integrity of scholarly publishing and close loopholes in the review process (Section 8).

Manifestation_Text: The involvement of AI blurs the boundary between human intellectual contribution and machine-generated content, delivering systemic shocks to established academic governance frameworks〞including traditional definitions of 'authorship', mechanisms for scholarly accountability, and peer review. Concurrently, inconsistencies across institutional guidelines create regulatory gaps that undermine the overall credibility of science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish the top-level principle of 'irreplaceability of human intellect and responsibility': Major publishers and universities must explicitly issue policies prohibiting the listing of AI as an author and mandating that human authors bear ultimate responsibility for the accuracy, completeness, and originality of their content (Sections 5, 6, and Table 2). Ｌ Enforce transparency and end-to-end disclosure: Authors must comprehensively disclose the use of AI tools〞including the specific tools employed, timing of use, and precise purposes〞in the Acknowledgements, Methods section, or cover letter (as stipulated by COPE, Nature Portfolio, and others in Table 2). Ｍ Upgrade the mandate of Institutional Ethics Committees (IECs) and foster interdisciplinary collaboration: IECs must expand their scope of review and collaborate with computer scientists, ethicists, and legal scholars to develop dynamic ethical frameworks adaptable to rapid technological change (Section 7). Ｎ Promote multi-stakeholder governance and policy harmonization: Universities (e.g., MIT, Stanford) should proactively issue policy briefs; the University of Melbourne has called for governments, universities, and industry partners to establish Communities of Practice to address the limitations of single-institution guidelines and advance globally or sectorally aligned governance standards (Sections 6 and 8).

Manifestation_Text: AI and computational methods risk impoverishing global cultural narratives by flattening rich cultural meanings (decontextualization) and amplifying certain narratives while marginalizing others in quantitative analysis〞thereby reinforcing existing cultural hegemonies.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Methodological integration: Computational methods should not replace humanistic inquiry but rather be integrated with qualitative approaches to preserve contextual nuance and ensure diverse voices are heard (Couldry and Hepp, 2017). Ｌ Philosophical safeguards and human-centered core: Human每machine co-created cultural research requires combining advanced computational methods with philosophically informed safeguards to ensure the richness of human experience and community agency remain central.

Manifestation_Text: AI tools (e.g., LLMs) perform poorly on novel cultural analytical tasks; structuring complex cultural phenomena into datasets inevitably introduces bias; and an uncritical pursuit of big data may lead to the 'reductionist trap'〞a misplaced faith in the absolute neutrality and objectivity of data〞thereby compromising the rigor and scientific quality of academic research.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Critical evaluation and transparency: Emphasize the necessity of critically evaluating AI tools within cultural contexts and call for transparency and reflexivity in data-driven scholarship. Ｌ Rigorous data construction: Stress that cultural data must be not only 'big' but also 'rigorous and clever'; researchers must thoughtfully consider how to represent cultural phenomena as data to avoid the reductionist trap.

Manifestation_Text: AI research engenders 'elite capture' and 'humanities extraction' in the humanities〞i.e., the unilateral appropriation of humanistic methodologies and perspectives by the AI field without commensurate investment in the disciplines that cultivate them〞resulting in the commodification of humanities scholarship and systemic disruption to the broader disciplinary ecology and academic development institutions.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Enhance academic and societal awareness: Scholars and society at large must be educated to fully recognize the risks posed by 'humanities extraction' and commodification. Ｌ Reject superficial engagement: Warn against and resist shallow participation that fails to acknowledge the depth and complexity of the humanities, and advocate for authentic, deep integration of humanistic thinking into AI development.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated texts render academic 'knowledge' generic and homogenized, packaged in deceptively simplified forms that erase nuance in scholarly expression and thought.

AI bypasses the essential 'struggle' and deep thinking processes inherent in academic inquiry, leading scholars to formulate broad, hasty claims and weak arguments, and potentially eroding their capacity for informed judgment and evaluation of argument quality〞thereby directly diminishing the rigor and scientific quality of academic output.

AI induces implicit trust and ascribes moral agency to itself through anthropomorphic 'flattery' (e.g., praising the author as courageous or ethical) and emotional support, thereby alienating scholars from their intellectual dependence on authentic academic communities (e.g., mentors, peers) and blindly delegating intellectual agency to algorithmic 'ghost writers'.

Current AI usage disclosure norms are severely inadequate and misleading, failing to capture complex AI interactions spanning hundreds of pages; meanwhile, covert AI use by senior scholars leads to an oversaturation of publications that are difficult for editors and reviewers to detect, thereby delivering systemic shocks to macro-level academic governance〞including definitions of 'authorship', determinations of originality, and peer review practices.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Creating spaces for academic reflection: cultivating intellectual, professional, and pedagogical spaces where scholars can continuously reflect on how AI shapes their modes of thinking, the meaning of academic labor, and their own scholarly identity. Ｌ Restructuring teaching and assessment paradigms: educators must honestly confront the widespread adoption of AI by designing assessments that AI cannot easily complete (e.g., in-class pen-and-paper exams and oral examinations), and guiding students to use AI ethically〞as a tool to support thinking rather than to replace cognitively demanding tasks.

Manifestation_Text: The quality and accuracy of text generated by generative AI (GenAI) remain questionable; such outputs may be used to supplement〞or even fabricate〞data production and analysis, resulting in an inundation of pseudoscientific texts and directly undermining the authenticity and scientific quality of academic publishing.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Refining contribution attribution and disclosure mechanisms: journals should require authors to identify and attribute contributions at a finer granularity (e.g., adopting the CRediT taxonomy for author contributions) and mandate explicit disclosure of GenAI usage〞or even prohibit its use outright〞to distinguish between human creativity and machine-generated content. Ｌ Author-led ethical self-assessment: scholars are urged to engage in critical self-questioning when using GenAI〞clarifying their writing objectives and the ethical risks involved in integrating GenAI tools〞and to adopt responsible ethical stances.

Manifestation_Text: The intervention of GenAI dissolves the moral responsibility and bonds of mutual trust within the academic community〞both grounded in human intellectual agency〞making it difficult for authors to delineate their own intellectual contributions and rendering external accountability elusive and untraceable.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Strengthening individual accountability and identification: re-establishing authorial identity and restoring accountability ties rooted in individual agency through finer-grained contribution statements (e.g., CRediT) and rigorous journal-level scrutiny of GenAI usage (via mandatory disclosure or prohibition). Ｌ Reconstructing academic collaboration and incentive structures: acknowledging the erosion of traditional authorship, exploring alternatives that decouple academic rewards from conventional authorship attribution and instead recognize participation, service, and collective contributions〞thus forging new collaborative and trust-based bonds within the academic community even in the absence of traditional 'bylines'.

Manifestation_Text: The 'hypercommons' model underpinning Generative AI (GenAI) exerts institutional pressure on macro-level academic governance systems〞including authorship identity, intellectual property rights, and reward mechanisms〞while large technology companies extract collective data for private gain under opaque and exploitative conditions. This undermines both individual accountability and collective recognition, thereby threatening the overall credibility of the scientific system.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Safeguard existing institutional baselines: Leverage current academic norms and incentive structures〞such as journal policies mandating disclosure or prohibiting GenAI use〞to preserve individual authorship identity and accountability frameworks, preventing the proliferation of pseudoscientific texts from eroding scientific credibility. Ｌ Advance democratic technology governance and platform cooperativism: Advocate reclaiming control over digital design and governance by developing GenAI technologies that are collectively owned, transparent, and equitable〞replacing profit-driven corporations＊ opaque and exploitative black-box solutions〞and ensuring that the creation, training, and benefit distribution of the 'hypercommons' align with collective decision-making and democratic principles. Ｍ Fundamentally restructure academic evaluation systems: Decouple scholarly rewards from individual research outputs and explore new mechanisms to recognize collective contributions, adapting macro-level academic governance to a context where authorial identity is increasingly attenuated.

Manifestation_Text: AI algorithmic hallucinations cause a collapse in the authenticity and reproducibility of academic content. When generating text, AI may fabricate fictional concepts, persons, or references, presenting erroneous outputs as factual〞blurring the boundary between reality and fabrication.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish audit and guidance frameworks: Researchers must develop dedicated frameworks to understand, audit, and guide AI-driven creativity and experimental processes (Section V). Ｌ Implement 'controlled openness' and shared verification: In research practice, process transparency must be valued equally with outcome quality; systemic shared verification mechanisms should compensate for quality deficits inherent in AI-generated outputs (Sections IV, VI). Ｍ Affirm ultimate human responsibility: Emphasize that while AI can produce content, final 'interpretation and responsibility' must remain firmly vested in human actors (Section IV).

Manifestation_Text: The erosion of human creative agency and the emergence of 'authorless writing' disrupt academic resonance and undermine teacher每student trust in educational settings. Direct copying of AI-generated content dilutes authorial identity, rendering texts fragmented and soulless; simultaneously, students＊ use of AI for essay writing triggers teachers＊ heightened skepticism regarding assignment authenticity.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implement 'dual educational innovation': Not only establish frameworks for auditing AI, but also concurrently invest in cultivating uniquely human capacities〞including creativity, interpretive skill, and embodied judgment (Section V). Ｌ Reinforce 'embodied practices' and hands-on experience: Reconceptualize creativity within research training by elevating the pedagogical value of experiential learning grounded in physical experimentation. Direct interaction with instruments, materials, and unpredictable phenomena fosters intuition, judgment, and situational awareness〞cognitive capacities currently inaccessible to AI〞and thereby reconstitutes distinctively human epistemic bonds (Section V).

Manifestation_Text: The deconstruction of traditional academic authorship institutions and the failure of accountability mechanisms. Debates over AI as a 'collaborator'〞or even as a 'co-author'〞render authorial boundaries porous, making it impossible to identify responsible parties when academic outputs err, thereby inflicting systemic strain on macro-level academic accountability frameworks.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Paradigm shift in governance: Advocate transitioning research ethics from 'static prohibitive rules' toward an 'adaptive, system-oriented form of governance', shifting the ethical focus entirely from 'Who created it?' to 'Who is responsible for it?' (Sections IV, VI). Ｌ Shift toward collaboration-centered ethics and system-level verification: Drawing inspiration from industrialized collaborative models such as K-pop Song Camps and Andy Warhol＊s Factory, relocate ethical emphasis from the individual to the collective〞pursuing transparency, shared verification, and co-authorship (Sections II, VI). Ｍ Institutionalize process transparency: Adopt 'controlled openness'〞explicitly acknowledging AI or collaborative system involvement〞and elevate process transparency to a core metric in academic evaluation (Section IV).

Manifestation_Text: Existing academic governance systems and publishing evaluation frameworks reveal systemic failures and institutional blind spots in responding to emerging technological ethical challenges such as those posed by AI. Specifically: (1) Traditional ethics review systems (e.g., IRBs/RECs) exhibit limitations〞for instance, U.S. IRBs are explicitly instructed not to assess long-term societal risks associated with large-scale technological deployment; (2) Journal publishing policies suffer from widespread gaps and weak enforcement: 54% of journals lack ethics reporting statements, and 51% of published papers omit any mention of ethical considerations; (3) Industry standards (e.g., COPE) suffer from inadequate awareness and implementation: 28% of editors are unaware of COPE, 38% provide no explicit ethical guidance to reviewers, and 18% have published research raising ethical concerns.
Mitigation_Text:
Drawing on co-creation with an editorial reference group, the article proposes a suite of editorial policy levers designed to reshape publishing evaluation systems and academic governance frameworks (see Table 1 and the article＊s core arguments throughout):
Ｋ Prescriptive and reflexive interventions: Revise author guidelines and submission templates to mandate disclosure of ethical information and assessment of potential downstream consequences, and expand peer-review criteria to include evaluation of risks and consequences.
Ｌ Capacity building and training: Provide ethics training, workshops, and benchmark case studies for reviewers and researchers〞especially early-career authors.
Ｍ Stakeholder engagement: Develop soft policies encouraging interaction with affected stakeholders across the full lifecycle of AI tools〞from design and evaluation to implementation.
Ｎ Create spaces for dialogue and reflection: Institutionalize discussions on downstream consequences and normative issues through editorials, symposia, and dedicated article categories, welcoming diverse perspectives.
Ｏ Incentivize 'slow research': Support more rigorous, long-term ethical deliberation via policies promoting data/code sharing, replication studies, and post-publication review.

Manifestation_Text: AI-assisted writing of substantive academic content undermines the integrity of the academic integrity system and the validity of degree-granting institutions, and threatens the overall credibility of science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish compliant AI detection policies: Universities urgently need to adopt AI detection policies that uphold the principle of 'presumption of innocence' and align with data protection laws. Ｌ Uphold the human authorship boundary: Academic evaluation and management systems must strictly reserve scholarly authorship as an intellectual process that cannot be outsourced to machines.

Manifestation_Text: The replacement of core human creative processes by AI-generated content compromises the independence of academic output; meanwhile, algorithmic 'memory' and stylistic imitation mechanisms pose serious risks of substantive plagiarism and copyright infringement, diminishing the originality and authentic quality of academic content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Technology developers provide similarity identification tools: The article suggests that if AI systems themselves offer tools capable of identifying similarities between generated content and copyrighted works, such tools could mitigate these risks of infringement and quality degradation (though the authors also note that declining user copyright awareness may weaken demand for such verification tools).

Manifestation_Text: AI hallucinations, factual fabrication, and false positives from detection tools directly compromise the authenticity and scientific quality of academic publications; overreliance on generative AI leads to the erosion of research originality and critical thinking.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop targeted technical assessment tools: The article notes that programs are being developed to evaluate specific sections where generative AI is used〞not merely relying on authors＊ self-declarations. Ｌ Clarify usage boundaries in publishing: Journal editors and publishers have explicitly stated, at conferences, their support for authors〞especially those whose first language is not English〞to use generative AI to enhance accessibility and comprehension of ideas, while strictly prohibiting its use to draft manuscripts.

Manifestation_Text: The widespread adoption of generative AI, combined with the existing high-pressure 'publish or perish' culture, systematically amplifies global academic misconduct (e.g., data falsification, paper mills) and retraction crises; simultaneously, AI hallucinations and deficiencies in knowledge retrieval cause retracted or refuted erroneous research to persistently circulate within macro-level societal systems〞including public policy, legal decision-making, and consumer choices〞severely damaging the overall credibility of science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish disciplinary guardrails and theoretical guidance frameworks: The abstract emphasizes that the macromarketing community bears responsibility for establishing 'guardrails' for the responsible use of generative AI in scientific research, thereby safeguarding trust and the pursuit of truth; the main text proposes integrating the Hunt-Vitell (H-V) ethical decision-making model and Jones＊s moral intensity model to provide a systematic theoretical framework guiding generative AI use. Ｌ Reconstruct academic citizenship culture: The authors call upon the marketing academic community〞and the broader academic ecosystem〞to assume leadership roles by implementing appropriate education and training initiatives that systematically foster good academic citizenship behaviors, thereby addressing at the root level the systemic incentives for misconduct driven by publication pressure.

Manifestation_Text: Ethical scrutiny of AI use and 'AI shaming' exacerbate racial bias in academia, imposing disproportionate psychological burdens and additional demands for marginalized groups (e.g., Black and women of color) to 'prove their effort', thereby hindering their participation and access to resources in academic and professional domains.
Mitigation_Text: Transform 'shaming' from a moral punishment directed at individuals into institutional reform through policy frameworks, educational interventions, and governance structures〞eliminating excessive scrutiny and structural barriers faced by marginalized groups and advancing more inclusive academic norms.

Manifestation_Text: The 'ersatz fluency' and grammatical polishing provided by AI tools mask the author＊s genuine ignorance or insufficient understanding, thereby undermining academic assessment systems〞such as product-based grading〞and diminishing the authentic intellectual engagement and scientific/learning quality underlying scholarly output.

In academic and professional communities, the 'shame' associated with AI use erodes trust bonds among students, instructors, and peers. It compels users to conceal their AI usage (secrecy), fostering suspicion across academia (e.g., instructors treating all polished submissions as suspect) and transforming what should be a collaborative, trust-based scholarly environment into an isolated one characterized by 'effort anxiety' and mutual surveillance.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implement comprehensive educational initiatives that integrate digital literacy with ecological and social literacy to alleviate structural pressures that compel individuals to conceal AI use; Ｌ Foster environments that encourage open dialogue and responsible AI integration; Ｍ Reframe shame as collective accountability for systemic harms〞not as interpersonal suspicion or punishment.

Manifestation_Text: 1) A legitimacy crisis in academic evaluation systems: AI＊s intervention renders traditional academic assessment and grading systems〞based on 'visible effort' and 'final texts'〞ineffective, thereby undermining the legitimacy of existing academic governance structures. 2) Systemic moral displacement: Societal scrutiny and shaming of individual users for 'cheating' obscure the true systemic harms embedded in AI development〞including high-carbon-emission data centers, exploitative labor in the Global South (e.g., content moderators in Kenya), and corporate knowledge monopolies ('green colonialism').
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Policy and governance level: Enforce stricter reporting guidelines and impose carbon taxes on data centers; integrate sustainability benchmarks into AI research funding; establish globally coordinated emission standards. Ｌ Corporate accountability and transparency: Require companies to disclose supply chain practices and energy consumption, and subject corporate conduct to collective oversight. Ｍ Educational interventions: Integrate digital literacy with ecological literacy to raise awareness among students and professionals about AI＊s hidden operational costs. Ｎ Ethical paradigm shift: Redirect shame toward institutional reform and collective accountability targeting technology corporations and governance structures.

Manifestation_Text: Technological barriers and resource inequalities exacerbate inequities in academic publishing opportunities. Scholars in resource-constrained settings, facing 'metrics-only' publication pressures, may lack access to advanced AI tools, computational resources, and institutional guidance〞forcing them into difficult ethical compromises between integrity and publication demands, thereby deepening global inequities in academia.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Provide resource and training support: Institutions should offer AI training, transparent guidelines, and supportive resources to bridge knowledge gaps and foster a more inclusive research ecosystem. Ｌ Promote equitable access: Advance fair access to AI tools to ensure AI benefits are realized across diverse academic contexts, thereby mitigating inequalities arising from resource disparities.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic recommendation and literature retrieval systems lead to homogenization and marginalization of academic perspectives. AI research assistants and algorithmic curation tools inherently embed popularity and visibility biases, privileging established mainstream sources〞thus narrowing the epistemic landscape, limiting exposure to marginalized or emerging scholarly work, and reinforcing entrenched hierarchies in knowledge production.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop differentiated ethical frameworks: Recognize the heterogeneity of AI systems and formulate tailored ethical frameworks to safeguard the diversity, creativity, and integrity essential to academic inquiry. Ｌ Defend critical heterodoxy: Actively uphold autonomy, inclusivity, and protection of 'critical heterodoxy' in academic inquiry to counteract algorithm-driven epistemic homogenization.

Manifestation_Text: AI 'hallucinations' and algorithmic flaws lead to the fabrication and distortion of scholarly content. Generative AI may produce bibliographic references that appear legitimate but are entirely fabricated, or generate statistical summaries and datasets lacking empirical grounding. If such seemingly coherent yet unverified content remains undetected, it risks contaminating the scientific record and misleading subsequent research.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandatory human verification: Human researchers must conduct indispensable, rigorous verification of all AI-generated data, references, and analytical results to prevent the inadvertent dissemination of false information. Ｌ Critical engagement and augmentation: Researchers must critically evaluate AI outputs, ensuring that generated content is accompanied by reflective reasoning, methodological rigor, and novel interpretation〞thereby preserving epistemic reliability.

Manifestation_Text: The cognitive substitution effect and concealment of AI use undermine epistemic trust within the academic community. When researchers outsource evaluative or interpretive judgment to AI (cognitive substitution), they weaken the development of scholarly expertise; simultaneously, undisclosed deep AI involvement obscures the source of intellectual contribution, misleads reviewers and readers, and erodes interpersonal academic trust grounded in human rational judgment and moral reflection.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish clear disclosure and attribution guidelines: Develop explicit guidelines on disclosing AI contributions, assigning authorship, and defining responsibility to uphold transparency and safeguard epistemic integrity. Ｌ Strengthen the oversight role of peers and editors: Peer reviewers, journal editors, and institutions must play a pivotal role in establishing AI-use standards, detecting potential misuse, and promoting transparency.

Manifestation_Text: A metric-driven academic system and the systemic failure of traditional safeguards. Under macro-level pressures to maximize publication counts and citation metrics, AI tools incentivize speed over reflective scholarship. Meanwhile, the 'gray zone' of human每AI collaboration〞such as AI-assisted rewriting to evade plagiarism detection or selective reporting of AI-generated data〞renders conventional editorial review and academic misconduct prevention mechanisms ineffective, causing broad disruption to academic governance systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Update institutional policies and governance frameworks: Institutions must urgently revise policies to establish an ethical governance framework encompassing both individual and structural accountability, ensuring AI adoption aligns with professional standards and sustains public trust in scholarly research. Ｌ Implement systemic education and cultural interventions: Bridge knowledge gaps through educational programs, professional development initiatives, and institutional policies; standardize expectations for AI integration; and cultivate a research culture that promotes responsible, transparent, and ethically grounded AI use.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated peer review reports lack substantive validation (substituting 'plausible prose' for 'patient verification'), and hidden 'prompt injection' instructions embedded in manuscripts can manipulate AI tools, subjecting the review process to active adversarial attacks〞directly degrading the quality and scientific validity of academic publishing assessments.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish secure infrastructure and content sanitization: Restrict the processing of external inputs and ensure automated assistance occurs only within controlled environments. Ｌ Clarify AI＊s auxiliary role: Specify that generative AI may serve solely as a supportive and triage tool〞never as a substitute for core human judgment. Ｍ Implement proportional, evidence-oriented auditing: Ensure substantive alignment between review comments and manuscript evidence. Ｎ Introduce procedural hygiene: Design systems to treat manuscripts as untrusted inputs and embed adversarial defense mechanisms.

Manifestation_Text: 'Outsourcing' of reviewer cognitive effort and 'accountability laundering'. Reviewers delegate core evaluative tasks〞such as interpretive summarization and identification of limitations〞to AI, reducing the human signature to a mere formal stamp of legitimacy. This weakens the substantive intellectual connection between reviewers and their reports, undermining the human-centered epistemic trust and accountability bonds essential to peer review.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reinforce ultimate human accountability: Institutional guidelines and editorial policies must explicitly state that reviewers bear final responsibility for report content, and that critical and original evaluation cannot be delegated to generative systems. Ｌ Shift toward process-based governance: Enhance observability and traceability of the review judgment process through secure infrastructure and specific transparency〞anchoring trust not merely in text-detection methods, but in institutional design.

Manifestation_Text: The traditional macro-regulatory mechanism〞based on 'text-based enforcement/policing' and 'abstract prohibitions'〞has failed, giving rise to 'performative compliance.' Because AI-generated text is difficult to detect, blanket prohibitions drive review practices underground (e.g., using un-auditable external tools), exacerbating confidentiality risks and eroding the governance capacity and institutional learning capability of academic publishing evaluation systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Abandon single-mode text policing and abstract prohibitions: Acknowledge the limitations of prohibition- and detection-only approaches, and avoid grounding governance on unreliable text detectors. Ｌ Build an auditable hybrid governance model: Centered on confidentiality, reviewer accountability, secure infrastructure, granular disclosure, and evidence-anchored auditing, this model enhances the verifiability of AI-assisted workflows at the system level. Ｍ Shift institutional design from 'textual products' to 'judgmental practices': Treat peer review as a socio-technical practice requiring governance〞not merely as a textual output.

Manifestation_Text: The 'black-box' operation of AI summarization tools, their lack of provenance mechanisms, and occasional logical errors〞compounded by the low accuracy of AI detection tools〞directly undermine the methodological rigor, transparency, and content authenticity of academic research.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Prioritize tools with provenance functionality: Scholars〞especially doctoral students and early-career researchers〞are advised to prioritize 'document-focused' AI tools (e.g., NotebookLM, Scholarcy, AskYourPDF) that support citation tracking and provenance tracing to safeguard methodological transparency. Ｌ Tool adaptation and human review as fallback: Encourage scholars to explore and experiment with diverse AI tools to match individual research needs; crucially, all AI-assisted outputs must undergo rigorous human review and editing, with full authorial responsibility for final published content (e.g., compliant implementation of the 'Declaration of Generative AI').

Manifestation_Text: AI＊s increasing involvement in academic writing and learning has triggered a crisis of trust between instructors and students, leading to the erosion of students＊ intellectual agency and the emergence of 'learned helplessness'.

The unreliability of AI detection tools and the proliferation of AI-generated submissions threaten the viability of traditional academic integrity review mechanisms and thesis evaluation systems, thereby undermining macro-level academic governance frameworks.

AI algorithmic flaws (e.g., hallucinations, incorrect citations) and non-compliant usage (e.g., translation plagiarism) directly compromise the authenticity and scientific quality of scholarly publications, while existing plagiarism-detection tools are largely ineffective against such violations.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implement rigorous human review: Conduct dual citation verification, data cross-validation, and detailed methodological confirmation for AI-generated or AI-restructured content. Ｌ Mandate multi-tool detection: Until effective domain-specific tools become available, journal editorial offices must combine multiple plagiarism-detection tools leveraging distinct databases and analytical algorithms. Ｍ Delimit AI＊s functional boundaries: Restrict AI strictly to supportive functions (e.g., literature searching, outline generation); core interpretation, methodological selection, and critical revisions must be performed exclusively by domain experts. Ｎ Strengthen cross-lingual human verification: During peer review, use translation tools to reverse-check whether identical keywords, titles, or abstracts exist in publications in other languages.

Manifestation_Text: The covert use of AI and AI-enabled translation plagiarism dilute academic responsibility, exposing existing copyright laws, academic integrity policies (e.g., COPE and ORI guidelines), and scholarly evaluation systems to systemic failure〞and thereby eroding the scientific community＊s overall credibility.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Shift toward a 'radical transparency' governance model: Propose an integrated management framework that transcends the traditional human每machine binary, mandating public disclosure of the type, model, version, and source of AI-generated content; Ｌ Integrate ethical and legal mechanisms: Embed COPE＊s ethical principles into formal governance structures and align them with the legal mechanisms of the EU AI Act, implementing risk-based compliance workflows; Ｍ Enact unified legislation and enforcement mechanisms: Call for immediate and harmonized legislative action to clarify platform providers＊ responsibilities and establish legal procedures for addressing attempted intellectual property appropriation and other forms of plagiarism; Ｎ Introduce technological provenance tools: Employ digital watermarking to assign unique identifiers for traceability and leverage blockchain technology for timestamping and copyright certification; Ｏ Conduct academic education initiatives: Deliver training on responsible research practices and incorporate issues of translation plagiarism into open scholarly discourse.

Manifestation_Text: The covert intervention of AI and the failure of automated detection tools undermine the trust-based bond among human experts in peer review and erode academic trust among authors, editors, and readers.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reinforce the core value of the 'human factor': Human verification must not be overlooked in anti-plagiarism and peer review processes; manual checks should persist to compensate for algorithmic blind spots and restore professional mutual trust between reviewers and editorial offices; Ｌ Establish a structured AI-use disclosure mechanism: Require authors to explicitly detail the nature and scope of AI contributions in their contribution statements, enabling readers and editors to accurately assess the extent of AI support〞and thereby repair and rebuild trust within the scholarly community.

Manifestation_Text: The facile generation of misleading or entirely fabricated scholarly articles containing false data using generative AI circumvents the relatively low quality-control thresholds of preprint servers, resulting in the proliferation of low-quality and fraudulent scholarly content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Strengthen the filtering function of traditional peer review: The authors note that although fake articles may occasionally pass through certain journals, traditional journals＊ peer review processes generally exhibit higher probabilities of identifying and rejecting such articles〞hence, traditional publishing＊s quality-control mechanisms should not be abandoned outright. Ｌ Community-based cautious citation and scrutiny: The scientific community should exercise restraint when citing or utilizing preprints lacking peer review, carefully examining data availability and study protocols. Ｍ Dynamic correction mechanisms for preprints: Preprint authors are encouraged to actively engage with the community; revise or appropriately retract preprints when serious errors are identified by readers (Engage, revise, and redact when appropriate).

Manifestation_Text: Malicious actors exploit generative AI to mass-produce pseudoscientific articles and publish them as preprints, exacerbating the spread of disinformation and conspiracy theories〞and delivering systemic shocks to the scientific community＊s overall credibility, the evidentiary foundation of policymaking, and public trust in the preprint ecosystem.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Community vigilance against propaganda manipulation: The scientific community must remain highly vigilant against manipulative efforts aimed at influencing scientists or the public by disseminating propaganda disguised as scientific preprints. Ｌ Media collaboration and public education: The research community must proactively collaborate with and educate media professionals〞clarifying which information channels are reliable and how to distinguish robust research from preprints of uncertain quality〞to prevent media amplification of pseudoscience. Ｍ Uphold the reputational endorsement of traditional journals: To counter the proliferation of disinformation and information overload, stakeholders beyond academia must be informed about the reputational authority and gatekeeping role of established traditional journals〞as a systemic defense against generative AI每driven information pollution.

Manifestation_Text: AI algorithmic flaws (e.g., hallucinations) combined with automated generation lacking substantive human oversight result in scholarly outputs that lack authenticity and scientific rigor〞producing 'science-like output' rather than genuine science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Resist full automation: The authors explicitly call for resisting the 'Research Automaton', opposing the complete delegation of research processes to AI. Ｌ Build hybrid cognitive constellations: Advocate for the judicious and deliberate use of AI within a 'hybrid cognitive constellation', positioning AI as a tool to 'augment'〞not replace〞human capabilities. Ｍ Ensure substantive human involvement: Emphasize the necessity of meaningful human engagement across all core stages of scientific research to safeguard the authenticity and quality of final scholarly outputs.

Manifestation_Text: The rupture of academic intellectual inheritance, the atrophy of early-career researchers＊ skills, and the alienation of collaborative bonds within the academic community〞bonds historically grounded in human intellectual passion and interaction.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reconceptualizing science as a vocation: Guiding the academic community to re-recognize science not merely as a technical process but as a way of life and a ＆vocation,＊ emphasizing the intrinsic value of the research process for the individual. Ｌ Preserving formative tasks involving ＆struggle＊: Institutions and mentors should deliberately retain those ＆messy, slow, and frustrating tasks＊ characteristic of traditional research〞such as manually surveying the full literature landscape, deeply engaging with theoretical frameworks, and handling data〞because these labor-intensive processes constitute essential formative elements for cultivating researchers＊ capabilities and sustaining academic intellectual inheritance; they must not be easily bypassed by AI.

Manifestation_Text: The distortion of macro-level academic evaluation systems by techno-solutionism, and the systemic risk of long-term erosion of scientific innovation capacity and public credibility.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Resisting techno-solutionism: Policymakers, academic institutions, and publishers must fundamentally resist the tendency to apply ＆techno-solutionism＊ to scientific research, refusing to recast non-problems (e.g., traditional research processes) as technical problems requiring technological fixes. Ｌ Upholding science＊s normative status: Reaffirming science＊s institutional position as a ＆normative activity,＊ ensuring that humans remain central agents within the scientific system. Ｍ Accepting efficiency trade-offs: The academic community must collectively agree〞in institutional design〞that safeguarding science＊s intrinsic value as a ＆process＊ and its long-term innovative capacity justifies deliberate compromises and sacrifices in short-term effectiveness and productivity.

Manifestation_Text: AI algorithmic flaws and ＆hallucinations＊ leading to fabricated references and synthetic plagiarism, thereby undermining the authenticity and traceability of scholarly content. The text notes that generative AI (GenAI) can synthesize and recombine existing texts without generating direct textual similarity (i.e., synthetic plagiarism), and can generate fabricated references. When authors fail to independently verify AI-generated content, this directly threatens the reliability of scholarly claims and scientific quality.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandatory human verification and accountability: Major publishers (e.g., Elsevier, SAGE, Wiley) explicitly require authors to verify the accuracy, fairness, original sources, and intellectual property compliance of AI outputs, ensuring final human accountability for content. Ｌ Context-sensitive editorial review: The article calls for editorial governance not to rely solely on AI-detection tools or quantitative metrics, but rather to treat it as a ＆qualitative, context-sensitive practice＊ grounded in human judgment, aimed at assessing AI＊s actual epistemic and scholarly quality impacts.
