Manifestation_Text: The failure of existing academic detection systems and governance mechanisms leads to the collapse of academic accountability, triggering a 'toxic online disinhibition effect'.
Using AI tools to deceive evaluators and derive pleasure from such deception alienates and undermines the bond of mutual trust inherent in academic assessment.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Targeted psychological intervention: Implement personalized counseling and support programs for students exhibiting sadistic and other 'dark triad' traits to correct the psychological mechanism whereby they derive pleasure from deception. Ｌ Enhance interpersonal relatedness within the academic environment: Responsibly integrate generative AI into teaching to strengthen students＊ sense of 'relatedness' within the academic community, thereby repairing and reinforcing interpersonal trust in academic contexts.

Manifestation_Text: Unfair academic evaluation and distorted resource allocation. In highly competitive technological universities, AI-enabled cheating distorts standards for assessing academic achievement, placing students who exert genuine effort and refrain from using AI shortcuts at a clear disadvantage in grading and academic resource distribution〞thereby undermining the fairness of academic evaluation.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduce technological countermeasures and monitoring: Institutions should invest in AI-driven detection systems (e.g., Turnitin) and AI-based online proctoring systems to combat digital cheating (Chapter 2.3). Ｌ Optimize teaching and assessment environments: Universities should consider improving course design and alleviating external environmental pressures to address root causes〞such as excessive course difficulty or time constraints〞that motivate students to cheat (Chapter 4.6).

Manifestation_Text: Compromised authenticity of academic content and hollowing-out of knowledge and skills. Students use AI to generate fabricated citations and references to falsely enhance academic credibility, while bypassing critical thinking and the learning process〞resulting in academic assignments lacking authentic scholarly quality and graduates deficient in core domain-specific knowledge and competencies.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Upgrade AI detection technologies: Institutions should invest in more advanced AI-driven detection systems, as these tools are better able to identify subtle markers left by AI-generated content (Chapter 2.3). Ｌ Deliver AI literacy education: Integrate AI literacy into curricula to educate students about the potential risks of AI misuse and guide them to use AI to augment learning〞not circumvent it (Chapter 2.3).

Manifestation_Text: Erosion of the trust bond within the academic community and the emergence of a low-trust culture. The widespread use of AI for cheating severely undermines trust among students, between students and faculty, and across the broader academic community. Students commonly perceive their environment as rife with cheating behavior, fostering a low-trust culture characterized by high tolerance for academic misconduct.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Rebuilding a culture of academic integrity: Institutions must place high priority on cultivating students＊ ethical decision-making capabilities and foster a campus culture〞particularly in technical universities〞that emphasizes integrity and personal responsibility (Chapter 1 and Section 2.3). Ｌ Establishing clear ethical boundaries: Developing and implementing explicit guidelines for acceptable AI use to help students distinguish between legitimate academic assistance and unethical cheating (Chapter 1).

Manifestation_Text: Undermining of the ethical foundation of education and systemic devaluation of degree credibility. AI-enabled cheating (e.g., AI-giarism) blurs the boundary between legitimate assistance and academic misconduct, posing a systemic challenge to existing academic integrity management systems; this results in technical degrees failing to reflect students＊ authentic competencies, thereby inflicting profound institutional impacts on graduates＊ long-term career development and on universities＊ overall societal reputation.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Top-level policy and institutional restructuring: Universities must review and implement new ethical guidelines, formulate institutional policies and supporting resources that promote responsible AI use, and ensure students fully understand the consequences of academic misconduct (Section 2.3). Ｌ Collaborative, multi-stakeholder educational adaptation: Educators must adapt to technological change by deeply integrating AI ethics education into curricula, upholding ethical standards in academic environments while harnessing the benefits of AI technologies (Chapter 1 and Section 2.3).

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated content often contains factual errors and fabricated citations (＆hallucinations＊), and students increasingly outsource higher-order cognitive tasks to AI〞leading to severe deterioration in the authenticity of academic output and the quality of educational assessment.

Cognitive dissonance among students and faculty regarding the boundaries of AI use, coupled with erosion of academic mutual trust, leads to the breakdown of the trust-based relationship underpinning traditional educational assessment.
Traditional academic integrity management systems and anti-cheating detection frameworks〞grounded in ＆deterrence theory＊〞face systemic failure due to the low detectability of AI-generated misconduct.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Shifting governance focus toward internal psychological constraints: Given the ineffectiveness of external formal sanctions (e.g., detection and punishment), the article proposes〞in sections such as ＆2.5. Informal sanctions＊〞amplifying the deterrent effect of ＆informal sanctions＊ (e.g., guilt, shame, embarrassment) as internal psychological costs. Ｌ Activating moral self-concept: It is recommended to intervene in students＊ ＆moral disengagement＊ mechanisms to activate their positive self-concept, thereby inducing psychological discomfort when confronted with the temptation to cheat using AI〞thus compensating, at the systemic level, for the limitations of external technical detection mechanisms. Ｍ Implications for detection software design: The abstract notes that the study＊s findings may inform plagiarism detection software designers in enforcing academic integrity in the ChatGPT era (though specific technical improvements are not elaborated in the text).

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI-generated content (e.g., plagiarism, fabrication) and algorithmic evasion (e.g., text obfuscation via carefully engineered 'strict prompts') directly undermines the authenticity of academic and educational materials and degrades or nullifies the performance of existing AI detection tools. Moreover, AI-generated misinformation compromises the reliability of content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Propose an NLP framework based on stylometry analysis (Stylometry Analysis / SCD): Authenticate content authenticity by extracting intrinsic writing-style features〞not merely surface-level textual patterns. Ｌ Construct and open-source a large-scale benchmark dataset: Generate a machine-written text corpus containing outputs from both 'ordinary' and 'strict' prompts, and publicly release the associated code to establish a baseline for improving detection tools＊ efficacy against sophisticated AI-generated texts.

Manifestation_Text: Excessive AI intervention erodes communicative interaction and collaborative bonds between instructors and students, as well as among students themselves, in educational settings; it also undermines the interpersonal trust underpinning academic assessment〞specifically, the principle of 'student-independent completion'〞triggering a crisis of trust due to ghostwriting or AI-assisted writing.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduce author change detection and author recognition techniques: Leverage stylometric change detection (SCD) to automatically identify author transitions and attribute specific contributions within multi-author documents. Ｌ Automate collaboration auditing: Employ technical means to detect potential cases of 'illegal or legal collaboration' in the production of educational content, thereby technically supporting authorship verification and restoring/safeguarding interpersonal trust mechanisms in academic assessment.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of generative AI exerts systemic pressure on macro-level academic integrity systems〞including core principles such as honesty, trust, fairness, and accountability〞as well as on educational evaluation frameworks, rendering traditional academic governance and accountability mechanisms vulnerable to failure.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish a systematic technical verification infrastructure: Develop an NLP verification framework targeting four core tasks〞human-vs.-AI text classification, single- vs. multi-author classification, etc.〞to enhance academic institutions＊ capacity for automated auditing of AI-generated content. Ｌ Promote open-source development and community co-construction: Publicly release generated datasets, source code, and related materials on GitHub to provide academia and detection agencies with a unified technical baseline for countering AI-enabled academic misconduct, thereby supporting and repairing macro-level academic integrity governance systems.

Manifestation_Text: Academic texts generated by generative AI often exhibit shallow reasoning, contextual disconnection, and absence of citations; furthermore, the emergence of 'humanized AI texts' tools renders AI-generated content increasingly indistinguishable, directly threatening the authenticity and scientific quality of scholarly publishing.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop a specialized detection tool based on statistical features: Train classification models (e.g., Gotcha GPT) using metrics such as perplexity and burstiness to accurately identify short-form AI-generated texts. Ｌ Integrate human judgment with semantic signals: Rather than relying solely on detectors, combine expert human review with identification of telltale AI-text signals〞including repetitive vocabulary, unnatural phrasing, awkward abbreviations, generic tone, and contradictory statements〞to comprehensively expose academic misconduct.

Manifestation_Text: Unreliable AI detection tools producing high false-positive rates (i.e., erroneous accusations) severely damage interpersonal trust between instructors and students, and between reviewers and authors, leading to deteriorating classroom climates; additionally, uploading unpublished manuscripts to third-party online detection platforms breaches confidentiality norms essential to peer review.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implement multi-tool verification and expert review: Instructors should employ as many AI detection tools as possible and seek a second opinion from an AI-detection expert to avoid wrongful accusations. Ｌ Adopt localized, privacy-preserving tools: Use open-source, offline tools (e.g., Gotcha GPT) that do not require uploading files to the internet, thereby safeguarding author copyright and upholding confidentiality ethics in peer review. Ｍ Emphasize the irreplaceability of human judgment: Explicitly state that AI detectors cannot substitute for human judgment; manual review must be integrated to prevent erosion of interpersonal trust.

Manifestation_Text: Misjudgments by AI detection tools and the escalating adversarial arms race between AI text generation/humanization techniques are undermining macro-level academic governance systems and scholarly publishing evaluation frameworks. False accusations may trigger legal disputes between academia and publishing institutions or universities〞and even derail the careers of early-career researchers〞thereby eroding the credibility of the scientific publishing system.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish a graduated disciplinary mechanism for academic misconduct: The authors propose a standardized procedural framework for suspected violations〞'flag on first occurrence, warn on second, act rigorously on third'〞to avoid systemic risks arising from one-size-fits-all approaches. Ｌ Continuous iteration and domain-specific model training: To keep pace with rapidly evolving AI humanization techniques, detection models must be continually retrained and updated using discipline-specific, language-specific (e.g., Portuguese), and balanced datasets to sustain the effectiveness of academic evaluation systems.

Manifestation_Text: Generative AI is being misused to fabricate data ('data fabrication') and commit scientific fraud. Due to the proliferation of evasion techniques, papers containing fabricated content may bypass textual scrutiny and be published, directly compromising the authenticity and scientific quality of scholarly publications. Moreover, AI detection tools themselves suffer from serious algorithmic flaws (e.g., high false-positive rates), even misclassifying classic scientific literature authored by human scholars in the 1960s as AI-generated〞rendering quality-control tools in scholarly publishing ineffective.
Mitigation_Text: It is essential to move beyond mere textual detection and instead examine more specifically the origin and quality of the data, while rigorously verifying the reproducibility of the results.

Manifestation_Text: The stealthiness and accessibility of AI-generated text exacerbate structural flaws inherent in the distorted 'publish or perish' academic evaluation system, distorting the assessment of academic careers into a narrow pursuit of publication quantity. Concurrently, the unreliability of AI detection tools〞namely their inability to reliably identify AI-generated text and their tendency to misclassify human-authored text〞places existing academic integrity review and publishing governance systems at risk of total failure, thereby undermining the overall credibility of the scientific community.
Mitigation_Text: Adopt a critical approach to re-examining and reforming academic evaluation systems for scientific careers, fundamentally shifting evaluation criteria away from the volume of articles published toward methodological rigor, data quality, and the originality of the work.

Manifestation_Text: Misjudgments by automated AI detection tools (e.g., Turnitin) lead to unjust punishment and inequitable evaluation of individual scholars. Legitimate human-authored scholarly works are erroneously flagged as AI-generated (false positives), while AI-generated texts evade detection (false negatives), allowing algorithms to directly intervene in〞and distort〞the fair allocation of academic assessment outcomes.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduce hybrid evaluation frameworks: Automated detection tools should not be used in isolation; rather, model outputs must be integrated into a systematic evaluation process. Ｌ Strengthen expert judgment and institutional guidelines: This process must be supported by expert judgment and institutional guidelines designed to safeguard originality, and must incorporate human oversight to ensure fair and accurate evaluation.

Manifestation_Text: AI algorithmic deficiencies (e.g., hallucinations) and non-compliant usage directly produce low-quality or fraudulent scholarly content. AI can generate deceptive medical articles indistinguishable from human-authored works; it carries hallucination risks when generating references; and AI-generated abstracts are typically of poor quality〞seriously undermining the authenticity and scientific efficacy of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandatory manual verification: Even when automated detectors perform well, manual verification remains indispensable to compensate for algorithmic limitations. Ｌ Incorporate qualitative analysis: Use qualitative analysis as a complement to automated methods to identify the lower scientific quality characteristic of AI-generated texts. Ｍ Adopt a balanced strategy: Implement a balanced strategy to uphold academic authenticity.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI language models has given rise to novel forms of academic misconduct, lowering the perceived cost of misconduct and triggering 'moral disengagement', thereby fundamentally undermining and disrupting both the educational integrity system and macro-level academic governance frameworks. Meanwhile, AI-induced authorship ambiguity challenges traditional conceptions of academic misconduct and accountability mechanisms.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop institutional comprehensive strategies: Academic institutions must adopt comprehensive strategies to address emerging forms of academic misconduct, striking a balance between technological advancement and the preservation of academic integrity. Ｌ Implement transparent policies and human oversight: Establish transparent policies and ensure that the critical role of human educators is not obscured by technology. Ｍ Clarify AI＊s instrumental role: AI should serve solely as a prescreening tool and must never replace expert judgment, to prevent systemic errors.

Manifestation_Text: The high false positive rate of existing AI detection tools leads to unfair academic penalties imposed on authentic student work.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop detection models that balance accuracy and fairness: The authors propose an XLNet-CNN hybrid architecture designed to 'balance accuracy with fairness', eliminating false negatives and optimizing detection logic to prevent authentic student work from being misclassified. Ｌ Provide transparent and adaptable assessment tools: Offer educators 'transparent, practical, and adaptable' solutions to accurately distinguish human-written from AI-generated text, thereby ensuring fairness in academic assessment allocation.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated text evades traditional plagiarism detection systems, posing a systemic threat to the credibility of academic assessments and macro-level academic integrity frameworks.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Systemic upgrading of detection frameworks: Academic institutions are urged to shift from reliance on conventional plagiarism detection tools (e.g., Turnitin) toward specialized AI detection frameworks (e.g., the XLNet-CNN framework proposed in this paper) to keep pace with rapidly evolving large language models (LLMs). Ｌ Responsible integration of AI into education: While upholding the foundational principle of 'preserving academic integrity', institutions should acknowledge and guide the constructive potential of LLMs in education, facilitating the evolution of academic governance systems toward AI-readiness.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated text exhibits intrinsic quality deficiencies, including deep discourse incoherence, semantic/grammatical inconsistencies, and mechanical repetition.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Deploy multidimensional feature capture and filtering mechanisms: Adopt a hybrid architecture (XLNet-CNN) integrating autoregressive (AR) sequence dependency learning with bidirectional contextual modeling to precisely identify quality deficiencies in AI-generated text〞both at the level of local statistical cues (e.g., n-grams) and global semantic structure. Ｌ Strengthen quality assurance in high-risk scenarios: Achieve exceptionally high detection accuracy (e.g., eliminating false negatives) to effectively intercept AI-generated content failing to meet academic quality standards within 'high-stakes academic contexts', thereby safeguarding the authenticity of scholarly output.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic flaws in AI (e.g., hallucination) and non-compliant usage lead to fabricated citations and misleading data, directly compromising the authenticity and scientific quality of academic content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduce human oversight and verification: Emphasize the necessity of human oversight and verification of AI outputs. Ｌ Advocate stricter regulation and responsible AI usage: Call for stricter regulation of AI-generated content and the promotion of responsible AI usage.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated text closely mimics human writing, making it difficult for instructors to distinguish the authenticity of student assignments, thereby raising doubts about students＊ academic integrity and undermining mutual trust and the assessment relationship between teachers and students in educational settings.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Providing actionable detection tools: This paper develops a RoBERTa-CNN hybrid model and an n-gram BOW differential language model to offer educators reliable tools for identifying AI-generated text, thereby restoring trust in academic assessment (Page 3, Contributions). Ｌ Implementing multi-dimensional rigorous review: It is recommended to conduct rigorous examination of writing patterns and consistency, along with potential external validation methods.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of generative AI renders traditional academic anti-cheating systems〞such as text-matching-based plagiarism detection tools〞ineffective, causing systemic disruption to macro-level academic integrity management frameworks and assessment systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Upgrading technological paradigms and infrastructure: A shift is proposed from conventional text-matching approaches to novel detection frameworks grounded in deep learning and statistical probability (e.g., the RoBERTa-CNN continuous-value prediction model and the GTLR statistical detection method presented in this paper) to strengthen the technical defenses of academic governance. Ｌ Advocating macro-level ethical and regulatory policies: In light of ethical concerns surrounding AI-generated content, stricter regulatory policies and responsible AI usage guidelines are called for to prevent systemic academic misconduct (Page 5).

Manifestation_Text: Academic content quality deterioration and authenticity crises arising from AI algorithmic flaws (e.g., fabrication of research) and students＊ diminished intellectual engagement.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Developing and upgrading AIGC detection technologies: The paper comprehensively reviews and proposes multiple technical countermeasures, including watermarking-based approaches (embedding encrypted pseudo-random function signatures into generated text), zero-shot detection, and classifier-based training methods, to identify and intercept low-quality or fabricated AI-generated content. Ｌ Constructing high-quality benchmark datasets: The authors point out current dataset limitations and recommend developing a benchmark dataset covering multiple domains and incorporating ＆modified/anti-detection ChatGPT responses＊, ensuring detection models can handle complex real-world scenarios and enhancing overall detection efficacy.

Manifestation_Text: Systemic disruption caused by AI misuse to authorship systems in academic publishing, mechanisms for attributing legal responsibility, and existing evaluation frameworks within educational institutions.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Revising top-level publishing policies: The paper notes institutional responses from the scientific publishing community〞for instance, prominent journals have ＆strictly banned listing ChatGPT as a co-author＊〞to uphold academic accountability mechanisms and authorship norms. Ｌ Establishing standardized detection and evaluation systems: The authors call for addressing the current fragmentation and lack of unified standards among AIGC detection tools, advocating the development of standardized benchmark datasets that incorporate evasion techniques, thereby enabling fair and consistent evaluation of diverse detection methods and providing robust technical support for academic management systems.

Manifestation_Text: Academic mutual trust between teachers and students〞grounded in authentic learning outcomes〞is eroded, and educational assessment devolves into a ＆cat-and-mouse game＊ pitting AI tools against detection algorithms.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Adapting pedagogical and assessment paradigms: The paper observes that some educators struggle to adjust teaching and assessment practices to deter plagiarism; the authors propose exploring long-term solutions grounded in ＆educational approaches＊ to adapt to evolving academic environments. Ｌ Deploying robust, evasion-resistant detection tools: By integrating underlying generative interventions such as ＆watermarking＊, signatures are embedded that are ＆invisible to end users yet decryptable and verifiable＊, thereby technically eliminating students＊ ability to deceive instructors using paraphrasing tools and assisting teachers in restoring the reliability of assessment.

Manifestation_Text: Bias in AI systems and detection algorithms exacerbates inequities in academic assessment and resource allocation based on race, gender, or cultural background.
Mitigation_Text: The authors recommend establishing a robust AI ethics framework for education, explicitly incorporating the principles of 'inclusiveness' and 'non-discrimination' to ensure equitable access to AI tools and prevent algorithmic bias; they further emphasize the need for a 'human-centered approach' in AI design to safeguard the rights and interests of all student populations.

Manifestation_Text: Current detection models inadequately represent texts produced by non-native English speakers (L2) and across diverse cultural contexts, leading to the marginalization or misclassification of academic outputs from specific linguistic and cultural groups.
Mitigation_Text: To address this issue, the paper mentions employing multi-dimensional linguistic features〞including repetition and readability〞for L2 language detection; the present authors, however, train their model on a large-scale, multi-source dataset (e.g., from Hugging Face and Kaggle) with broader coverage and apply class-weighted cross-entropy loss to mitigate data distribution imbalance, thereby enhancing the model＊s inclusivity and accuracy in representing diverse texts.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic flaws and unreliability in existing AI detection tools compromise the integrity of content authenticity verification in academic assessment.
Mitigation_Text: The authors propose developing more advanced and accurate hybrid detection algorithms〞specifically, the BART-CNN model introduced in this paper〞by integrating automated hyperparameter optimization techniques (e.g., Bayesian optimization, random search) and fine-tuning on large-scale, cross-domain datasets, thereby significantly improving the robustness, generalizability, and classification accuracy of detection models to remedy the quality-of-service deficiencies of current tools.

Manifestation_Text: The proliferation and high fidelity of AI-generated content have inflicted systemic disruption upon macro-level academic integrity systems, the credibility of assessment frameworks, and traditional academic governance mechanisms.
Mitigation_Text: The authors call for 'careful regulation' and 'strong data protection measures', advocating for a comprehensive AI ethics framework grounded in principles such as accountability, transparency, security, and responsibility; they also stress that effective AI governance in education must incorporate 'interdisciplinary perspectives' to ensure that diverse insights shape macro-level academic governance policies and practices.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic flaws and high false-negative rates in AI detection tools undermine academic integrity verification services. These tools exhibit confusion when confronted with 'AI-paraphrased text' and 'AI-generated text embedded with contextual information', fail to provide the kind of 'conclusive evidence' (e.g., source attribution) offered by conventional plagiarism detection software, and cannot trace the authentic origin of AI-generated content〞thereby directly diminishing the efficacy of authenticity verification in academic publishing and assessment.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Focus on core detection capability: AI detectors should concentrate on domains where they can substantiate 'paraphrasing of others＊ work' to prevent misuse of the tools. Ｌ Underlying model improvement: Substantial improvements to AI models are required to validate the effectiveness claims of detection tools, thereby better supporting educators and researchers.

Manifestation_Text: The trust mechanism in academic evaluation〞grounded in 'concrete evidence'〞is undermined by probabilistic black-box algorithms, triggering a crisis of trust between educators/reviewers and students/authors. Since AI detection tools cannot, unlike traditional plagiarism software, pinpoint explicit sources of copied content, authors erroneously flagged as having used AI are unable to exonerate themselves, thereby eroding the mutual trust that binds the academic community.

Chaotic market competition among detection tools, conflicts of interest, and the conceptual ambiguity surrounding the traditional definition of 'originality' exert systemic pressure on macro-level academic governance frameworks and scholarly publishing evaluation systems. The detection domain lacks standardized protocols, and many companies simultaneously offer both AI generation and AI detection services〞acting as both players and referees. Moreover, ethical debates over the equivalence between non-native English speakers＊ use of AI for language polishing and their use of paid language editing services challenge existing academic evaluation standards.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop inclusive policies: Rather than discarding AI tools outright, policies should be formulated to integrate them beneficially into existing knowledge ecosystems. Ｌ Reform standards for evaluating scientific originality: Within the scientific context, greater weight should be assigned to the originality of ideas and research conditions〞not merely linguistic expression〞thereby ethically delineating the appropriate boundaries for non-native English speakers＊ use of AI to improve readability. Ｍ Clarify red lines for academic misconduct: Policies and tool development must explicitly define 'using AI to rewrite others＊ work and claiming it as one＊s own' as blatant cheating, and allocate resources strategically to combat such behavior.

Manifestation_Text: Automated scoring algorithms amplify demographic biases, resulting in inequitable allocation of scoring resources; meanwhile, AI-assisted writing undermines the fundamental fairness of examination scoring.
Mitigation_Text: Develop and deploy high-accuracy, cross-model AI detectors to safeguard fairness. The abstract and conclusion of the cited paper state: 'detectors trained on essays generated from one model can often identify texts from others with high accuracy', indicating that effective detection models〞capable of precisely identifying AI-generated text〞can, in practice, ensure equitable distribution of scoring resources.

Manifestation_Text: Existing automated scoring engines (e.g., e-rater) suffer from severe algorithmic limitations and failures when confronted with AI-generated texts, rendering them incapable of accurately assessing genuine writing proficiency and deep thinking〞leading to distorted evaluation outcomes (e.g., assigning artificially inflated scores to AI-generated texts).
Mitigation_Text: Enhance feature engineering and weight calibration in automated scoring engines. The paper＊s 'Abstract' explicitly proposes concrete system improvements: 'identify areas for improvement, including the development of new features to capture deeper thinking and recalibrating feature weights'.

Manifestation_Text: Learners＊ excessive reliance on AI tools bypasses essential cognitive processes, leading to the deterioration of critical thinking skills and undermining the foundation of mutual trust in educational assessment〞trust rooted in authentic human intellectual output.

The proliferation of AI-generated text has inflicted a systemic, institutional impact on academic integrity and test security in high-stakes standardized examinations (e.g., GRE, TOEFL), threatening the credibility of macro-level educational assessment systems.
Mitigation_Text: Build a robust, cross-model AI-text detection defense. The paper empirically demonstrates〞through RQ3 and the abstract〞that 'detectors trained on essays generated from one model can often identify texts from others with high accuracy, suggesting that effective detection could remain manageable in practice.' It recommends continuously refining detection techniques grounded in linguistic and perplexity-based features to maintain practical, effective deterrence against AI-enabled cheating, thereby safeguarding examination security and the academic integrity system.

Manifestation_Text: The educational trust bond between teachers and students is distorted into a 'courtroom-style' relationship characterized by evidentiary burden and preventive suspicion. The low detectability of AI cheating forces instructors to shift from 'educational guides' to 'policy enforcers,' imposing an excessively high and disproportionate evidentiary burden upon them〞ultimately eroding mutual trust.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Shift policy paradigms from 'punitive' to 'educative': The authors strongly recommend abandoning current policy clauses saturated with legalistic language and punitive measures, and instead integrating educative strategies into academic integrity management. Ｌ Introduce process-oriented and preventive assessment mechanisms: Encourage instructors to adopt early-intervention approaches (e.g., mandating submission of drafts with formative feedback) to prevent misconduct before it occurs, thereby repairing and proactively reinforcing academic interactions between teachers and students. Ｍ Implement the principle of 'proportionality' in sanctions: Institutions are advised to review existing policies to ensure that the severity of academic integrity sanctions corresponds proportionally to the actual seriousness of student violations, avoiding irreversible damage to the foundational trust between teachers and students caused by excessive punishment.

Manifestation_Text: Macro-level academic governance systems and policy frameworks exhibit severe lag and systemic failure in responding to generative AI, placing higher education institutions＊ academic integrity governance systems at risk of collapse.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop agile and adaptive policy frameworks: Academic institutions are urged to abandon blunt, blanket bans and instead formulate agile policies capable of rapidly evolving alongside AI technological advancements, while acknowledging ethical distinctions across diverse AI application contexts. Ｌ Establish comprehensive institutional support apparatuses: Emphasize the necessity of providing frontline instructors with adequate institution-level support〞including optimized detection tools and clear operational guidelines〞to empower effective policy implementation and prevent the unilateral transfer of macro-level institutional enforcement costs onto individual instructors. Ｍ Integrate a multi-dimensional, holistic governance framework: Advocate for a balanced framework that synthesizes educational strategies, technical detection tools, and cultural sensitivities to systematically reshape and sustain academic integrity standards in the AI era.

Manifestation_Text: Generative AI tools (GAITs) are widely exploited for academic cheating and contract cheating, leading to devaluation of higher education institutions＊ academic assessment systems, compromised credentialing validity, and triggering systemic trust crises and institutional reputational damage.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Refocus governance priorities: Educational institutions should shift emphasis away from a narrow 'parochial emphasis on AI detection' toward 'fostering an understanding of the motivations driving such misconduct' (p. 3). Ｌ Develop targeted institutional strategies: Implement targeted institutional strategies to address the multiple factors that increase students＊ intent to cheat (Abstract section). Ｍ Advance authentic assessment reform: Apply research findings to educational policy and intervention design to promote the development and implementation of 'authentic assessment' in higher education during the AI era (Discussion section, p. 12).

Manifestation_Text: Students＊ non-compliant use of GAITs〞directly substituting their own writing and intellectual contributions, and even misrepresenting authorship〞compromises the originality and authenticity of academic assessment outputs (e.g., essays, reports), thereby diminishing the ultimate efficacy of academic content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Clarify usage boundaries and evolve policies: Educational institutions must continually refine institutional policies to help students clearly distinguish between 'permissible supportive use' and 'prohibited misuse constituting academic misconduct' (p. 4). Ｌ Promote responsible and transparent AI use: Recognizing that detection alone is insufficient to safeguard academic integrity, institutions must transition toward promoting 'responsible and transparent use' of AI and seamlessly integrate this principle into higher education (pp. 3 and Abstract).

Manifestation_Text: The convenient generative capability of AI tools, coupled with their non-compliant use, directly triggers plagiarism, academic fraud, and loss of originality, thereby diminishing the final quality and authenticity of academic content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Conduct institution-wide ethics and skills training: Academic institutions should provide training on the ethical and effective use of AI tools to ensure they support〞rather than undermine〞academic integrity (Abstract 每 Practical implications; Page 6). Ｌ Establish a clear ethical framework: The use of AI tools must be accompanied by a well-defined ethical framework and guiding policies to regulate the quality and compliance of generated content (Page 2).

Manifestation_Text: The proliferation of AI-generated content has imposed broad institutional impacts on traditional academic values, academic integrity systems, and macro-level university management policies, compelling educational institutions to adopt defensive restrictive measures.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop and implement clear macro-level policies: Academic institutions must formulate explicit policies and ethical frameworks to govern AI use and reconstruct academic integrity systems (Page 2). Ｌ Organizational-level stress management and goal orientation: Organizations should focus on stress management initiatives and foster balanced approaches to individual goal setting, thereby mitigating the potential negative ethical impacts of ChatGPT adoption at the systemic management level (Abstract 每 Practical implications).

Manifestation_Text: The disproportionate false positives produced by AI detection tools unjustly compromise the fairness of academic assessment for neurodivergent students. In academic integrity reviews, erroneous determinations made by AI detection systems place neurodivergent students (e.g., those with ADHD or AuDHD) and non-native English speakers at risk of being falsely accused of academic misconduct, resulting in algorithmic injustice and substantive harm in the allocation of grades, academic reputation, and other resources.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Restrict technological use and provide alternatives: There is a call to restrict the use of monitoring and detection technologies in online learning environments and to offer alternative examination and assessment methods. Ｌ Shift toward inclusive assessment: Advocates propose replacing punitive technological surveillance with inclusive assessment practices.

Manifestation_Text: AI detection algorithms harbor inherent biases and misrepresentations regarding the expressive styles of specific cognitive and linguistic groups. Relying on statistical features such as 'perplexity' and 'burstiness', AI detection tools erroneously characterize the distinctive writing styles and cognitive expressions of neurodivergent individuals (e.g., those on the autism spectrum) and non-native English speakers as 'machine-generated' or 'academically dishonest', thereby marginalizing non-standard forms of knowledge expression within academic norms.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduce epistemic plurality: In the abstract and conclusion, the authors propose adopting this framework〞not to enforce standardized knowledge expression, but to recognize that diverse cognitive styles enrich, rather than impair, academic quality. Ｌ Paradigm shift in policy: Advance academic integrity policies from a compliance-based model toward an inclusive approach that honours neurodiversity.

Manifestation_Text: Inherent algorithmic flaws in AI detection tools severely undermine their efficacy as instruments for academic integrity review. Despite claims of high accuracy, these tools heavily rely on unreliable statistical metrics, rendering them highly prone to false positives and incapable of accurately distinguishing between human-authored text〞particularly that of neurodivergent individuals〞and AI-generated text, thereby directly compromising the authenticity and accuracy of academic evaluation.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mitigate risks associated with low-quality technologies: The article recommends 'limit[ing] the use of surveillance technologies' and 'offer[ing] alternative examination methods'〞that is, shifting assessment modalities to avoid the misjudgment risks posed by flawed AI detection tools, rather than placing blind trust in these defective technological systems.

Manifestation_Text: The integration of AI monitoring and detection technologies undermines the trust bond between teachers and students and alienates the educational environment. Remote proctoring and AI detection tools are deployed as 'solutions' to prevent academic misconduct, yet they inherently construct a surveillance environment that exacerbates the trust deficit between educators and learners, imposes psychological pressure on neurodiverse students, and erodes the collaborative educational relationship grounded in human intelligence and dignity.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ A fundamental shift in educational philosophy: advocating a transition from punitive, competition-driven approaches toward pedagogical practices centered on human rights, dignity, and inclusion. Ｌ Establishing trust-based practices: actively promoting 'human-centred, trust-based, and accessible pedagogical practices' to restore the teacher每student trust relationship damaged by surveillance technologies.

Manifestation_Text: Current macro-level academic integrity governance frameworks constitute systemic exclusion and ableism against neurodiverse populations. Existing academic integrity policies〞grounded in compliance and punishment〞as well as standardized assessment designs and mandatory monitoring technologies, systematically overlook the specific needs of neurodiverse students, contradicting the overarching societal goal of educational equity and thereby undermining the legitimacy of academic governance systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Restructuring the academic integrity framework: reconceptualizing academic integrity through the lens of 'epistemic plurality', moving beyond traditional punitive approaches. Ｌ Systemic policy evolution: calling for a shift in academic integrity from 'compliance-based models' to 'inclusive approaches', recognizing neurodiversity as a form of human variation that enriches the academic community〞not as a deficit requiring correction.

Manifestation_Text: Students conceal their use of AI and submit AI-generated text as original personal work (akin to contract cheating or plagiarism), blurring the boundary between human and machine contributions and obscuring students＊ authentic capabilities〞thereby directly compromising the authenticity of academic assessment content and diminishing the ultimate quality of educational outcomes.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Updating definitions of plagiarism and academic integrity: institutions must explicitly incorporate AI-generated content into definitions of plagiarism and provide concrete guidelines for proper attribution. Ｌ Optimizing declaration mechanism design: simplifying the declaration process to allow students to detail how AI assisted them at specific stages of their workflow, rather than merely checking a checkbox laden with negative connotations. Ｍ Delivering ethics and competency education: educating students about the ethical implications of AI-assisted work and clarifying acceptable boundaries and illustrative examples of AI use.

Manifestation_Text: The covert use of AI and punitive declaration mechanisms erode academic trust between teachers and students. Students perceive AI declarations as 'admission-of-plagiarism traps', fearing unfair grading bias; meanwhile, instructors fall into suspicion about whether students＊ actual intellectual engagement can be accurately assessed〞leading to the alienation of the collaborative, honest, and transparent teacher每student relationship essential for evaluation and academic partnership.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establishing a 'bidirectional transparency' mechanism: institutions must transparently communicate to students the evaluation criteria for AI declarations and the specific consequences of non-compliance, thereby dispelling the fear that 'declaration equals confession'. Ｌ Cultivating a culture of trust and dialogue: facilitating open discussions between teachers and students about AI use, setting clear expectations, and shifting the policy focus from 'punitive deterrence' to 'supportive guidance'. Ｍ Standardizing faculty implementation: ensuring consistent and equitable enforcement of declaration policies across all teaching staff to eliminate grading bias and trust crises arising from individual instructor preferences.

Manifestation_Text: The proliferation of generative AI〞and a non-compliance rate among students as high as 74%〞has delivered a systemic shock to higher education＊s macro-level academic governance frameworks, assessment systems, and academic integrity norms. Peer pressure has normalized and even rendered AI use 'mandatory', resulting in the institutional failure of traditional concepts of authorship, originality, and written assessment paradigms.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Developing clear and consistent macro-level policies: policymakers must issue explicit, coherent, and evidence-informed guidelines on AI use to eliminate discrepancies in implementation across courses and instructors. Ｌ Adapting academic assessment practices: institutions must respond to AI＊s disruption of conventional written assignment paradigms by revising assessment practices to accommodate technological change while ensuring compliance. Ｍ Reframing the institutional context of declarations: decoupling AI declarations from the traditional 'plagiarism warning' context to eliminate associated stigma and suspicion, and systematically redefining academic integrity norms.

Manifestation_Text: AI-driven automation of content creation and the deterioration of authenticity in academic output. Students＊ excessive reliance on generative AI (GenAI) to automatically produce complex academic content makes it increasingly difficult to distinguish AI-generated material from human-authored original work, thereby undermining independent critical thinking and analytical reasoning abilities〞and directly compromising the authenticity and scientific quality of academic learning outcomes.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Curriculum and pedagogical restructuring: Integrate GenAI ethics into teacher training and curriculum design, and redesign assessment practices to foster critical thinking and self-regulated learning. Ｌ Enhancing AI literacy: Deliver critical AI literacy courses and evidence-informed discussions on AI ethics to equip students with rigorous skills for verifying GenAI outputs. Ｍ Technological support and disclosure: Implement AI-use disclosure policies and AI-detection mechanisms as supportive tools.

Manifestation_Text: Alienation of the pedagogical interaction bond and intellectual collaboration relationship between students and instructors. Overreliance on GenAI as a purely computational tool may lead students into passive learning, eroding the ＆meaningful student-instructor interactions＊ that constitute the core of traditional education〞interactions grounded in human intellectual collaboration〞and thereby placing pedagogical trust and interpersonal collaborative bonds at risk of being replaced or marginalized by algorithmic mediation.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Promoting an AI每human co-learning model: Adopt the concept of ＆living intelligence＊ to develop an AI每human collaborative learning model aligned with constructivist and sociocultural learning theories, positioning AI as a collaborative cognitive agent. Ｌ Conducting pilot evaluations: Higher education institutions (HEIs) must implement pilot studies to assess whether AI-driven assessment successfully fosters independent learning and meaningful interpersonal teaching interactions while safeguarding intellectual authenticity.

Manifestation_Text: The failure of traditional academic assessment systems and systemic lag in institutional governance frameworks. GenAI is reshaping knowledge production and assessment strategies, rendering conventional assessment models〞reliant on written assignments and examinations〞vulnerable to AI-generated content. Concurrently, HEIs＊ responses to GenAI tend to be reactive rather than strategic, lacking clear guidelines and consensus on AI use, thereby subjecting macro-level academic integrity governance systems to structural disruption.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establishing transparent and adaptive governance frameworks: Institutions should develop transparent, adaptive, and discipline-responsive governance frameworks and establish GenAI ethics committees. Ｌ Cross-departmental policy coordination and standardization: Integrate GenAI ethics into curriculum design, faculty development, and cross-departmental policy frameworks; standardize academic integrity frameworks based on empirical evidence to align institutional strategy with AI innovation. Ｍ Developer每educator collaboration: Foster collaboration between AI developers and educators to enhance algorithmic transparency and establish equitable GenAI governance mechanisms.

Manifestation_Text: Macro-level academic governance systems〞particularly academic integrity policies〞lack regulatory provisions and practical guidance regarding the misuse of generative AI, resulting in severe institutional lag and policy gaps that threaten the credibility of higher education qualifications and institutional reputations.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Refining policy details and definitions (at the Detail level): Policymakers must explicitly incorporate specific definitions, usage boundaries, and guiding principles for generative AI and contract cheating into academic integrity policies to eliminate regulatory gaps. Ｌ Advancing an educational paradigm shift (at the Approach level): Move beyond the currently dominant (80%) punitive approach by integrating educational strategies〞embedding AI ethics into academic integrity culture building rather than relying solely on post-hoc sanctions. Ｍ Strengthening shared responsibility and institutional support (at the Responsibility & Support level): Broaden the policy＊s target audience beyond students alone to include faculty and administrative leadership across the entire educational community, and provide institution-level educational resources to guide students and instructors in conducting teaching and research with integrity in the AI era.

Manifestation_Text: Unethical use of generative AI in assignments and assessments distorts authentic representations of student academic performance, hindering educators＊ ability to accurately evaluate individuals＊ genuine learning outcomes〞and thereby directly diminishing the quality and authenticity of academic assessment and educational services.
Algorithmic systems may introduce structural inequities through biased or uneven allocation of opportunities, resulting in distributive harms to academic resources or learning opportunities.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Enhance AI literacy to help students understand how these tools operate and their limitations; Ｌ Implement inclusive AI policies to ensure equitable access.

Manifestation_Text: AI systems replicate social and cultural inequities present in their training data, producing biased outputs that may marginalize specific student groups; language models reproduce stereotypes and narrow demographic representations.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Embed bias awareness and ethical AI training into curricula; Ｌ Strengthen inclusive training practices and governance mechanisms.

Manifestation_Text: Factual inaccuracies (hallucinations) generated by AI raise concerns about reliability and epistemic trust; overreliance on AI undermines the development of critical thinking, reduces meaningful cognitive engagement, leads to surface-level learning, and directly diminishes the ultimate quality of academic output.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Guide trust calibration and verification workflows to support responsible use; Ｌ Position AI as a complement〞not a substitute〞for critical thinking; Ｍ Implement educational interventions emphasizing clear citation norms and structured guidance.

Manifestation_Text: Overreliance on generative AI reduces human interaction, thereby weakening the bonds of mutual trust and collaboration grounded in human intellectual exchange between instructors and students or among students within educational settings.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Reform assessment design to balance AI use with academic integrity〞for example, by introducing or strengthening oral/authentic assessments (see recommendations under 'Future Research'); Ｌ Guide trust calibration in teaching policies to reconfigure boundaries of trust between humans and machines, as well as among humans.

Manifestation_Text: The complexity of ChatGPT blurs traditional boundaries of authorship and originality, challenging existing academic norms; simultaneously, policy frameworks across academic institutions are fragmented, inconsistent, and still evolving, placing macro-level academic governance systems, assessment practices, and academic integrity regulations at risk of obsolescence.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop and implement inclusive and unified AI policies; Ｌ Redefine authorship standards and embed ethical guidance into teaching practice; Ｍ Conduct comprehensive, evidence-based reviews and revisions of institutional policies, assessment practices, and academic integrity regulations.

Manifestation_Text: The proliferation of AI-generated peer review reports has led to a decline in review quality, while the surge in AI-related submissions has resulted in 'premature generalization and insufficient theorization', thereby diminishing the scientific and conceptual quality of published papers.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduce the RAISE reporting framework: Implement the 'Reporting AI in Scholarship for Education (RAISE)' framework〞a structured 30-item checklist requiring authors to explicitly report AI interventions, research design, and contextual details〞to enhance interpretability and validity of AI-integrated research. Ｌ Enforce rigorous publication standards and conceptual depth: Explicitly state that 'novelty alone is insufficient for publication' and mandate that AI-related studies demonstrate conceptual depth, methodological transparency, and critical engagement. Ｍ Expand editorial capacity to safeguard review quality: Recruit associate editors to effectively manage peer review processes, synthesize feedback, and ensure consistency and quality in editorial decision-making.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI poses systemic challenges to academic ethics governance systems and the foundational principles of publishing equity〞including researchers＊ evasion of ethical review in AI studies involving human participants, and the systemic threats posed by AI-generated review reports and surging submission volumes to journal quality and fairness thresholds.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Institutionalize mandatory ethics reporting and intervention: Integrate a mandatory ethics declaration field into the submission system, requiring transparent documentation of ethical approval and informed consent procedures, aligned with SAGE＊s Publishing Ethics Policy; apply corrective and educational editorial interventions for perfunctory or incomplete responses. Ｌ Institutionalize the Ethics and Risk Matrix: Adopt the 'Ethics and Risk Matrix' from the RAISE framework as a standardized requirement for supplementary materials or appendices, embedding systematic risk assessment into the publication process for AI-related research. Ｍ Structural adaptive management: Strengthen institutional resilience in peer review management through structural adjustments〞such as hiring associate editors〞to uphold fairness and sustainability of the scholarly evaluation system amid escalating submission volumes.

Manifestation_Text: Well-funded institutions monopolize algorithmic rankings on AI-powered scientific discovery platforms (e.g., Elicit.com) by purchasing advertising slots, resulting in diminished visibility and inequitable distribution of academic resources for early-career researchers and scholars in underfunded disciplines.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Progressive bidding models: Offer up to 90% fee discounts for early-career researchers and scholars based in low-income economies. Ｌ Redistributive financing: Impose a modest levy (capped at 5% of advertising revenue) on high-value bids to fund equity-oriented initiatives.

Manifestation_Text: AI advertising algorithms amplify the voices of dominant market or academic actors, leading to homogenization, marginalization, or erasure of knowledge systems from specific disciplines (e.g., humanities) or marginalized communities within scientific discovery platforms.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Visibility reserves: Mandate reservation of a fixed proportion (e.g., 30%) of advertising slots for humanities or underfunded disciplines. Ｌ Visibility Gini Coefficient audit: Quantify and audit advertising allocation inequality across institution types, geographic regions, and disciplines using the Gini coefficient, ensuring it remains below a target threshold (e.g., <0.3).

Manifestation_Text: AI systems, when generating abstracts and synthesizing scientific content, conflate advertising-driven visibility with academic rigor〞causing 'signal pollution'〞and may even treat unreviewed blogs or fabricated papers equivalently to high-quality, peer-reviewed publications, directly undermining the ultimate efficacy and scientific integrity of scholarly publishing outputs.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Scholarly relevance thresholds: Restrict eligibility for advertising promotion exclusively to publications meeting academic benchmarks〞such as peer-reviewed status and minimum citation counts. Ｌ Rigor-weighted promotion algorithm: Assign substantially greater weight to methodological rigor (汐) than to financial bidding (汕) in ranking scores〞for example: Final_Score = (0.7 ℅ Rigor_Index) + (0.3 ℅ Log_Scaled_Bid). Ｍ Dissonance threshold: Cap the proportion of promoted content in single-page search results (e.g., ≒20%) to prevent cognitive overload and signal conflict.

Manifestation_Text: Introducing market-based real-time bidding layers directly into the algorithmic ranking of AI-powered scientific discovery platforms disrupts the traditional academic evaluation and governance system〞grounded in peer review, journal reputation, and citation accumulation〞replacing its 'slow signals' with commercialized speed. This exerts a systemic shock to the overall credibility of science and the macro-level knowledge dissemination infrastructure.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Algorithmic Segregation: Technically isolate advertising ranking logic from organic relevance algorithms to prevent commercial bias from infiltrating scientific ranking. Ｌ Third-Party Independent Auditing: Academic consortia (e.g., COPE, FORCE11, COS) conduct behavioral input-output audits to verify algorithmic objectivity. Ｍ Algorithmic Impact Statements: Platforms must publish annual statements disclosing metrics such as the proportion of results exceeding discordance thresholds and the visibility Gini coefficient, establishing macro-level accountability mechanisms. Ｎ Labeled Disclosures: Implement high-contrast visual labels (e.g., 'Sponsored') to explicitly distinguish paid from organic results, thereby reconstructing system-wide transparency norms.

Manifestation_Text: Deficiencies in AI algorithms (e.g., hallucinations) and non-compliant usage (e.g., using AI to generate core scholarly contributions or fabricating evidence with synthetic media) directly undermine the authenticity, rigor, and scientific quality of scholarly publishing content.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Strict Boundary Definition for Use: Generative AI (GenAI) is permitted only for auxiliary tasks (e.g., language editing, formatting checks); its use to generate substantive scholarly contributions〞such as core arguments, literature synthesis, or interpretation of results〞is strictly prohibited. Ｌ Mandatory Methodological Reflection and Robustness Checks: When GenAI is employed in the research process, authors must reflect on its influence on decision-making and implement rigorous validity safeguards〞including human verification, audit trails, triangulation, or inter-rater reliability assessments. Ｍ Transparent Labeling and Use Restrictions for Synthetic Media: AI-generated or AI-modified media must be explicitly and transparently labeled, and their use to disguise or distort empirical evidence is strictly forbidden.

Manifestation_Text: Covert use of AI erodes the trust bond among members of the scholarly community (authors, reviewers, editors)〞a bond historically grounded in human intellect, confidentiality, and accountability〞thereby fostering unwarranted suspicion and threatening the confidentiality of peer review.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandatory and Specific Disclosure Mechanisms: Authors must detail GenAI usage (including tools, versions, purposes, etc.) in the acknowledgments and cover letter, rendering responsibility 'legible'〞thus shielding authors from vague integrity accusations and alleviating reviewers＊ suspicions. Ｌ Upholding the Central Role and Confidentiality Boundary of Humans in Peer Review: Reviewers and editors are strictly prohibited from uploading submitted manuscripts or review reports to external, unregulated GenAI tools, safeguarding author privacy and preserving the confidentiality and trustworthiness of the review process. Ｍ Non-Transferable Accountability: Named human authors bear full responsibility for the scholarly record; GenAI cannot be listed as an author, ensuring that interpersonal accountability is not dissolved by algorithmic intermediation.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI and the absence of unified governance have given rise to an 'AI-generated knowledge bubble', causing widespread systemic disruption to macro-level journal publishing standards consistency, academic governance frameworks, and the overall credibility of science.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish Unified and Enforceable Publishing Standards and Policies: Journals must adopt explicit 'Six Commitments' to fill policy vacuums, ensuring clarity, consistency, and defensibility across submission, review, and publication processes〞and preventing AI from becoming an ungoverned default infrastructure. Ｌ Advance a Paradigm Shift in Governance: In a 'post-detection' scholarly environment, shift academic integrity management from 'artefact-based inference' to 'accountability-based transparency', treating transparency as the minimum condition for sustaining systemic trust. Ｍ Reaffirm Human Epistemological and Ethical Commitments: Recast authorship as an epistemological and ethical commitment〞not merely a measure of output〞to prevent the macro-level scholarly evaluation system from being distorted by raw AI-generation volume.

Manifestation_Text: AI algorithmic deficiencies (e.g., hallucinations) and non-compliant usage degrade scholarly content quality and compromise peer review effectiveness. Specific manifestations include: AI-generated text masking methodological flaws through linguistic polishing (Hidden methodological errors); AI tools generating plausible yet hallucinated fabricated data, images, or references (Undetected fabrication); and synthetic data or AI-drafted content bypassing standard peer review, while reviewers struggle to distinguish AI- from human-authored content (Reviewer detection challenges).
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implement Structured AI Auditing and Reporting Frameworks: Submitted manuscripts must undergo structured AI-use auditing aligned with frameworks such as CONSORT-AI and SPIRIT-AI. Ｌ Mandate Methodological Transparency: The methods section must explicitly describe how the AI system was trained, validated, and audited, ensuring reproducibility. Ｍ Introduce Transparency Badges: Journals adopt measures such as 'Reproducibility Badges' to incentivize researchers who share open data or code.

Manifestation_Text: The delegation of human intellectual agency and the blurring of academic accountability/authorship. Specifically: (1) Overreliance on AI for critical thinking and writing (deskilling and overreliance), leading to the erosion of domain-specific expertise; (2) AI rewriting or direct extraction of content blurs authorship (blur authorship), raising concerns about originality and complicating intellectual property rights and academic accountability.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish AI＊s assistive role: Emphasize that AI must remain strictly assistive〞complementing, not replacing, human expertise. Ｌ Reinforce ultimate author accountability: Authors must retain full accountability for all academic claims, ensuring complete understanding and endorsement of their work; responsibility must not be delegated to AI.

Manifestation_Text: Systemic proliferation of AI misuse and an institutional crisis of scientific credibility at large. Unlike isolated human errors, AI flaws are systemic, scalable, and difficult to detect. A flood of AI-generated submissions overwhelms journals, while ambiguous guidelines lead to underreporting of AI contributions (lack of transparency), eroding scholarly confidence in published work and inflicting broad damage on the macro-level scientific trust ecosystem.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implement a no-penalty mandatory transparency disclosure mechanism: Journals should adopt mandatory transparency policies encouraging authors to disclose AI tools used〞without penalizing researchers or biasing editorial decisions. Ｌ Global alliance每led coordinated governance: Standardize ethics training in scholarly publishing through global alliances such as the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) to harmonize international ethical standards. Ｍ Reform academic evaluation and incentive systems: Align with initiatives such as the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA); academic systems must shift reward structures to prioritize methodological rigor, mentorship excellence, and transparent practices〞rather than publication volume〞in funding and promotion decisions, thereby eliminating systemic incentives for AI misuse.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated academic text lowers the barrier to academic misconduct, enabling the production of seemingly credible papers without substantial human intellectual input〞thereby exacerbating risks of plagiarism and fraud. Simultaneously, models may generate inaccurate or misleading academic citations (＆hallucinated citations＊), directly undermining the authenticity, originality, and ultimate scientific quality of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandate structured documentation and transparency: Academic publishing entities (e.g., top-tier journals and conference program committees) should revise submission guidelines to require structured documentation (e.g., dataset datasheets, model cards) and reproducibility checklists, revealing potential biases and limitations inherent in AI-generated content. Ｌ Interdisciplinary ethics and impact review: Introduce interdisciplinary review panels〞including experts from humanities and social sciences〞to systematically assess both technical capabilities and ethical consistency, as well as potential societal consequences, thereby elevating quality standards for AI research. Ｍ Risk warning and stakeholder communication: Developers must prominently display, in plain non-technical language on paper and model release pages, explicit explanations of safety assumptions, scope of applicability, and potential misuse risks〞to prevent user misinterpretation.

Manifestation_Text: AI-generated content triggers severe ambiguity and accountability vacuums in responsibility attribution, causing fundamental mismatches in existing academic authorship definitions, copyright assignment, and scholarly governance frameworks. Concurrently, the current peer-review system reveals institutional limitations when evaluating cutting-edge AI research with broad societal implications〞due to reviewers＊ narrow, predominantly technical backgrounds〞potentially undermining the overall scientific credibility and macro-level evaluation framework for AI research over time.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Clarify legal rights and responsibility frameworks: National legislatures and judicial systems should amend copyright laws and related regulations to explicitly define the copyright status and liability chain for AI-generated content, delineate the boundaries of ＆fair use＊ for training data, and establish developers＊ primary responsibility for data compliance and users＊ ultimate responsibility for output content. Ｌ Build an independent verification and auditing ecosystem: Led by national standardization bodies (e.g., NIST) and professional associations (e.g., ACM, IEEE), develop benchmarking and auditing standard frameworks to conduct independent third-party performance and security audits of major model releases〞thereby building community trust. Ｍ Strengthen ethics and impact assessment mechanisms: Academic publishers and funding agencies should establish standing interdisciplinary review expert pools (including legal, ethical, and sociological experts) and mandate inclusion of societal impact assessments in final project reports.

Manifestation_Text: The widespread adoption of generative AI introduces new ambiguity and institutional disruption to traditional authorship definitions and accountability mechanisms, giving rise to novel forms of academic misconduct and rendering static, conventional publishing ethics checklists obsolete and ineffective.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Build a dynamic, scalable, versioned governance system: Publishing ethics must evolve beyond static checklists into a ＆living governance system＊, calibrated and iterated via formalized consensus mechanisms (e.g., Delphi protocols) to continuously integrate emerging AI-related ethical issues. Ｌ Clarify policy boundaries and accountability principles for AI use: Journals must explicitly define, in their policies, disclosure requirements for AI assistance (what must be disclosed), prohibited behaviors (what is prohibited), and accountability allocation methods (how accountability is assigned), aligning with the latest updates from authoritative international guidelines such as those of the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE). Ｍ Anchor human翋极孮�� as the foundational principle: Embed accountability principles explicitly within standards systems, stipulating that AI tools cannot satisfy authorship criteria and that ultimate responsibility must always rest with human authors and reviewers.

Manifestation_Text: Non-compliant use of AI tools〞such as uploading unpublished, confidential manuscripts to public or unapproved AI models〞severely undermines the confidentiality-based trust bond within the academic community that is grounded in peer review; simultaneously, deep AI involvement may lead human authors and reviewers to blindly cede intellectual agency, thereby alienating the interpersonal academic trust relationship.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish strict confidentiality constraints and a negative list: explicitly prohibit, within the publishing workflow, the uploading of confidential manuscript content or review materials to unapproved or non-compliant AI tools, thereby restoring and safeguarding the confidentiality bond underpinning peer review. Ｌ Implement audit trails for AI-assisted editorial behavior: under the Advanced standard element, require audit trails for 'AI-assisted editorial actions' to ensure verifiability of interpersonal trust and operational transparency throughout editing and reviewing processes. Ｍ Strengthen accountability mechanisms for human intellectual agents: mandate, within workflow elements, the principle of human fallback〞clearly stipulating that, regardless of the extent of AI assistance in writing or reviewing, final academic responsibility and intellectual attribution must〞and can only〞rest with humans, preventing blind delegation of accountability to algorithms.

Manifestation_Text: AI-assisted writing and reviewing may introduce covert academic misconduct, data fabrication, or quality deficiencies; yet traditional journals〞constrained by limited resources or abstract policies〞lack effective technical screening and workflow interception mechanisms, directly diminishing the ultimate efficacy, authenticity, and scientific quality of scholarly publications.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Translate AI ethics requirements into auditable workflow control points: reject abstract principle statements and instead adopt an operational syntax of 'Actor每Action每Evidence每Escalation', embedding AI disclosure and review requirements directly into submission systems, editorial checklists, and specific workflow events (e.g., screening, revision) to realize actionable quality control. Ｌ Introduce advanced technical detection and forensic tools: encourage resource-capable journals to adopt Advanced standard elements〞for example, deploying a 'structured image forensics workflow'〞to technologically identify and intercept AI-generated false data or images, thereby safeguarding publication quality. Ｍ Enforce mandatory AI-assistance disclosure and transparency review: institutionalize AI usage disclosure as a core workflow element, requiring authors and reviewers to transparently declare the specific contributions of AI in manuscript preparation or analysis, enabling editors and readers to accurately assess the scientific reliability of the content.

Manifestation_Text: Narrative reviews generated by AI exhibit severe methodological and substantive flaws, leading to deterioration in scholarly publishing quality. Specific manifestations include: complete absence of conceptual or methodological foundations; citation of irrelevant literature; systematic use of hyperbolic language; superficial or disjointed content; and even direct retention of AI prompts within the text.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Define red lines for AI use and mandate disclosure: explicitly authorize AI tools solely for language polishing and content organization support〞and require full disclosure〞while strictly prohibiting their use in data generation, analysis, and synthesis tasks demanding human critical thinking and judgment. Ｌ Trigger high-level early review: for manuscripts exhibiting hallmark features of AI generation (e.g., lack of methodological grounding, irrelevant citations, hyperbolic language, retained prompts), initiate higher editorial scrutiny and early investigation. Ｍ Adhere to publisher-level macro guidelines: guide authors to consult and comply with Elsevier＊s official policy on generative AI use.

Manifestation_Text: The proliferation of AI-written papers under pressure for 'rapid publication' inflicts systemic damage on academic integrity systems and scientific credibility. A large number of unscrupulous authors exploit AI to mass-generate papers for submission, exacerbating the scientific community＊s 'replicability crisis' and 'validity crisis' in evidence synthesis, thereby eroding the foundational trust upon which the scholarly publishing system depends.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Implement deterrent new editorial policies: introduce and rigorously enforce new editorial policies〞particularly for narrative reviews〞to raise submission thresholds and deter authors with questionable integrity from submitting AI-generated papers. Ｌ Advocate industry-wide strengthening of editorial stewardship: call upon other journals to widely adopt specialist editorial policies specifically designed to address the 'validity crisis' in evidence-synthesis publications, collectively rebuilding scientific credibility and trust. Ｍ Continuously optimize editorial workflows: commit at the journal level to ongoing optimization of editorial workflows and enhancement of standards development, to adapt to evolving evidence-synthesis practices and the macro-level systemic challenges posed by AI technologies.

Manifestation_Text: Algorithmic flaws and biases inherent in AI detection tools result in unfair academic evaluation of non-native English-speaking students.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Ethical use of detection tools: within the 'digital infrastructure' component of the ecosystem model proposed by authors, emphasize the ethical use of detection tools〞avoiding uncritical reliance. Ｌ Investment in infrastructure and capacity building: in the 'Implications' section, call for national- and institutional-level investment in digital infrastructure and faculty capacity development to bridge the technological divide.

Manifestation_Text: The 'hallucinations' of AI algorithms and the homogenization of generated content directly degrade the scientific quality and authenticity of academic work.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Assessment Design Reform: Propose the adoption of authentic, process-based, and 'AI-resilient' assessment designs within the ecosystem model, alongside the integration of review and calibration practices. Ｌ Embedding Academic and AI Literacy Education: Integrate academic writing instruction and ethical AI literacy education into curricula, clearly defining boundaries for permitted, conditionally permitted, and prohibited AI use to enhance academic output quality at its source.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of AI tools intertwines with local cultural dynamics, blurring the boundary between academic collaboration and cheating, and exacerbating interpersonal trust crises and reporting dilemmas between students and faculty.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Culturally Sensitive Peer Education: Within the 'Student Engagement and Culture' component of the ecosystem model, recommend involving student representatives in integrity governance and implementing peer education and culturally sensitive awareness-raising activities. Ｌ Institutional Safeguards to Reduce Interpersonal Strategic Behavior: Mitigate faculty members＊ interpersonal and emotional pressures when addressing AI misconduct by establishing clear, coherent policies and ensuring consistent, fair enforcement〞thereby enhancing institutional certainty.

Manifestation_Text: The proliferation of AI-enabled academic misconduct exposes fragmentation and governance vacuums in macro-level academic management systems, undermining the overall credibility and quality objectives (SDG 4) of higher education systems.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Development of a National Framework: At the national policy level, advocate for the development of a national academic integrity framework and dedicated AI governance guidelines.
