Ｌ Institution-Level Cross-Departmental Coordination: Recommend that institutions establish cross-departmental integrity committees or offices to review and harmonize policies, embedding integrity into quality assurance and strategic planning. Ｍ Construction of an Ecosystem Model: Fully implement the 'Academic Integrity Ecosystem Model', comprising seven core components〞governance, assessment, literacy, student culture, faculty development, infrastructure, and AI ethics〞to achieve whole-institution, systemic integrity governance.

Manifestation_Text: Although GenAI-generated content appears fluent on the surface, it contains significant inaccuracies ('hallucinations'); if adopted without rigorous verification, it directly undermines the authenticity and scientific quality of academic outputs.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Cultivating Critical AI Literacy (CAIL): Through the 'Analyzing GenAI Tools and Their Outputs' skill in the CAIL framework, educate users to recognize AI＊s intrinsic system functionalities, limitations of training data, and potential errors. Ｌ Strengthening Critical Thinking Practices: Within the 'Creating New Content' skill dimension, mandate practices that foster critical engagement with AI-generated content, ensuring human oversight and quality control over final outputs.

Manifestation_Text: The underlying training data and algorithms of GenAI inherit and amplify pre-existing inequalities and biases embedded in human-authored texts, thereby suppressing and erasing the representation of already marginalized populations and communities during knowledge production.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Assessing Socio-Political Impacts: Incorporate a dedicated skill in the CAIL framework requiring users to recognize broad societal issues related to AI (e.g., data poverty) and understand how AI shapes social structures and access to resources. Ｌ Integrating Critical Pedagogy: Drawing on Freirean theory, position CAIL as an ethically grounded approach to integrating GenAI〞actively confronting and deconstructing entrenched biases within educational systems to advance more equitable, human-centered knowledge creation.

Manifestation_Text: The explosive growth of Generative AI (GenAI) tools has outpaced the adaptive capacity of existing ethical and regulatory frameworks, resulting in systemic failure and a crisis of trust in traditional academic integrity policies, assessment systems, and governance structures within higher education institutions.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Develop a multi-dimensional AI ecosystem education policy framework: Drawing on frameworks from UNESCO and Chan, reconstruct institutional policies across three dimensions〞pedagogical, governance, and operational〞while ensuring currency and flexibility. Ｌ Adopt a dual-track approach of ＆Legislate or Educate＊: Combine institution-level policy regulation (e.g., clearly defining red lines for academic integrity) with institution-wide critical AI literacy education to establish ethically grounded human每AI collaboration norms. Ｍ Implement participatory action research (PAR) for co-governance: Engage multiple stakeholders〞including faculty, staff, students, and senior leadership〞in deep, iterative participation in policy development and reflective practice to ensure accountability and inclusive institutional design.

Manifestation_Text: Hallucinations and false data generation by GenAI tools have triggered a crisis of authenticity in student academic output. Overreliance on GenAI for assessment tasks undermines the authenticity of scholarly work and fuels widespread plagiarism; meanwhile, approximately 33% of students remain unaware that these tools may generate fabricated information, significantly compromising the final quality and scientific reliability of academic learning and assessment outcomes.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Enhance student AI literacy: Higher education institutions should offer systematic AI literacy courses enabling students to deeply understand the application boundaries, biases, and limitations of GenAI, and to distinguish responsible use from unethical use (e.g., practices at the University of Sydney, RMIT University, and Nanjing University). Ｌ Strengthen critical thinking training: Embed critical thinking as a core learning outcome, equipping students with the capacity to evaluate the reliability of GenAI-generated content (e.g., modular teaching approaches at the University of Bath and the University of Technology Sydney). Ｍ Adopt authentic assessments and project-based assessments: Employ real-world-context-based evaluation methods〞including case studies, simulations, and experiential learning〞to prompt students to demonstrate genuine understanding rather than resorting to AI-enabled shortcuts.

Manifestation_Text: The integration of GenAI erodes the trust-based, human-intellect-centered bonds and collaborative responsibilities within the academic community. When students delegate intellectual agency to AI tools, they undermine the honesty, trust, and mutual accountability inherent in educator每student and peer每peer relationships, thereby alienating the interpersonal foundations of traditional academic communities.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Promote collaborative learning: Design group-based collaborative tasks that foster dynamic social environments where students challenge each other＊s assumptions and co-construct knowledge, thereby building trust anchored in peer review and collective accountability (e.g., practices at Stanford University and the University of Melbourne). Ｌ Deploy adaptive learning platforms: Leverage personalized learning pathways to strengthen students＊ self-efficacy and sense of ownership over their learning, encouraging reliance on their own capabilities rather than dishonest means. Ｍ Support educators＊ professional development: Ensure educators participate in targeted professional development programs that equip them with the competencies necessary to cultivate cultures of honesty and ethical conduct, thereby repairing and sustaining academic trust between educators and students.

Manifestation_Text: The misuse of GenAI has delivered systemic and institutional shocks to macro-level academic governance systems, the effectiveness of university assessment frameworks, and the overall culture of academic integrity. Most current institutional policies remain at a superficial level〞focusing narrowly on ＆what works＊〞and lack comprehensive consideration of how GenAI affects student learning, leading to the collapse of traditional assessment systems, institutional policy lag, and systemic erosion of academic integrity culture.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establish comprehensive GenAI institutional policies: Universities must move beyond traditional ＆prohibition＊ approaches or superficial guidelines to develop multi-dimensional policies covering education, enforcement, and encouragement〞clearly delineating compliant uses of GenAI and definitions of academic misconduct. Ｌ Invest in technological infrastructure: Institutions must build robust technical systems capable of effectively detecting and responding to AI-generated content to safeguard fairness and validity in assessment. Ｍ Cultivate a culture of academic integrity: Through co-creation involving multiple stakeholders〞including students, educators, and institutional leaders〞establish shared commitments to integrity, transforming academic integrity from a regulatory constraint into an embedded organizational culture. Ｎ Address four systemic challenges: Institutions must systematically tackle strategic, operational, cultural, and financial challenges arising during the implementation of comprehensive academic integrity frameworks.

Manifestation_Text: Cognitive biases embedded in large language model (LLM) training data contribute to the marginalization of minority groups, while low female participation in AI development leads to inequities in knowledge production and perspective representation.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Foster critical thinking and information literacy: Require educators to cultivate students＊ critical thinking, data literacy, and information literacy skills〞enabling them to understand tool limitations and actively identify and question biased information. Ｌ Integrate an EDI lens: As emphasized in the article abstract, the principles of Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) must be mandatorily embedded in both the application and governance of GenAI.

Manifestation_Text: GenAI generates inaccurate information, fabricates academic citations and references (hallucinations), and the system itself cannot assume academic responsibility for such false outputs.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Mandatory human verification mechanism: The article explicitly states that, given AI＊s inability to assume responsibility, humans are expected to verify the factual accuracy of AI-generated outputs when reading and using them (se espera que los seres humanos verifiquen la informaci車n al leer sus resultados). Ｌ Education on cognitive limitations: Systematic training is provided to help educational stakeholders deeply understand the capabilities and limitations of GenAI.

Manifestation_Text: AI-assisted writing suppresses authentic human voices, circumvents genuine learning processes, and undermines the trust and certification nexus in academic assessment〞namely, the mutual recognition of individual intellectual achievement.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Introduction of supplementary verification mechanisms: In high-stakes summative assessments, educators must not rely solely on student declarations but instead obtain supplementary, verifiable evidence confirming that students completed tasks autonomously (acceso a fuentes complementarias y verificables que corroboren la realizaci車n aut車noma). Ｌ Transparency in AI usage boundaries: Students are encouraged to explicitly declare their use of AI; when used transparently and disclosed openly, AI functions as a legitimate assistive tool, thereby restoring academic integrity and mutual trust between instructors and students.

Manifestation_Text: GenAI can bypass existing text similarity detection tools, and currently no reliable AI-detection software exists〞rendering traditional definitions of ＆plagiarism＊ and academic integrity management systems ineffective and subject to systemic disruption.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Conceptual and institutional redefinition: The academic community must redefine the concept of ＆plagiarism＊ (redefinici車n) to successfully adapt to GenAI-driven educational environments, rather than clinging to outdated detection criteria. Ｌ Implementation of systemic, multi-level governance (the 4M framework): Grounded in the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) framework, organizational cultural change is advanced at the micro (individual), meso (departmental), macro (institutional), and mega (national/international) levels; formal ethical policies are developed; and concrete practical guidance resources and support networks are provided to educational stakeholders.

Manifestation_Text: AI models reproduce and disseminate societal biases and toxic content from their underlying training data, generating discriminatory outputs that marginalize specific groups and reinforce harmful stereotypes.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Cultivation of critical thinking and AI literacy: Educational institutions should foster a culture of critical thinking to ensure students possess the capacity to identify and challenge questionable or biased content. Ｌ Systemic digital literacy training: Writing Centers (WCs) should lead discussions, workshops, and courses on digital literacy, systematically explaining GenAI tools and encouraging critical evaluation of GenAI outputs. Ｍ Enhancement of user ethical awareness: Users must be made acutely aware〞when selecting and deploying these tools〞of the biases and broader societal implications embedded in their choices.

Manifestation_Text: GenAI ＆hallucinations＊, fabricated references, and dissemination of disinformation/misinformation directly compromise the factual accuracy and scientific quality of academic writing.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Establishment of fact-checking and cross-verification mechanisms: Robust fact-checking protocols are developed and taught; users are trained to integrate GenAI tools with verified library databases to ensure factual accuracy and enhance output reliability. Ｌ Instruction in prompt engineering: Through workshops and similar formats, students are taught effective prompt-writing techniques, emphasizing the formulation of intelligent ＆machine questions＊ to elicit optimal ＆machine answers＊, thereby maximizing GenAI＊s potential while minimizing low-quality outputs.

Manifestation_Text: Students＊ excessive reliance on and blind trust in AI undermine the value of personalized guidance provided by human writing center (WC) tutors, eroding individual voice, intellectual curiosity, and self-awareness in academic interaction.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Restructure WC pedagogy and culture: Tutors should engage students in deep discussions about the value of creativity, individuality, and pride in one＊s work, directly intervening to address overreliance on large language models (LLMs) and uncritical trust in technology. Ｌ Uphold the 'human-in-the-loop' principle: Emphasize that nuanced understanding and personalized guidance offered by human tutors are irreplaceable, positioning the WC as a complementary resource that integrates technological advantages with human expertise. Ｍ Strengthen in-person interpersonal interaction: Grounded in evidence that students〞especially post-pandemic〞prefer face-to-face learning and perform better in such settings, reaffirm interpersonal interaction as central to writing instruction.

Manifestation_Text: AI-induced covert plagiarism, the failure and misclassification of detection tools, and confusion surrounding copyright ownership and legal accountability collectively exert systemic pressure on the broader academic integrity system, assessment frameworks, and legal infrastructure.
Mitigation_Text: Ｋ Lead academic integrity policy revision: WC experts should actively join academic integrity committees to spearhead discussions on the evolving definitions of plagiarism and authorship, driving institutional updates to generative AI (GenAI) usage policies and definitions of academic misconduct. Ｌ Clarify course-level rules and legal accountability: Support faculty in establishing clear GenAI usage restrictions and conditions for each course, explicitly assigning students full legal and academic responsibility for the content they submit. Ｍ Shift toward authentic assessment: Promote a transformation in assessment practices by leveraging GenAI to design complex, real-world tasks〞thereby circumventing simplistic AI-assisted cheating at the systemic level. Ｎ Establish cross-institutional communities of practice: Build networks and partnerships with other WCs to share policy experiences and evidence-based best practices, ensuring institutional decisions align with macro-level standards across the academic community.
